# Queue

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/queue/

# Queue

A queue runs slow work in the background, so the request can answer at once.

You put a slow task, like an email or a report, on a queue as a **job**. A **worker** process then takes each job and runs it. The `dox_queue` package has a `redis` driver and a `sync` driver. The `database` driver is in the `dox_queue_database` package.

## Setup

A new app already has the queue. In an older app, run this command:

```bash
dox add queue
```

The default driver is `database`. Add `--driver=redis` or `--driver=sync` to pick another one. The command writes the config, the provider, `bin/queue.dart` and a sample job. It never overwrites a file.

With `database`, it also adds `dox_queue_database` and the migration of the jobs tables, so run `dox add orm` first. With `redis`, it adds the `REDIS_*` keys.

### Configuration

The queue config picks the driver and lists your jobs:

```dart title="lib/config/queue.dart"
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';

import '../generated/jobs.g.dart';

QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  /// sync, database or redis
  driver: 'database',

  /// every @Job class, from lib/generated/jobs.g.dart
  jobs: jobRegistry,
);
```

`dart run build_runner build` writes `jobRegistry`. `Queue.config` gives this config in your code.

- `sync`: `dispatch()` runs the job at once. There is no worker, no retry and no delay. Use it for tests and local work.
- `database`: jobs are rows in the `jobs` table. It needs `dox_queue_database`, and Postgres, MySQL 8+, MariaDB 10.6+ or SQLite.
- `redis`: jobs are in Redis.

!!! warning "Keep `retryAfter` bigger than your longest job"
    A job that runs longer than `retryAfter` (default 90 seconds) looks crashed, so a second worker runs it again.

### All options

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `driver` | `sync` | `sync`, `database` (needs `dox_queue_database`) or `redis` |
| `jobs` | empty | `jobRegistry` from `lib/generated/jobs.g.dart` |
| `redis` | 127.0.0.1:6379 | `RedisOptions` for the `redis` driver. See [Redis driver](#redis) |
| `prefix` | `dox_queue:` | the start of every Redis key |
| `connection` | default | the dox_orm connection name, for `dox_queue_database` |
| `retryAfter` | 90 seconds | when a worker does not finish a job in this time, another worker can take it |
| `inProcess` | false | run a worker in the web server. See [Running jobs in the web server](#running-jobs-in-the-web-server) |
| `workerQueues` | `['default']` | the queues of the in-process worker |
| `workerConcurrency` | 1 | jobs at once in the in-process worker |
| `workerTimeoutGrace` | none | the `--timeout-grace` wait of the in-process worker |
| `serializeSync` | false | the `sync` driver saves the job and reads it back before it runs |
| `connections` | none | more queue connections by name. See [Queue connections](#queue-connections) |
| `afterCommit` | false | push jobs from a transaction only after the commit. See [Dispatching after the commit](#dispatching-after-the-commit) |
| `failedAtTimestamp` | false | the `failed_at` column is a timestamp. See [The failed_at column](#the-failed_at-column) |

### The provider

The provider sets up the queue in every isolate. Put it in `lib/providers/`:

```dart title="lib/providers/queue_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';

import '../config/queue.dart';

class AppQueueProvider extends QueueProvider {
  AppQueueProvider() : super(queueConfig);
}
```

### The worker file

The worker runs from `bin/queue.dart`. It starts the providers of your app, but not the HTTP server:

```dart title="bin/queue.dart"
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';

/// run queued jobs: `dart run bin/queue.dart [work] [flags]`.
Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await QueueWorker(app: appConfig).run(args);
}
```

### Database driver

The `database` driver, [job batches](#job-batching) and [dispatching after the commit](#dispatching-after-the-commit) need the `dox_queue_database` package:

```bash
dart pub add dox_queue_database
```

Then make your queue provider extend `DatabaseQueueProvider`:

```dart title="lib/providers/queue_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_queue_database/dox_queue_database.dart';

import '../config/queue.dart';

class AppQueueProvider extends DatabaseQueueProvider {
  AppQueueProvider() : super(queueConfig);
}
```

Make the `jobs`, `failed_jobs` and `job_batches` tables. Batches need the `job_batches` table with every driver:

```bash
dox queue:table
dox migrate
```

The migration looks like this:

```dart title="db/migration/2026_10_25_000000_create_queue_tables.dart"
// ignore_for_file: file_names
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue_database/dox_queue_database.dart';

class CreateQueueTables extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await QueueTables.up(schema);
    await QueueTables.upBatches(schema);
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await QueueTables.downBatches(schema);
    await QueueTables.down(schema);
  }
}
```

To keep the jobs in another database connection, use `QueueConfig(connection: 'postgres')`.

#### Adding the pop indexes to an old table

A `jobs` table from an earlier migration can be slow to poll. Add the missing indexes with a new migration:

```dart title="db/migration/2026_11_20_000000_add_queue_pop_index.dart"
// ignore_for_file: file_names
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue_database/dox_queue_database.dart';

class AddQueuePopIndex extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await QueueTables.popIndex(schema);
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {}
}
```

#### The connection column

`failed_jobs.connection` keeps the name of the [queue connection](#queue-connections). An older table without it still works, but `failed --connection=X` then lists all failed jobs. Add the column, then restart the workers:

```dart
await schema.table('failed_jobs', (Table table) {
  table.string('connection').nullable();
});
```

#### The failed_at column

`failed_jobs.failed_at` is an integer with unix time in milliseconds. For a UTC timestamp, set `failedAtTimestamp: true` in the migration and in the queue config:

```dart
await QueueTables.up(schema, failedAtTimestamp: true);
```

```dart
QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'database',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  failedAtTimestamp: true,
);
```

!!! warning "The setting and the column must match"
    If they do not match, the failed job commands throw a StateError, and a job that fails all its tries stays in `jobs` and runs again after `retryAfter`.

On MySQL and MariaDB, a `TIMESTAMP` cannot hold a time after 2038-01-19. To change an existing integer column, stop all workers, run the SQL for your database, set `failedAtTimestamp: true`, then start the workers.

SQLite (3.35 or newer):

```sql
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs ADD COLUMN failed_at_utc TIMESTAMP;
UPDATE failed_jobs SET failed_at_utc =
  strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%fZ', failed_at / 1000.0, 'unixepoch');
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs DROP COLUMN failed_at;
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs RENAME COLUMN failed_at_utc TO failed_at;
```

Postgres:

```sql
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs ALTER COLUMN failed_at TYPE TIMESTAMP
  USING to_timestamp(failed_at / 1000.0) AT TIME ZONE 'UTC';
```

MySQL and MariaDB:

```sql
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs ADD COLUMN failed_at_utc TIMESTAMP NULL;
UPDATE failed_jobs SET failed_at_utc = FROM_UNIXTIME(failed_at DIV 1000);
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs DROP COLUMN failed_at;
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs CHANGE failed_at_utc failed_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL;
```

### Redis driver {#redis}

Set the driver to `redis` and give the Redis server:

```dart
QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'redis',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  redis: RedisOptions(
    host: env.redisHost,
    port: 6379,
    commandTimeout: Duration(seconds: 5),
    maxQueuedCommands: 1000,
  ),
);
```

`commandTimeout` (default 10 seconds) fails a command that gets no reply, and null turns it off. `maxQueuedCommands` limits the commands that wait for a connection. It is off by default.

To read the Redis server from the env, use `QueueConfig.redisFromEnv()`:

```dart
QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'redis',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  redis: QueueConfig.redisFromEnv(),
);
```

It reads `REDIS_URL`, like `rediss://user:password@host:6380/0`, where `rediss` turns on TLS. Without `REDIS_URL`, it reads `REDIS_HOST`, `REDIS_PORT`, `REDIS_USERNAME`, `REDIS_PASSWORD` and `REDIS_TLS`.

## Creating jobs

### Generating job classes

Make a new job file in `lib/app/jobs/`:

```bash
dox make:job SendWelcomeEmail
```

### Class structure

A job is a class with `@Job()` that extends `DoxJob`. The worker calls its `handle()` method:

```dart title="lib/app/jobs/send_welcome_email.job.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';

@Job()
class SendWelcomeEmail extends DoxJob {
  SendWelcomeEmail({required this.userId});

  final int userId;

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    MailService mail = Dox().ioc.get<MailService>();
    await mail.sendWelcome(userId);
  }
}
```

Run `dart run build_runner build` after you add or change a job.

### Job data

The parameters of the unnamed constructor are saved with the job. Each parameter needs a field or getter with the same name. These types work:

- `int`, `double`, `num`, `String`, `bool`
- `DateTime`
- enums (saved by name)
- `List` and `Map<String, ...>` of these, also nested
- `dynamic` and `Object` (the value must be JSON)
- the nullable types of all of them

Save an id, not an object. Load the user in `handle()`, so you get the newest data.

### Using services in a job

A job is made again from its saved data, so get services in `handle()` from the container:

```dart
UserService users = Dox().ioc.get<UserService>();
```

### Setting the number of tries

A job runs one time by default. Set `tries` to try again when `handle()` throws, and `backoff` to wait between the tries:

```dart
/// run up to 3 times
@override
int get tries => 3;

/// wait 10 seconds before the 2nd try, 60 seconds before the 3rd
@override
List<Duration> get backoff => const <Duration>[
  Duration(seconds: 10),
  Duration(seconds: 60),
];
```

The last `backoff` entry is used for all later tries. Three more settings change the retries:

- `retryUntil` retries until a time, in place of a number of tries.
- `maxExceptions` fails the job after this many tries that threw an error.
- `failOnTimeout` fails the job at once when a try times out.

### Setting a timeout

`timeout` is the maximum run time of one try. The default is the worker `--timeout`, 60 seconds:

```dart
@override
Duration? get timeout => const Duration(seconds: 30);
```

### Choosing the queue

Jobs go on the `default` queue. Give a job its own queue, so a worker can run it first or apart:

```dart
@override
String get queue => 'emails';
```

### Handling failed jobs

`failed()` runs one time, after the last try failed:

```dart
@override
Future<void> failed(Object error, StackTrace stack) async {
  // tell someone, or clean up
}
```

### Encrypting job data

Add the `ShouldBeEncrypted` mixin to encrypt the data of the job with the app key. The worker needs the same key, or one of `AppConfig.previousKeys`:

```dart
@Job()
class ChargeCard extends DoxJob with ShouldBeEncrypted {
  // ...
}
```

The job name, the queue and the id stay plain text.

### Renaming a job class

The class name is saved with each job. When you rename a class, keep the old name with `name`:

```dart
@Job(name: 'SendWelcomeEmail')
```

## Dispatching jobs

Call `dispatch()` to put a job on the queue. It gives the job id. `Queue.dispatch()` does the same:

```dart
await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: user.id).dispatch();
await Queue.dispatch(SendWelcomeEmail(userId: user.id));
```

### Delayed dispatching

Use `delay` to wait before the job runs. You can also pick another queue:

```dart
await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatch(
  delay: Duration(minutes: 10),
  queue: 'emails',
);
```

To wait until a time, use `delayUntil`. Give `delay` or `delayUntil`, not both:

```dart
await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatch(
  delayUntil: DateTime.utc(2030, 1, 1, 9),
);
```

### Conditional dispatching

`dispatchIf` dispatches only when the condition is true, and `dispatchUnless` only when it is false. They give null when the job was not dispatched:

```dart
await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatchIf(user.wantsEmail);
await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatchUnless(user.isBlocked);
```

### Synchronous dispatching

Run the job now, in this process, with no queue. `Queue.dispatchSync(job)` does the same:

```dart
await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatchSync();
```

### Dispatching after the response

Run the job in this process after the response is sent. `Queue.dispatchAfterResponse(job)` does the same:

```dart
SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatchAfterResponse();
```

It gives nothing, so do not `await` it. The job has no retry, and it is lost if the server stops first.

### Dispatching after the commit

A job dispatched in a transaction can run before the commit, or after a rollback. Use `afterCommit: true` to push it after the commit. This needs [`dox_queue_database`](#database-driver):

```dart
await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  User user = await User().create(<String, dynamic>{'email': email});
  await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: user.id).dispatch(afterCommit: true);
});
```

A rollback drops the job, and outside a transaction it is pushed at once. It waits only for a transaction on the default dox_orm connection. To do this for every dispatch, set `QueueConfig(afterCommit: true)`. Chains and batches also take `afterCommit`.

### Queueing an email

To send an email later, you do not need a job class. With [dox_mailer](mail.md#queue-an-email), call `Mail.queue()`:

```dart
await Mail.queue(message);
await Mail.later(Duration(minutes: 10), message, queue: 'emails');
```

## Running the worker

Start a worker to run the jobs:

```bash
dart run bin/queue.dart
```

`--queue` picks the queues, and the first one goes first. `--concurrency` runs more jobs at once on one thread:

```bash
dart run bin/queue.dart work --queue=emails,default --concurrency=4
```

For CPU heavy jobs, run more worker processes. The `dox` CLI runs the same file: `dox queue:work`, `dox queue:failed`, `dox queue:retry <id|all>`, `dox queue:forget <id>`, `dox queue:flush`, `dox queue:clear [queue]`, `dox queue:restart` and `dox queue:prune-failed`.

### Worker flags

| Flag | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--queue=high,default` | `default` | the queues to work. The first one goes first |
| `--concurrency=4` | 1 | jobs at once in this process |
| `--once` | off | run one job, then stop |
| `--tries=3` | 1 | tries of a job that does not set `tries` |
| `--timeout=60` | 60 | maximum run time in seconds of a job that does not set `timeout` |
| `--sleep=3` | 3 | seconds to wait when the queues are empty |
| `--max-sleep=30` | off | double the sleep on each empty poll, up to this many seconds |
| `--stop-when-empty` | off | stop when the queues are empty |
| `--timeout-grace=10` | none | after a timeout, wait up to this many seconds for the old run to end |
| `--backoff=1,5,10` | none | seconds to wait before each retry of a job that does not set `backoff` |
| `--max-jobs=1000` | off | stop after this many jobs |
| `--max-time=3600` | off | stop after this many seconds |
| `--memory=256` | off | stop when the process uses more than this many MB |
| `--connection=name` | main | the [queue connection](#queue-connections) to use |

After `--max-jobs`, `--max-time` and `--memory`, let your process manager start the worker again.

### Stopping the worker

Press Ctrl+C, or send SIGTERM. The worker waits for the running jobs, then stops. A second signal stops it at once.

### Restarting after a deploy

The worker keeps your code in memory, so restart it after each deploy:

```bash
dart run bin/queue.dart restart
```

Each worker stops after its current jobs, and your process manager starts it again. The workers and the command must share a cache store, like `file` on one machine, or `redis`.

### Running the worker in production

Run the binary that `dox build` makes in `build/bundle/bin/queue`. It takes the same commands and flags:

```bash
cd build/bundle
./bin/queue work --concurrency=4
```

Run it as its own process, next to the web server. For example, with Docker Compose:

```yaml
services:
  web:
    build: .
    command: /app/bin/server
  worker:
    build: .
    command: /app/bin/queue work --concurrency=4
```

Set your process manager to restart it when it stops.

### Running jobs in the web server

A small app can skip the worker process. With `inProcess: true`, the first isolate of the web server also runs jobs:

```dart
QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'database',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  inProcess: true,
);
```

The jobs share the isolate with web requests, so heavy jobs make those requests slow.

## Dealing with failed jobs

When `handle()` throws or times out, the worker waits the `backoff` time and tries again, up to `tries` times. After the last try, the job goes to the failed jobs, and `failed()` runs.

!!! info "A timeout does not stop the code"
    Dart cannot stop a running `Future`, so `handle()` continues after a timeout. Write jobs that are safe to run two times.

To wait for the old run, start the worker with `--timeout-grace=SECONDS`. Keep `timeout` plus the grace time below `retryAfter`.

### Retrying failed jobs

List the failed jobs, and put one or all of them back on their queue:

```bash
dart run bin/queue.dart failed
dart run bin/queue.dart retry 6f1c0e...
dart run bin/queue.dart retry all
```

### Deleting failed jobs

`forget` deletes one failed job, and `flush` deletes all of them. `prune-failed` deletes failed jobs older than `--hours=N` (default 24):

```bash
dart run bin/queue.dart forget 6f1c0e...
dart run bin/queue.dart flush
dart run bin/queue.dart prune-failed --hours=48
```

### Controlling the job from handle()

Add the `InteractsWithQueue` mixin, then call one of these in `handle()`:

| Call | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `attempts()` | how many times a worker took the job. The first run gives 1 |
| `release(delay)` | put the job back on its queue. It runs again after `delay` |
| `fail(error)` | fail the job now, with no retry. `failed()` runs |
| `delete()` | delete the job, with no retry and no `failed()` |

```dart
@Job()
class SendReport extends DoxJob with InteractsWithQueue {
  SendReport({required this.reportId});

  final int reportId;

  @override
  int get tries => 5;

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    ReportApi api = Dox().ioc.get<ReportApi>();
    if (await api.isBusy()) {
      release(Duration(seconds: 30));
      return;
    }
    if (!await api.hasReport(reportId)) {
      delete();
      return;
    }
    await api.send(reportId);
  }
}
```

`release()` counts as a try, so set `tries` above 1. In a test file, write `this.fail(...)`, because `package:test` also has a `fail()`.

### Clearing jobs from a queue

Delete all jobs of a queue, also the running ones. The default queue is `default`:

```bash
dart run bin/queue.dart clear emails
```

## Job middleware

Job middleware wraps `handle()` of a job, for rules that many jobs share. Add the `HasMiddleware` mixin and list the middleware. The first one runs first:

```dart
@Job()
class SendReport extends DoxJob with HasMiddleware {
  SendReport({required this.reportId});

  final int reportId;

  @override
  int get tries => 5;

  @override
  List<JobMiddleware> get middleware => <JobMiddleware>[
    RateLimited('report-api', 10, Duration(minutes: 1)),
  ];

  // ...
}
```

The built-in middleware keeps its counts and locks in the default cache store. All workers must share it, so do not use the `memory` store. A middleware that puts the job back counts as a try.

### Rate limiting

`RateLimited(key, max, per)` runs `max` jobs of `key` in each `per` window at most. The other jobs go back on the queue:

```dart
RateLimited('report-api', 10, Duration(minutes: 1)),
```

### Preventing job overlaps

`WithoutOverlapping(key)` runs one job of `key` at a time:

```dart
WithoutOverlapping(
  'report-$reportId',
  releaseAfter: Duration(seconds: 30),
  expireAfter: Duration(minutes: 10), // longer than the longest run
),
```

`releaseAfter` (default zero) puts the other jobs back after this time. With null, they are dropped. `expireAfter` frees the lock after this time, so a crash cannot keep it forever.

### Throttling exceptions

`ThrottlesExceptions(key, maxAttempts:, decay:, retryAfter:)` is for jobs that call a service that is down. After `maxAttempts` errors (default 10), jobs of `key` wait until `decay` is over (default 10 minutes):

```dart
ThrottlesExceptions('report-api',
    maxAttempts: 5, decay: Duration(minutes: 5)),
```

### Writing your own middleware

Extend `JobMiddleware`. Call `next()` to continue, or `release(job, delay)` to put the job back:

```dart
class SkipAtNight extends JobMiddleware {
  @override
  Future<void> handle(DoxJob job, JobNext next) async {
    if (DateTime.now().hour < 6) {
      release(job, Duration(hours: 1));
      return;
    }
    await next();
  }
}
```

If you do not call `next()`, the job is skipped and counts as done.

## Unique jobs

Add the `ShouldBeUnique` mixin to keep one job of a class and `uniqueId` on the queue. While one waits or runs, `dispatch()` pushes nothing and gives `''`:

```dart
@Job()
class UpdateSearchIndex extends DoxJob with ShouldBeUnique {
  UpdateSearchIndex({required this.productId});

  final int productId;

  @override
  String get uniqueId => '$productId';

  @override
  Duration? get uniqueFor => Duration(hours: 1);

  // ...
}
```

Set `uniqueFor`, or the lock of a crashed worker never ends. The lock is in the default cache store, so the web app and the workers must share it.

To free the lock when a worker starts the job, use `ShouldBeUniqueUntilProcessing`.

## Job chaining

A chain runs jobs one after the other. When a job fails for good, the rest of the chain is dropped and the catch job runs:

```dart
await Queue.chain(<DoxJob>[
  ResizeImage(imageId: 1),
  UploadImage(imageId: 1),
  TellUser(imageId: 1),
]).catchError(TellAdmin(imageId: 1)).dispatch(queue: 'images');
```

`dispatch()` gives the id of the first job. `delay` counts for the first job only. Each job carries the data of the jobs after it, so keep chains short.

### Handling chain failures

The catch handler is a job too. Add the `CatchesError` mixin to read the error:

```dart
@Job()
class TellAdmin extends DoxJob with CatchesError {
  TellAdmin({required this.imageId});

  final int imageId;

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    await alertAdmin('image $imageId failed: $caughtError');
  }
}
```

The catch job runs one time, in the worker, with no retry. `queue:retry` of the failed job continues the chain.

## Job batching

A batch runs many jobs and does something when they are all done. Batches need [`dox_queue_database`](#database-driver) and the `job_batches` table, with every driver:

```dart
Batch batch = await Queue.batch(<DoxJob>[
  ImportRows(from: 0),
  ImportRows(from: 1000),
  ImportRows(from: 2000),
])
    .name('import')
    .then(ImportDone())
    .catchError(ImportFailed())
    .whenComplete(CleanUpImport())
    .dispatch(queue: 'imports');

print(batch.id);
```

### Batch callbacks

| Callback | Runs |
| --- | --- |
| `before(job)` | one time, at `dispatch()`, before the jobs are pushed |
| `progress(job)` | each time a job is done. With `allowFailures()`, also when one fails |
| `then(job)` | one time, when every job is done |
| `catchError(job)` | one time, when the first job fails for good |
| `whenComplete(job)` | one time, when every job ran, done or failed |

Each callback is a job. It runs one time, with no retry. Add `Batchable` to read the batch, and `CatchesError` to read the error:

```dart
@Job()
class ImportFailed extends DoxJob with Batchable, CatchesError {
  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    Batch? batch = await this.batch();
    await alertAdmin('import ${batch?.name} failed: $caughtError');
  }
}
```

### Defining batchable jobs

Add the `Batchable` mixin to read the batch of a job. `batchId` is the id, and `batch()` reads the batch:

```dart
@Job()
class ImportRows extends DoxJob with Batchable {
  ImportRows({required this.from});

  final int from;

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    Batch? batch = await this.batch();
    if (batch?.cancelled ?? false) return;
    await importRows(from);
  }
}
```

### Inspecting batches

`Queue.findBatch(id)` reads a batch, or gives null. A `Batch` has these fields:

| Field | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `id`, `name` | the id and the name |
| `totalJobs` | how many jobs the batch has |
| `pendingJobs` | how many jobs are not done. Failed jobs are counted, because you can retry them |
| `failedJobs` | how many jobs failed |
| `processedJobs` | how many jobs are done |
| `progress` | the percent of done jobs, from 0 to 100 |
| `finished` | true when every job ran, or the batch was cancelled |
| `cancelled` | true after `cancel()`, or after a first failure |
| `createdAt`, `cancelledAt`, `finishedAt` | the times of these steps |

```dart
Batch? batch = await Queue.findBatch(id);
```

### Cancelling batches

The first job that fails for good cancels the batch. Add `allowFailures()` to continue. You can also call `cancel()`. The jobs still run, so a `Batchable` job reads `cancelled` to skip its work:

```dart
await batch.cancel();
```

### Adding jobs to a batch

`add(jobs)` adds jobs to a batch, for example from a job of the batch. It throws a StateError when the batch is finished or cancelled:

```dart
await batch.add(<DoxJob>[ImportRows(from: 3000)]);
```

### Chains in a batch

Use `chain(jobs)` to put a chain in a batch. The batch counts the chain as one job:

```dart
await Queue.batch(<DoxJob>[ImportUsers()])
    .chain(<DoxJob>[ImportOrders(), SumOrders()])
    .dispatch();
```

### Pruning batches

Delete batches that finished or were cancelled more than `--hours` ago (default 24). `--unfinished` also deletes old batches that never finished:

```bash
dart run bin/queue.dart prune-batches --hours=48
dart run bin/queue.dart prune-batches --hours=48 --unfinished=168
```

In code, use `Queue.pruneBatches(before, unfinishedBefore:)`.

## Queue events

Listen to the steps of a job, for example to log or count jobs:

```dart
Queue.before(
    (QueueEvent event) => print('start ${event.name} ${event.id}'));
Queue.after((QueueEvent event) => print('done ${event.name}'));
Queue.failing((QueueEvent event) => alert(event.name, event.error));
```

| Hook | When |
| --- | --- |
| `Queue.queued` | `dispatch()` pushed a job |
| `Queue.before` | a worker starts a job |
| `Queue.after` | a worker finished a job and deleted it |
| `Queue.released` | a worker put a job back (`release()` or a retry) |
| `Queue.exceptionOccurred` | `handle()` threw and the job will be tried again |
| `Queue.failing` | a job failed for good |
| `Queue.looping` | a worker is about to take the next job |
| `Queue.stopping` | a worker stops |

Each isolate has its own listeners, so register them in a provider. `Queue.forgetListeners()` removes all listeners. A listener gets a `QueueEvent`:

| Field | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `type` | the kind of event |
| `job` | the job. Null for `looping` and `stopping` |
| `name` | the job name of the registry |
| `id` | the job id |
| `queue` | the queue name |
| `attempts` | the try number. 0 for `queued`, `looping` and `stopping` |
| `error`, `stack` | the error and its stack trace, for `exceptionOccurred` and `failing` |
| `delay` | the wait, for `queued` and `released` |
| `batch` | the `Batch`, for the [batch events](#batch-events) |

The `sync` driver, `dispatchSync()` and `dispatchAfterResponse()` fire no job events.

### Batch events

In a batch event, `event.batch` is the batch after the step:

```dart
Queue.batchProgress((QueueEvent event) {
  Batch batch = event.batch!;
  print('${batch.name}: ${batch.progress}%');
});
Queue.batchFailed(
    (QueueEvent event) => alert(event.batch!.id, event.error));
```

| Hook | When |
| --- | --- |
| `Queue.batchDispatched` | the batch was saved, before its jobs are pushed |
| `Queue.batchProgress` | a job (or a chain) of the batch is done. With `allowFailures()`, also when one failed |
| `Queue.batchFailed` | the first job failed for good |
| `Queue.batchCancelled` | the batch was cancelled |
| `Queue.batchFinished` | every job ran, done or failed |

Each event fires one time for each step, also with many workers.

## Queue connections

The config is the main connection. Add more queue stores in `connections`:

```dart
QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'redis',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  connections: <String, QueueConfig>{
    'database': QueueConfig(driver: 'database'),
  },
);
```

Pick a connection when you dispatch:

```dart
await SendReport(reportId: 1).dispatch(connection: 'database');
```

Run a worker for each connection. Every command of `bin/queue.dart` takes `--connection`:

```bash
dart run bin/queue.dart work
dart run bin/queue.dart work --connection=database
dart run bin/queue.dart failed --connection=database
```

An entry uses only `driver`, `redis`, `prefix`, `connection`, `retryAfter`, `serializeSync` and `failedAtTimestamp`. The in-process worker runs only the main connection. `Queue.driverOf(name)` gives the job store of a connection.

## Custom drivers

Write a `QueueDriverFactory` that makes your `QueueDriver`, and add it with `Queue.extend` before the first use of the queue:

```dart
class MyDriverFactory implements QueueDriverFactory {
  @override
  QueueDriver create(QueueConfig config, {String? name}) {
    return MyQueueDriver(config);
  }
}

Queue.extend('mine', MyDriverFactory()); // QueueConfig(driver: 'mine')
```

Call it in `setup()` of your queue provider, before `super.setup()`.

## Testing

### Running jobs in tests

Use the `sync` driver. `dispatch()` then runs the job at once:

```dart
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/jobs/send_welcome_email.job.dart';
import 'package:my_app/generated/jobs.g.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  setUp(() {
    Queue.configure(QueueConfig(driver: 'sync', jobs: jobRegistry));
  });

  test('sends the welcome email', () async {
    await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatch();
    // check the email was sent
  });
}
```

A job that uses `Dox()` needs `Dox().initialize(appConfig)` in `setUpAll`. Set `serializeSync: true` to save the job and read it back before it runs, like a worker. Then a job that is not in `jobRegistry` throws:

```dart
Queue.configure(
  QueueConfig(driver: 'sync', jobs: jobRegistry, serializeSync: true),
);
```

To test a job alone, call `handle()`:

```dart
await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).handle();
```

### Faking the queue

`Queue.fake()` keeps every `dispatch()` in a list and runs nothing:

```dart
late QueueFake queue;

setUp(() {
  queue = Queue.fake();
});

tearDown(Queue.restore);

test('signing up queues the welcome email', () async {
  await signUp(userId: 1);

  queue.assertPushed<SendWelcomeEmail>();
  queue.assertPushed<SendWelcomeEmail>(
    (SendWelcomeEmail job) => job.userId == 1,
  );
  queue.assertPushedTimes<SendWelcomeEmail>(1);
  queue.assertNotPushed<SendInvoice>();
});
```

| Method | Checks |
|---|---|
| `assertPushed<T>([test])` | a `T` job was pushed. With `test`, one of them passes it |
| `assertPushedTimes<T>(n)` | `n` `T` jobs were pushed |
| `assertNotPushed<T>()` | no `T` job was pushed |
| `assertNothingPushed()` | no job was pushed |
| `assertChained(<Type>[A, B])` | a chain of these job classes, in this order, was dispatched |
| `assertBatched([test])` | a batch was dispatched. `test` gets a `PendingBatch` |
| `assertBatchedChain(<Type>[A, B])` | a batch has a chain of these job classes, in this order |
| `assertBatchCount(n)` | `n` batches were dispatched |

`queue.pushed` gives the jobs, with the `job`, the `queue`, the `delay` and the `connection`. `queue.jobsOf<T>()` gives the `T` jobs, and `queue.clear()` removes them. `dispatchSync()` and `dispatchAfterResponse()` still run, and their jobs are in `queue.dispatchedSync` and `queue.dispatchedAfterResponse`.

The fake does not encode the job. So a job that is not in `QueueConfig.jobs` passes a faked test, but fails in a worker.

### Testing the queue itself

Use the `database` driver with SQLite `:memory:`, and run a worker that stops when the queue is empty:

```dart
await Worker(
  driver: Queue.driver,
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  options: WorkerOptions(stopWhenEmpty: true),
).run();
```

## Without Dox

`dox_queue` also works in a plain Dart app. Add `build_runner` and `dox_builder`, so it writes `lib/generated/jobs.g.dart`:

```bash
dart pub add dox_queue dox_core
dart pub add dev:build_runner dev:dox_builder
```

Write your jobs as in [Creating jobs](#creating-jobs), and run `dart run build_runner build`. Then set up the queue and run a worker:

```dart
import 'dart:async';
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';
import 'package:my_app/generated/jobs.g.dart';
import 'package:my_app/jobs/resize_image.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  // the worker logs with the Dox logger, so it needs an AppConfig
  Dox().initialize(AppConfig(appKey: 'not-used'));

  Queue.configure(QueueConfig(
    driver: 'redis',
    jobs: jobRegistry,
    redis: RedisOptions(host: '127.0.0.1', port: 6379),
  ));

  await ResizeImage(path: 'photo.png').dispatch();

  Worker worker = Worker(
    driver: Queue.driver,
    jobs: jobRegistry,
    options: WorkerOptions(queues: <String>['default'], concurrency: 4),
  );

  // Ctrl+C: finish the running jobs, then stop
  StreamSubscription<ProcessSignal> signal =
      ProcessSignal.sigint.watch().listen((_) => worker.stop());
  await worker.run();
  await signal.cancel();
  await Queue.close();
}
```

`WorkerOptions` takes the settings of the `work` flags, like `queues`, `concurrency`, `once`, `tries`, `timeout`, `sleep` and `stopWhenEmpty`. For the `database` driver, call `QueueDatabase.register()` before `Queue.configure()`, after you set up the default dox_orm connection.

## Next steps

- [Background work](../guides/background-work.md): pick the right tool for work after the response.
- [Scheduler](scheduler.md): run work on a timer.
- [Mail](mail.md): queue an email.

# Mail

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/mail/

# Mail

The `dox_mailer` package sends email from your app with SMTP, Amazon SES, Azure, Resend, Mailgun, Postmark or sendmail.

You make a `Message` and call `Mail.send()`, and a **transport** sends it. The config picks the transport, so you can change providers with no code change.

## Setup

### Install

Add the package. Add `--transport=smtp` (or `resend`, `mailgun`, `postmark`, `ses`) to pick a transport. The default is `log`:

```bash
dox add mailer
```

It writes the mail config and the provider, and adds `MAIL_MAILER`, `MAIL_FROM` and the transport keys to `.env`. It never overwrites a file.

### Configuration

A **mailer** is a name and a transport. `Mail.send()` uses the `defaultMailer`:

```dart title="lib/config/mail.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';

MailConfig mailConfig = MailConfig(
  /// the mailer of Mail.send()
  defaultMailer: Env.get('MAIL_MAILER', 'log'),

  /// for messages with no from address
  from: Address(Env.get('MAIL_FROM', 'hello@example.com'), 'My app'),

  mailers: <String, Transport>{
    'smtp': SmtpTransport(
      host: Env.get('MAIL_HOST', 'localhost'),
      port: Env.get<int>('MAIL_PORT', 587),
      username: Env.get<String?>('MAIL_USERNAME'),
      password: Env.get<String?>('MAIL_PASSWORD'),
    ),

    /// prints emails, sends nothing
    'log': LogTransport(),
  },
);
```

```bash title=".env"
MAIL_MAILER=smtp
MAIL_FROM=hello@example.com
MAIL_HOST=smtp.example.com
MAIL_PORT=587
MAIL_USERNAME=me
MAIL_PASSWORD=secret
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `defaultMailer` | `log` | the mailer of `Mail.send()` |
| `mailers` | a `log` mailer | each mailer name and its transport |
| `from` | none | the from address of a message that has none |
| `replyTo` | none | the reply-to addresses of a message that has none |

`Mail.config` gives this config in your code.

### The mail provider

The provider sets up the mailers in every isolate. Put it in `lib/providers/`:

```dart title="lib/providers/mail_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';

import '../config/mail.dart';

class AppMailProvider extends MailProvider {
  AppMailProvider() : super(mailConfig);
}
```

When the server stops, the provider closes the SMTP connections and HTTP clients.

## Sending mail

Make a `Message` and give it to `Mail.send()`:

```dart
import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';

await Mail.send(
  Message(
    to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com', 'Ann Lee')],
    subject: 'Welcome',
    text: 'Hello Ann, welcome!',
    html: '<p>Hello Ann, <b>welcome</b>!</p>',
  ),
);
```

A message needs a from address, a recipient, and a text or HTML body. When the send fails, `send()` throws a `MailException` with the `statusCode` and the `body` of the server answer. It gives a `SentMessage` with the `messageId`.

### Using another mailer

Send with a mailer that is not the default:

```dart
await Mail.mailer('ses').send(message);
```

### Short ways to send

For a short plain text email, use `Mail.raw()`:

```dart
await Mail.raw('Your code is 1234',
    to: 'ann@example.com', subject: 'Your code');
```

`Mail.to()` starts an email for a [mailable](#mailables). `to()`, `cc()` and `bcc()` take an `Address`, an email text, or a list of these:

```dart
await Mail.to('ann@example.com')
    .cc('Bob Lee <bob@example.com>')
    .bcc(<String>['audit@example.com'])
    .send(WelcomeMail(user));
```

`queue()` and `later()` also work here, like `Mail.to(email).queue(WelcomeMail(user))`.

### The message

| Field | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `from` | an `Address`. Null: `MailConfig.from` |
| `to`, `cc`, `bcc` | lists of `Address` |
| `replyTo` | a list of `Address` |
| `subject` | text |
| `text` | the plain text body |
| `html` | the HTML body |
| `attachments` | a list of `Attachment` |
| `headers` | more headers, like `{'X-Campaign': 'fall'}` |
| `tags` | tags for the reports of the provider. See [Tags and metadata](#tags-and-metadata) |
| `metadata` | key and value data for the provider, like `{'user_id': '42'}` |

A subject or header with a line break is an error, so user input cannot add headers.

An `Address` is an email and an optional name. `Address.parse` reads one from text, and `Address.list` reads many:

```dart
Address('ann@example.com', 'Ann');
Address.parse('Ann <ann@example.com>');
Address.list(<String>['ann@example.com', 'bob@example.com']);
```

### Attachments

Add files with `attachments`. The content type comes from the file extension, or from `contentType`:

```dart
Message(
  to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com')],
  subject: 'Your invoice',
  text: 'The invoice is attached.',
  attachments: <Attachment>[
    Attachment(pdfBytes, 'invoice.pdf'),
    Attachment.fromFile('storage/terms.pdf'),
  ],
);
```

To attach a file from a storage disk, read its bytes first:

```dart
Uint8List? pdf = await Storage().disk('s3').get('invoices/42.pdf');
Attachment(pdf!, 'invoice.pdf');
```

### Inline images

Give the file a `cid`, and use it in the HTML with `cid:`:

```dart
Message(
  to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com')],
  subject: 'Hello',
  html: '<img src="cid:logo.png"> Hello!',
  attachments: <Attachment>[
    Attachment.fromFile('assets/logo.png', cid: 'logo.png'),
  ],
);
```

Mailgun uses the file name as the cid, so use a cid with the extension, like `logo.png`.

### HTML from a view

Render a [view](../the-basic/views.md) template to HTML:

```dart
String html =
    View.render('emails/welcome', <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann'});
await Mail.send(Message(to: to, subject: 'Welcome', html: html));
```

## Mailables

A **mailable** is one kind of email in its own class, like the welcome email. Make one with the CLI. Add `--no-view` for a plain text body. See [`dox make:mail`](../reference/cli.md#dox-makemail):

```bash
dox make:mail Welcome
```

It writes `lib/app/mail/welcome_mail.dart` and `resources/views/emails/welcome.dox.html`. Override the getters you need:

```dart
class WelcomeMail extends Mailable {
  WelcomeMail(this.user);

  final User user;

  @override
  List<Address> get to => <Address>[Address(user.email, user.name)];

  @override
  String get subject => 'Welcome';

  @override
  String? get view => 'emails/welcome';

  @override
  Map<String, Object?> get data => <String, Object?>{'name': user.name};
}
```

| Getter | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `to`, `cc`, `bcc`, `replyTo` | the addresses |
| `from` | the sender. Null: the `from` of the mail config |
| `subject` | the subject |
| `html`, `text` | the body as text, when there is no template |
| `view` | a [dox_view](../the-basic/views.md) template for the HTML body |
| `textView` | a dox_view template for the plain text body |
| `markdown` | a dox_view template with Markdown. See [Markdown mail](#markdown-mail) |
| `data` | the variables of the templates |
| `attachments` | the files |
| `mailer` | the mailer name, like `ses`. Null: the default mailer |

### Sending a mailable

Call `send()`, or put the mailable on the queue with `queue()` or `later()`:

```dart
await WelcomeMail(user).send();
await WelcomeMail(user).queue();
await WelcomeMail(user).later(Duration(minutes: 10));
```

`queue()` and `later()` render the templates at once. They take the options of [`Mail.queue()`](#queue-an-email).

### Changing the message

`toMessage()` gives the email as a `Message`. Override it to set more, like headers or tags:

```dart
@override
Message toMessage() {
  return super.toMessage().copyWith(tags: <String>['welcome']);
}
```

### Markdown mail

Write the email in Markdown. One template gives an HTML email with a layout and a plain text part:

```markdown title="resources/views/emails/welcome.dox.html"
# Hi {{ name }}

Thanks for joining. Here is what you can do next:

- Fill in your profile
- Invite your team

[Open your profile]({{ profileUrl }})

<a href="https://example.com/dashboard" class="button">Open the app</a>
```

Then set the `markdown` getter:

```dart
@override
String? get markdown => 'emails/welcome';
```

`<a class="button">` shows as a button. Do not indent the Markdown in `@if` or `@each`, because 4 spaces make a code block.

`{{ }}` escapes HTML and Markdown, and a link with an unsafe URL, like `javascript:`, loses its URL. Raw HTML in the template, like `<a href="{{ url }}">`, is not checked, so write links as `[text]({{ url }})`. To put Markdown from a value in the email, give a `SafeString`.

### Custom layout

Override `layout()` to use your own look. It gets the HTML of the Markdown and gives the full page:

```dart
import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';
import 'package:dox_view/dox_view.dart'; // View, SafeString

abstract class AppMail extends Mailable {
  @override
  String layout(String body) {
    return View.render('emails/layout',
        <String, Object?>{'body': SafeString(body)});
  }
}
```

### A simple email with no template

`MailMessage` is a mailable for a few lines and a button. It uses the Markdown layout:

```dart
await (MailMessage(
        subject: 'Invoice paid',
        to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com')])
      ..line('We got your payment.')
      ..action('View invoice', 'https://example.com/invoices/1')
      ..line('Thank you!'))
    .send();
```

- `cc:` in the constructor adds cc addresses.
- `attach(Attachment(...))` adds a file.
- `error()` makes the buttons red.
- `greeting` (default `Hello!`) starts the email, and `salutation` (default none) ends it.

Lines can use Markdown, like `**bold**`. `action()` throws an ArgumentError for an unsafe URL. To send one email on more channels, see [Notifications](notifications.md).

## Queue an email

A queue worker sends the email later, so the request does not wait:

```dart
await Mail.queue(message);
```

To send it after a time, use `Mail.later()`. Both give the job id:

```dart
await Mail.later(Duration(minutes: 10), message);
```

To pick another mailer and another queue:

```dart
await Mail.mailer('ses').queue(message, queue: 'emails');
```

This uses [dox_queue](queue.md), so you need its `QueueProvider` and a worker. The worker must also run your `MailProvider`, or the job fails with "Mail is not set up". The message is checked at once, so a bad message fails in the request.

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `queue` | `default` | the queue name |
| `encrypt` | false | encrypt the job data with the app key. The worker needs the same key |

The full email, with its attachments, is saved in Redis or in the `jobs` table. So keep attachments small. An email has personal data, so use `encrypt: true` if other people can read the queue.

With `encrypt: true`, the send error of a failed job is encrypted too. Read it with `RedactedMailError.decrypt(job.error)`. To use a queue other than dox_queue, call `Mail.useQueue(queue)`.

## Transports

### SMTP

```dart
'smtp': SmtpTransport(
  host: 'smtp.example.com',
  port: 587,
  username: Env.get('MAIL_USERNAME'),
  password: Env.get('MAIL_PASSWORD'),
  encryption: SmtpEncryption.starttls,
),
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `host` | required | the server |
| `port` | 465 for `tls`, 587 for `starttls`, 25 for `none` | the port |
| `username`, `password` | none | the login. No username: no login |
| `encryption` | `starttls` | `none`, `starttls` (TLS after connect) or `tls` (TLS from the start) |
| `allowInsecure` | false | accept a self-signed TLS certificate. Only for test servers |
| `auth` | PLAIN, or LOGIN when the server has no PLAIN | `SmtpAuth.plain`, `SmtpAuth.login` or `SmtpAuth.xoauth2` |
| `localDomain` | `localhost` | the name of this machine, for `EHLO` |
| `timeout` | 30 seconds | the time to connect, and to wait for each reply |
| `keepAlive` | false | keep the connection open for the next message |

With `starttls`, the send fails when the server has no STARTTLS, so your password never goes in plain text. For Gmail or Outlook with OAuth 2, use `SmtpAuth.xoauth2` with the access token as the `password`.

For local work, [Mailpit](https://mailpit.axllent.org) catches all emails:

```dart
'mailpit': SmtpTransport(
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 1025,
  encryption: SmtpEncryption.none,
),
```

### Amazon SES

`SesTransport` uses SES API v1, and `SesV2Transport` uses SES API v2. Both send attachments and inline images:

```dart
'ses': SesV2Transport(
  key: Env.get('AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID'),
  secret: Env.get('AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY'),
  region: Env.get('AWS_REGION', 'us-east-1'),
),
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `key` | required | the AWS access key id |
| `secret` | required | the AWS secret access key |
| `sessionToken` | none | for temporary keys, like from a role |
| `region` | `us-east-1` | the AWS region of SES |
| `configurationSet` | none | the SES configuration set, to track events |
| `endpoint` | `https://email.<region>.amazonaws.com/` | another API address |

### Azure Communication Services

```dart
'azure': AzureTransport(
  endpoint: 'https://my-app.europe.communication.azure.com',
  accessKey: Env.get('AZURE_EMAIL_KEY'),
),
```

Or use the connection string from the Azure portal:

```dart
'azure': AzureTransport.fromConnectionString(
  Env.get('AZURE_EMAIL_CONNECTION_STRING'),
),
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `endpoint` | required | the address of your resource |
| `accessKey` | required | the access key of the resource |
| `apiVersion` | `2023-03-31` | the API version. Inline images need a newer version |
| `disableTracking` | false | turn off open and click tracking |

### Resend

```dart
'resend': ResendTransport(apiKey: Env.get('RESEND_API_KEY')),
```

### Mailgun

Use the region of your Mailgun domain: `MailgunRegion.us` (the default) or `MailgunRegion.eu`:

```dart
'mailgun': MailgunTransport(
  apiKey: Env.get('MAILGUN_API_KEY'),
  domain: 'mg.example.com',
  region: MailgunRegion.eu,
),
```

### Postmark

`messageStream` is optional. Without it, Postmark uses the default stream:

```dart
'postmark': PostmarkTransport(
  serverToken: Env.get('POSTMARK_TOKEN'),
  messageStream: 'outbound',
),
```

### sendmail

Send with the `sendmail` program of the server (Postfix, Exim, msmtp and others):

```dart
'sendmail': SendmailTransport(
  path: '/usr/sbin/sendmail',
  mode: SendmailMode.smtp,
),
```

| Mode | Command | How it works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SendmailMode.smtp` (default) | `sendmail -bs` | speaks SMTP on stdin and stdout |
| `SendmailMode.pipe` | `sendmail -t -i` | sends the message in. sendmail reads the recipients from the headers |

### Log

Print each email and send nothing. `output` sets where it prints, and `bothBodies: true` also shows the HTML body:

```dart
'log': LogTransport(bothBodies: true, output: stderr.writeln),
```

### Array

Keep each email in a list and send nothing. See [Testing](#testing):

```dart
'array': ArrayTransport(),
```

### Failover

`FailoverTransport` tries each transport in order, until one sends the email. If all fail, it throws the error of the last one:

```dart
SesV2Transport ses = SesV2Transport(key: '...', secret: '...');
SmtpTransport smtp = SmtpTransport(host: 'smtp.example.com');

MailConfig mailConfig = MailConfig(
  defaultMailer: 'main',
  mailers: <String, Transport>{
    'main': FailoverTransport(<Transport>[ses, smtp]),
  },
);
```

Give `onError` to get the error of each transport that fails.

## Tags and metadata

Each transport uses `tags` and `metadata` in its own way:

| Transport | `tags` | `metadata` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SES | not used | message tags |
| Resend | tags with the value true | tags |
| Mailgun | `o:tag` | variables (`v:name`) |
| Postmark | the first tag | metadata |
| Azure, SMTP, sendmail | not used | not used |

For SMTP and sendmail, use `headers`.

## Hooks

Run code before or after each email, for example to log it. Each isolate has its own hooks, so add them in `setup()` of your mail provider:

```dart
class AppMailProvider extends MailProvider {
  AppMailProvider() : super(mailConfig);

  @override
  void setup() {
    super.setup();
    Mail.clearHooks(); // a second setup() does not add each hook twice
    Mail.onSending((Message message) {
      print('sending "${message.subject}" to ${message.to}');
    });
    Mail.onSent((SentMessage sent) {
      print('sent ${sent.messageId}');
    });
  }
}
```

Hooks run for every mailer, for queued emails and with `Mail.fake()`. When an `onSending` hook throws, the email is not sent. When an `onSent` hook throws, the error is only logged.

## Sending all mail to one address

On a staging server, send every email to your own inbox with `Mail.alwaysTo()`. Call it in `setup()` of your mail provider:

```dart
class AppMailProvider extends MailProvider {
  AppMailProvider() : super(mailConfig);

  @override
  void setup() {
    super.setup();
    if (Env.get<String>('APP_ENV') == 'staging') {
      Mail.alwaysTo('qa@example.com');
    }
  }
}
```

The `to` of each email becomes that address, and `cc` and `bcc` are removed. `Mail.alwaysTo(null)` turns it off.

## Custom transports

Extend `Transport` and add it to `mailers`:

```dart
class MyApiTransport extends Transport {
  @override
  Future<SentMessage> send(Message message) async {
    // call your API here
    return SentMessage(message, messageId: 'id from the API');
  }
}
```

The message already has a from address. For a provider that takes raw MIME, `MimeBuilder().build(message)` gives the MIME text.

## Testing

`Mail.fake()` sends all mailers to one `ArrayTransport`, so nothing goes out:

```dart
import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  late ArrayTransport mail;

  setUp(() {
    mail = Mail.fake();
  });

  tearDown(() {
    Mail.restore();
  });

  test('sign up sends a welcome email', () async {
    await signUp('ann@example.com');

    expect(mail.messages, hasLength(1));
    Message message = mail.messages.single;
    expect(message.to.single.email, 'ann@example.com');
    expect(message.subject, 'Welcome');
  });
}
```

### Testing queued mail

Queued emails go to `mail.queued`, not to the job queue, so you need no queue setup:

```dart
await Mail.queue(message);

mail.assertQueued((Message m) => m.subject == 'Welcome');
mail.assertNothingSent();
```

Each item in `mail.queued` is a `QueuedMessage` with `mailer`, `message`, `id`, `delay`, `queue` and `encrypt`.

### Assertions

| Method | Checks |
|---|---|
| `assertSent([test])` | an email was sent. With `test`, one of them passes it |
| `assertSentCount(count, [test])` | `count` emails were sent. With `test`, `count` emails pass it |
| `assertNotSent(test)` | no sent email passes `test` |
| `assertNothingSent()` | no email was sent |
| `assertQueued([test])` | an email was queued. With `test`, one of them passes it |
| `assertNotQueued(test)` | no queued email passes `test` |
| `assertNothingQueued()` | no email was queued |

`test` is a `bool Function(Message)`. A failed check throws a StateError. `mail.clear()` removes the sent and the queued emails.

## Without Dox

`dox_mailer` also works on its own. Call `Mail.configure()` at the start, and `Mail.close()` at the end:

```dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  Map<String, String> env = Platform.environment;

  Mail.configure(MailConfig(
    defaultMailer: 'smtp',
    from: Address('hello@example.com', 'My app'),
    mailers: <String, Transport>{
      'smtp': SmtpTransport(
        host: env['MAIL_HOST'] ?? 'localhost',
        username: env['MAIL_USERNAME'],
        password: env['MAIL_PASSWORD'],
      ),
    },
  ));

  await Mail.send(Message(
    to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com')],
    subject: 'Hello',
    text: 'Hello Ann!',
  ));

  // closes open SMTP connections and HTTP clients
  await Mail.close();
}
```

- [Notifications](notifications.md): send one message on many channels.

# Notifications

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/notifications/

# Notifications

A notification tells a user about something, like "your invoice is paid", by email or by a channel you write.

Each notification is a class that holds the text and the channels. Notifications are in the `dox_mailer` package, so set up [mail](mail.md) first.

## Creating notifications

A notification extends `Notification`. The `via` method gives the channels, and `toMail` makes the email:

```dart
class InvoicePaid extends Notification {
  InvoicePaid(this.invoiceId);

  final int invoiceId;

  @override
  List<NotificationChannel> via(Object notifiable) {
    return <NotificationChannel>[const MailChannel()];
  }

  @override
  Mailable toMail(Object notifiable) {
    return MailMessage(subject: 'Invoice paid')
      ..line('We got your payment.')
      ..action('View invoice', 'https://example.com/invoices/$invoiceId');
  }
}
```

`toMail()` can return any mailable, like a `WelcomeMail` with a template.

## Sending notifications

### Making a model notifiable

Add the `Notifiable` mixin to the class that gets notifications. Its `routeNotificationFor` method gives each channel the destination:

```dart
class User extends Model<User> with Notifiable {
  @override
  Object? routeNotificationFor(String channel) {
    return channel == 'mail' ? Address(email!, name) : null;
  }
}
```

The mail route can be an `Address`, an email text like `Ann <ann@example.com>`, or a list of these. A `to` address on the mailable wins over the route.

### Sending to one user

Call `notify` on the model:

```dart
await user.notify(InvoicePaid(1));
```

### Sending to many users

Use `Notification.send` with a list:

```dart
await Notification.send(users, InvoicePaid(1));
```

### Sending to an address with no user

For a guest with no user row, give an `Address`:

```dart
await Notification.send(<Object>[Address('ann@example.com')],
    InvoicePaid(1));
```

## Handling errors

When one channel throws, the other channels and notifiables still get the notification. At the end, `Notification.send()` throws a `NotificationException`. Its `errors` list gives the notifiable, the channel and the error of each failure:

```dart
try {
  await Notification.send(users, InvoicePaid(1));
} on NotificationException catch (e) {
  for (NotificationError error in e.errors) {
    print('${error.channel}: ${error.error}'); // null channel: via()
  }
}
```

The error text has no email addresses, so it is safe for logs. With one notifiable and one error, like in `user.notify()`, you get the initial error, like a `MailException`.

## Queueing notifications

Override `shouldQueue` to send the email in the background. The mail channel then puts the email on [the queue](queue.md), like `Mail.queue()`:

```dart
@override
bool get shouldQueue => true;
```

The email is rendered at once, and the worker sends it. These getters set the queue options:

| Getter | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `queue` | null (`default`) | the queue name |
| `delay` | null | the worker sends the email after this wait |
| `encrypt` | false | encrypt the job data with the app key |

These options change only the mail channel. To queue your own channel, dispatch a job in it.

## Custom channels

To send a notification another way, like to a database table, write a channel. A channel implements `NotificationChannel` and gets the data from `toArray()`:

```dart
import 'dart:convert';

class DatabaseChannel implements NotificationChannel {
  @override
  Future<void> send(Object notifiable, Notification notification) async {
    // only a user has a row. An Address or an email text has none.
    if (notifiable is! User) return;
    AppNotification row = AppNotification()
      ..userId = notifiable.id
      ..data = jsonEncode(notification.toArray(notifiable));
    await row.save();
  }
}
```

Then add the channel to `via()`, and give the data in `toArray()`:

```dart
class InvoicePaid extends Notification {
  @override
  List<NotificationChannel> via(Object notifiable) {
    return <NotificationChannel>[const MailChannel(), DatabaseChannel()];
  }

  @override
  Map<String, Object?> toArray(Object notifiable) {
    return <String, Object?>{
      'type': 'invoice_paid',
      'invoice_id': invoiceId,
    };
  }

  // ...
}
```

## Testing

`Mail.fake()` also catches the emails of the mail channel:

```dart
ArrayTransport mail = Mail.fake();
await user.notify(InvoicePaid(1));
expect(mail.messages.single.subject, 'Invoice paid');
```

With `shouldQueue`, the email goes to `mail.queued`. Check it with `mail.assertQueued()`. See [Mail](mail.md#testing).

## Next steps

- [Mail](mail.md): mailables, templates and transports.
- [Queue](queue.md): run the workers that send queued email.

# Broadcasting

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/broadcasting/

# Broadcasting

Broadcasting sends server events to browsers and apps over Socket.IO, on public, private and presence channels.

A client subscribes to a **channel**. Your code sends an event to the channel, and every client in it gets the event. Broadcasting is part of the `dox_socketio` package. It is off by default.

## Setup

Do the [Socket.IO setup](../packages/socketio.md#setup) first. Then turn on broadcasting in the config:

```dart title="lib/config/socketio.dart"
SocketIoConfig socketIoConfig = SocketIoConfig(
  broadcasting: true,
  namespaces: <NamespaceHandler>[ChatNamespace()],
);
```

Broadcasting works on the `/` namespace. To use another namespace, call `Broadcast.listen(nsp)` with it. `Broadcast.event` sends through the last namespace it got.

### Channel rules

Private and presence channels need a rule for who can join. Each isolate keeps its own rules, so add them in a provider:

```dart title="lib/providers/broadcast_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_socketio/dox_socketio.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

class BroadcastProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Broadcast.channel('orders.{id}', (Object? user, String id) {
      return (user as User).id.toString() == id;
    });
  }
}
```

Run `dart run build_runner build`, so the container finds the provider. Without a rule, every private subscribe gets `Forbidden`. See [Authorizing channels](#authorizing-channels).

### The auth route

A client gets a channel token from the auth route. Add the route with your auth middleware:

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
@override
void register() {
  // POST /api/broadcasting/auth
  Broadcast.routes(middleware: <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware()]);
}
```

The router prefix goes in front of the path. Give `path:` to use another path. The route answers `{"auth": "<token>"}`, or 403 when the rule refuses. The token is signed with a key from `APP_KEY`, and it works for one socket, one channel and one minute.

### Limits

| Setting | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Broadcast.maxChannelLength` | 200 | the longest channel name a client can subscribe to |
| `Broadcast.maxChannelsPerSocket` | 100 | the most channels for one socket |
| `Broadcast.tokenLifetime` | 1 minute | how long a token from the auth route works |
| `Broadcast.presenceTimeout` | 2 seconds | how long a presence join or leave waits for other servers |
| `Broadcast.maxWhisperSize` | 10 KB | the biggest `data` of a [client event](#client-events), in bytes of JSON |

## Channel types

| Channel | Name | Who can subscribe |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Channel('news')` | `news` | any client |
| `PrivateChannel('orders.5')` | `private-orders.5` | a client that passes the rule |
| `PresenceChannel('chat.lobby')` | `presence-chat.lobby` | a client that passes the rule. Members see each other |

## Defining broadcast events

An event is a class with the `ShouldBroadcast` mixin:

```dart
class OrderShipped with ShouldBroadcast {
  OrderShipped(this.order);
  final Order order;

  @override
  List<Channel> broadcastOn() =>
      <Channel>[PrivateChannel('orders.${order.id}')];

  @override
  String broadcastAs() => 'order.shipped'; // default: the class name

  @override
  Map<String, Object?> broadcastWith() =>
      <String, Object?>{'id': order.id};
}
```

`broadcastOn` gives the channels. `broadcastWith` gives the JSON payload, an empty map by default. Do not start an event name with `client-`, because that prefix is for [client events](#client-events).

## Authorizing channels

`Broadcast.channel(pattern, rule)` adds a rule. The pattern has no `private-` or `presence-` prefix, and a `{name}` part matches any text with no dot. The rule gets the user, then one string for each `{name}` part. It can be async.

- A private rule returns true to allow.
- A presence rule returns a map of member info, with an `id`.
- Any other result, or an error, refuses.

This presence rule lets any logged in user join a chat room:

```dart
Broadcast.channel('chat.{room}', (Object? user, String room) {
  User u = user as User;
  return <String, Object?>{'id': u.id, 'name': u.name};
});
```

One rule serves both kinds, so `orders.{id}` checks `private-orders.1` and `presence-orders.1`. When more patterns match, the first rule wins.

### Your own auth endpoint

To write the auth route yourself, run the rule with `Broadcast.authorize`, and make the token with `Broadcast.authToken`:

```dart
Object? result = await Broadcast.authorize(user, 'private-orders.5');
if (result == null) throw ForbiddenHttpException();
String token = Broadcast.authToken(socketId, 'private-orders.5');
```

`authorize` gives null when the rule refuses. For a presence channel, it gives the member map. Give that map as the third argument of `authToken`.

## Broadcasting events

Use `broadcast` to send an event. `Broadcast.event` does the same:

```dart
await broadcast(OrderShipped(order));
await Broadcast.event(OrderShipped(order)); // the same
```

### Only to others

Use `toOthers` to skip the socket of the user who made the change. `Broadcast.socketId(req)` reads the socket id from the `X-Socket-ID` header:

```dart
await Broadcast.event(OrderShipped(order),
    toOthers: Broadcast.socketId(req));
```

## Receiving broadcasts

On the client, use `socket.io-client`. Subscribe in the `connect` handler, because after a reconnect the socket has no channels:

```js
import { io } from 'socket.io-client';

const socket = io('https://app.example.com', { transports: ['websocket'] });

socket.on('order.shipped',
  (channel, payload) => console.log(channel, payload));
socket.on('connect', () => {
  socket.emit('subscribe', { channel: 'news' }, (ack) => console.log(ack));
});
```

Events come as `(channel, payload)`, with the name from `broadcastAs`.

### Private and presence channels

Get a token from the auth route, then send it as a string in `auth`. A token works for one socket id, so get a new one in the `connect` handler:

```js
socket.on('connect', async () => {
  const res = await fetch('/api/broadcasting/auth', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: {
      'content-type': 'application/json',
      authorization: `Bearer ${apiToken}`,
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({
      socket_id: socket.id,
      channel_name: 'private-orders.5',
    }),
  });
  const { auth } = await res.json();
  socket.emit('subscribe', { channel: 'private-orders.5', auth },
    (ack) => console.log(ack));
});
```

A socket logged in with [`SocketAuth`](../packages/socketio.md#log-in-a-socket) needs no token. The rule then gets `socket.user`.

### Leaving a channel

Send `unsubscribe` with the channel name:

```js
socket.emit('unsubscribe', { channel: 'news' }, (ack) => console.log(ack));
```

### Subscribe errors

The ack of `subscribe` and `unsubscribe` is `{ok: true}` or `{ok: false, error}`:

| `error` | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `channel is missing` | no channel name |
| `channel name is too long` | over `Broadcast.maxChannelLength` |
| `too many channels` | over `Broadcast.maxChannelsPerSocket` |
| `already subscribing` | the server still checks the same channel |
| `Forbidden` | the rule refused, or the token is missing, wrong or old |
| `unsubscribed` | an `unsubscribe` came during the subscribe |
| `presence is not available` | another server did not answer in time |

## Presence channels

A presence channel tells its members who else is in it. The client gets three events:

| Event | Arguments | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `presence:subscribed` | `(channel, members)` | to the new socket, with all members |
| `presence:joining` | `(channel, member)` | to the others, when a member joins |
| `presence:leaving` | `(channel, member)` | to the others, when a member leaves |

A member is `{user_id, user_info}`, and `user_info` is the map from the rule:

```js
socket.on('presence:subscribed',
  (channel, members) => console.log(members));
socket.on('presence:joining',
  (channel, member) => console.log(member.user_info.name));
socket.on('presence:leaving',
  (channel, member) => console.log(member.user_id));
```

A user with two sockets is one member. The member list covers all isolates and servers that share the adapter.

## Queued broadcasting

A queued broadcast goes through your [queue](queue.md), so the request does not wait. Connect the two packages with a hook and a small job.

### 1. Mark the event

Use `ShouldBroadcastQueued` in place of `ShouldBroadcast`:

```dart
class OrderShipped with ShouldBroadcastQueued {
  OrderShipped(this.order);
  final Order order;

  @override
  List<Channel> broadcastOn() =>
      <Channel>[PrivateChannel('orders.${order.id}')];

  @override
  Map<String, Object?> broadcastWith() =>
      <String, Object?>{'id': order.id};
}

await broadcast(OrderShipped(order)); // goes to the queue
```

### 2. Write the job

The worker runs this job, and it sends the broadcast to the clients:

```dart title="lib/app/jobs/broadcast.job.dart"
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';
import 'package:dox_socketio/dox_socketio.dart';

@Job()
class BroadcastJob extends DoxJob {
  BroadcastJob({required this.payload});

  final Map<String, dynamic> payload;

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    await Broadcast.deliver(BroadcastPayload.fromJson(payload));
  }
}
```

Run `dart run build_runner build` to add the job to the job registry. See [queue setup](queue.md#setup) and [configuration](queue.md#configuration).

### 3. Set the hook

Add the hook to `setup()` of the `BroadcastProvider` from [Channel rules](#channel-rules):

```dart title="lib/providers/broadcast_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';
import 'package:dox_socketio/dox_socketio.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

import '../app/jobs/broadcast.job.dart';

class BroadcastProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Broadcast.channel('orders.{id}', (Object? user, String id) {
      return (user as User).id.toString() == id;
    });

    // puts ShouldBroadcastQueued events on the queue
    Broadcast.useQueue(queueBroadcast);
  }

  static Future<void> queueBroadcast(BroadcastPayload payload) async {
    await Queue.dispatch(BroadcastJob(payload: payload.toJson()));
  }
}
```

With no hook, a `ShouldBroadcastQueued` event is sent at once.

### 4. Use the Redis adapter

The worker is its own process, so it reaches the clients of the web server through Redis. Set the [Redis adapter](../packages/socketio.md#many-servers-redis-adapter) in `SocketIoConfig`. The web server and the worker share this config.

### 5. Run the worker

```bash
dart run bin/queue.dart
```

Deploy the worker with the web app. See [run the worker](queue.md#running-the-worker).

## Broadcasting from other processes

A command has no Socket.IO server. Set an emitter, so `Broadcast.event` sends through Redis:

```dart
Redis redis = Redis(RedisOptions(host: '127.0.0.1', port: 6379));
Broadcast.emitter = SocketIoEmitter(redis);

await Broadcast.event(OrderShipped(order));
```

The servers must use the [Redis adapter](../packages/socketio.md#many-servers-redis-adapter). For a namespace other than `/`, use `SocketIoEmitter(redis).of('/chat')`. With no server and no emitter, `Broadcast.event` throws a StateError.

## Client events

A **client event** (a whisper) goes from one client to the other members of a private or presence channel, like "is typing". The server only passes it on. It is off by default, because clients can then send messages to each other:

```dart
SocketIoConfig(broadcasting: true, whisper: true);
```

The client sends `client event` with `{channel, event, data}`. The event name must start with `client-`. The other sockets in the channel get `(channel, data)`:

```js
socket.emit('client event', {
  channel: 'presence-chat.lobby',
  event: 'client-typing',
  data: { name: 'Alice' },
}, (ack) => console.log(ack)); // the ack is optional

socket.on('client-typing', (channel, data) => console.log(channel, data));
```

Only a subscribed socket can whisper. The sender does not get its own whisper. A refused whisper gets `{ok: false, error}`, like `not subscribed`.

The names match the Echo client. Echo sends `auth` as headers, so log its socket in with [`SocketAuth`](../packages/socketio.md#log-in-a-socket) for private channels.

## Testing

`Broadcast.fake()` keeps the events and sends nothing:

```dart
test('shipping an order broadcasts', () async {
  BroadcastFake fake = Broadcast.fake();

  await shipOrder(order);

  fake.assertBroadcasted<OrderShipped>();
  fake.assertBroadcastedOn<OrderShipped>('private-orders.${order.id}');
  fake.assertBroadcastedTimes<OrderShipped>(1);
});
```

| Method | Passes when |
| --- | --- |
| `assertBroadcasted<T>([test])` | an event of type `T` was sent. With `test`, one of them passes it |
| `assertBroadcastedOn<T>(name)` | `T` was sent on the channel `name`, with its prefix |
| `assertBroadcastedTimes<T>(n)` | `T` was sent `n` times |
| `assertQueued<T>([test])` | `T` was sent as a queued event |
| `assertNotBroadcasted<T>()` | no `T` was sent |
| `assertNothingBroadcasted()` | no event was sent |

`fake.eventsOf<T>()` gives the events, `fake.delivered` gives the payloads of `deliver`, and `fake.clear()` removes them. `Broadcast.restore()` turns the fake off. Call `Broadcast.reset()` in `tearDown` to remove the rules, the emitter and the fake.

- [Socket.IO](../packages/socketio.md): namespaces, rooms and the Redis adapter.
- [Queue](queue.md): run the worker for queued broadcasts.

# HTTP/2

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/http2/

# HTTP/2

Dox serves HTTP/2 on the same port as HTTP/1.1, so one connection can send many requests at the same time.

Turn it on to serve [gRPC](grpc.md), when your proxy sends HTTP/2 to the app, or when Dox serves HTTPS itself. HTTP/2 is off by default.

## Setup

Set `http2` to true in the app config. The port then accepts HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, and your routes stay the same:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  http2: true,
  // ...
);
```

## Read the protocol of a request

`req.protocolVersion` is `2.0` for an HTTP/2 request, and `1.0` or `1.1` for HTTP/1.x:

```dart
Route.get('/protocol', (DoxRequest req) {
  return req.protocolVersion; // '2.0'
});
```

Test it with curl:

```bash
curl --http2-prior-knowledge http://localhost:3000/protocol
```

## Limit the open requests on one connection

`maxConcurrentStreams` is the most open requests on one connection. The default is 250:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  http2: true,
  maxConcurrentStreams: 100,
  // ...
);
```

## Use TLS

Browsers use HTTP/2 only with TLS. Dox can do the TLS itself. Set `tls` together with `http2`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  http2: true,
  tls: TlsOptions(certificatePath: 'fullchain.pem', keyPath: 'privkey.pem'),
  // ...
);
```

```text
browser  --HTTP/2 + TLS-->  Dox
```

The client selects HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1 in the TLS handshake (ALPN `h2` or `http/1.1`). See [Deployment: HTTPS without a proxy](deployment.md#https-without-a-proxy).

## Use a proxy

Without `tls`, Dox speaks **h2c**: HTTP/2 over plain TCP. Then your proxy does the TLS:

```text
browser  --HTTP/2 + TLS-->  proxy  --h2c or HTTP/1.1-->  Dox
```

For the Caddy and nginx config, see [Deployment: HTTP/2 and gRPC](deployment.md#http2-and-grpc).

## Protection

Dox has protection against the known HTTP/2 attacks by default:

- A cancelled request stays in the `maxConcurrentStreams` count until your handler stops. This stops the Rapid Reset attack.
- Too many resets, `SETTINGS` frames, `PING` frames or empty frames close the connection with `GOAWAY ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM`.
- A request body has the same limits as on HTTP/1.1. See [Size limits](../the-basic/request.md#size-limits).
- A connection with no open request closes after `idleTimeout`.

## Benchmark

On one isolate, HTTP/2 does approximately 1.6 times the requests of HTTP/1.1, when a client sends many requests on one connection.

The two HTTP/1.1 rows are almost the same, so `http2: true` does not make HTTP/1.1 clients slower.

| Load                                       | Requests a second |
| ------------------------------------------ | ----------------: |
| HTTP/1.1, 256 connections, `http2` off     | 364,000           |
| HTTP/1.1, 256 connections, `http2` on      | 373,000           |
| HTTP/2, 16 connections × 16 requests each  | 587,000           |
| HTTP/2, 4 connections × 64 requests each   | 465,000           |

With 4 isolates, HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 both do approximately 630,000 requests a second. This number is the limit of the load tool on 4 cores, not the limit of Dox. HTTP/2 gives the largest increase when the app has few isolates.

### Test setup

- The app has one route, `GET /`. This route sends `Hello, World!`.
- The app is an AOT build. The build command is `dart build cli`.
- All tests ran in Linux containers on one machine with 8 cores. The server used 4 cores. The load tool, [oha](https://github.com/hatoo/oha), used the other 4 cores.
- Each number is the median of 3 runs. Each run took 10 seconds, after a warm up of 3 seconds.


## Without Dox

With the [native server](native-server.md) on its own, give the same options to `NativeHttpServer.bind`. `http2ResetBurst` and `http2ResetRate` limit the resets of one connection. Raise them behind a proxy that sends many cancels:

```dart
NativeHttpServer server = await NativeHttpServer.bind(
  3000,
  http2: true,
  maxConcurrentStreams: 100,
  http2ResetBurst: 1000,
  http2ResetRate: 100, // a second
);
```

- [Deployment](deployment.md): HTTPS with or without a proxy.
