# gRPC

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/grpc/

# gRPC

gRPC lets your services call each other with typed messages, on the same port as your HTTP routes.

You write the calls one time in a `.proto` file, and each side gets typed code from it. A client in any language can call your app.

## Setup

Run the setup command in your app:

```bash
dox add grpc
```

It adds the packages, a sample `protos/greeter.proto` file, `lib/routes/grpc.dart` and `APP_HTTP2=true` in `.env`. To add the packages yourself, run `dart pub add dox_grpc protobuf grpc`.

gRPC works only over [HTTP/2](http2.md). A new app turns it on from the `APP_HTTP2` key:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  http2: env.appHttp2 ?? false,
  // ...
);
```

If your `AppEnv` has no `appHttp2` getter, add `bool? get appHttp2;` and run `dart run build_runner build`. Or set `http2: true`.

### Options

Give a `GrpcOptions` to `Grpc.register` to change the limits of one service:

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `maxReceiveMessageSize` | 4 MiB | The largest request message, also after unzip. |
| `maxSendMessageSize` | 4 MiB | The largest reply message. |
| `gzipResponses` | false | Gzip the replies for clients that accept gzip. |
| `idleTimeout` | 5 minutes | Stop a call with no message in or out for this time. null means no limit. |

A bigger message stops the call with `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`. An idle call stops with `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`. See [Changing the options](#changing-the-options).

## Write the .proto file

A `.proto` file gives the calls of a service and their messages. The setup command wrote this sample:

```proto title="protos/greeter.proto"
syntax = "proto3";

package greeter;

service Greeter {
  rpc SayHello (HelloRequest) returns (HelloReply);
}

message HelloRequest {
  string name = 1;
}

message HelloReply {
  string message = 1;
}
```

## Generate the Dart code

Install `protoc` and its Dart plugin one time. `~/.pub-cache/bin` must be on your `PATH`:

```bash
brew install protobuf
dart pub global activate protoc_plugin
```

Generate the code. Do this again after each change to the `.proto` file:

```bash
mkdir -p lib/generated
protoc --dart_out=grpc:lib/generated -Iprotos protos/greeter.proto
```

It writes the message classes and a `GreeterServiceBase` class to `lib/generated`.

## Write the service

Extend the generated base class. Each `rpc` of the `.proto` file is one method:

```dart title="lib/app/grpc/greeter_service.dart"
import 'package:dox_grpc/dox_grpc.dart';

import '../../generated/greeter.pbgrpc.dart';

class GreeterService extends GreeterServiceBase {
  @override
  Future<HelloReply> sayHello(
      ServiceCall call, HelloRequest request) async {
    return HelloReply(message: 'Hello ${request.name}');
  }
}
```

## Register the service

Call `Grpc.register` in the router that the setup command wrote. Keep the [health check](#health-check) as the first call:

```dart title="lib/routes/grpc.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_grpc/dox_grpc.dart';

import '../app/grpc/greeter_service.dart';

class GrpcRouter extends Router {
  @override
  void register() {
    Grpc.register(HealthService());
    Grpc.register(GreeterService());
  }
}
```

Run `dart run build_runner build` and start the app again.

The router must have no prefix, because a gRPC client always calls `/<package.Service>/<Method>`. So do not use the `api` router or a `Route.group`. A changed path throws a `StateError` at start.

## Call the service

Test a call with [grpcurl](https://github.com/fullstorydev/grpcurl). Give it the `.proto` file, because Dox has no server reflection:

```bash
grpcurl -plaintext -import-path protos -proto greeter.proto \
  -d '{"name": "Ann"}' localhost:3000 greeter.Greeter/SayHello
```

The reply is `{ "message": "Hello Ann" }`.

## Add auth

Your Dox middleware runs before each call. Put the services that need a login in `Route.middleware`, and keep the health check out of it:

```dart title="lib/routes/grpc.dart"
class GrpcRouter extends Router {
  @override
  void register() {
    Grpc.register(HealthService());

    Route.middleware(<dynamic>[AuthMiddleware()], () {
      Grpc.register(GreeterService());
    });
  }
}
```

A client sends its token as metadata. The middleware reads it as a header:

```dart title="lib/app/http/middleware/auth.middleware.dart"
class AuthMiddleware implements IDoxMiddleware {
  @override
  dynamic handle(IDoxRequest req) {
    String token = Env.get<String>('API_TOKEN');
    String sent = req.header('authorization') ?? '';
    if (!Hash.equals(sent, 'Bearer $token')) {
      throw HttpStatusException(401, message: 'Bad token');
    }
    return req;
  }
}
```

The client gets the gRPC status of the HTTP error, so 401 becomes `UNAUTHENTICATED`. See [HTTP errors and gRPC statuses](#http-errors-and-grpc-statuses).

### Middleware for a full router

Set the `middleware` of the router when all its services need it:

```dart title="lib/routes/grpc.dart"
class GrpcRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware()];

  @override
  void register() {
    Grpc.register(GreeterService());
  }
}
```

Then register the health check in a router with no middleware, and put it first in `routers` of the app config. See [Routers and providers](../the-basic/dependency-injection.md#routers-and-providers). The first `Grpc.register` of the app in `Route.middleware` throws a `StateError` at start.

## Call types

gRPC has four types of calls. The place of `stream` in the `.proto` file sets the type:

```proto title="protos/greeter.proto"
service Greeter {
  rpc SayHello (HelloRequest) returns (HelloReply);
  rpc SayHelloMany (HelloRequest) returns (stream HelloReply);
  rpc CollectNames (stream HelloRequest) returns (HelloReply);
  rpc Chat (stream HelloRequest) returns (stream HelloReply);
}
```

### Unary calls

One request and one reply. The method returns a `Future`:

```dart
@override
Future<HelloReply> sayHello(ServiceCall call, HelloRequest request) async {
  return HelloReply(message: 'Hello ${request.name}');
}
```

### Server streaming

One request and many replies. The method returns a `Stream`:

```dart
@override
Stream<HelloReply> sayHelloMany(
    ServiceCall call, HelloRequest request) async* {
  for (int i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
    if (call.isCanceled) return;
    yield HelloReply(message: 'Hello ${request.name} $i');
  }
}
```

### Client streaming

Many requests and one reply. The method gets a `Stream` of requests:

```dart
@override
Future<HelloReply> collectNames(
  ServiceCall call,
  Stream<HelloRequest> request,
) async {
  List<String> names = <String>[];
  await for (HelloRequest item in request) {
    names.add(item.name);
  }
  return HelloReply(message: 'Hello ${names.join(', ')}');
}
```

### Bidirectional streaming

Many requests and many replies. The method gets a `Stream` and returns a `Stream`:

```dart
@override
Stream<HelloReply> chat(
    ServiceCall call, Stream<HelloRequest> request) async* {
  await for (HelloRequest item in request) {
    yield HelloReply(message: 'Hello ${item.name}');
  }
}
```

## Return errors

Throw a `GrpcException` with a `GrpcStatus` and a message for the client:

```dart
throw GrpcException(GrpcStatus.notFound, 'No user 5');
```

The third argument is a list of protobuf messages. The client gets them as error details. A `GrpcError` from `package:grpc` also works.

Any other error stops the call with `INTERNAL` and goes to your exception handler. The client sees its text only when `APP_ENV` is `development` or `local`. A call to an unknown service or method gets `UNIMPLEMENTED`.

### Status codes

`GrpcStatus` has the 17 gRPC status codes. `code` is the number, `fromCode` gives the status of a number, and `fromHttp` gives the status of an HTTP error:

```dart
int code = GrpcStatus.notFound.code; // 5
GrpcStatus status = GrpcStatus.fromHttp(401); // unauthenticated
```

### HTTP errors and gRPC statuses

Dox changes an HTTP error of a middleware to a gRPC status:

| HTTP error | gRPC status |
| --- | --- |
| 400, 422 | `INVALID_ARGUMENT` |
| 401 | `UNAUTHENTICATED` |
| 403 | `PERMISSION_DENIED` |
| 404 | `NOT_FOUND` |
| 408, 504 | `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED` |
| 409 | `ABORTED` |
| 413, 429 | `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` |
| 501 | `UNIMPLEMENTED` |
| 502, 503 | `UNAVAILABLE` |
| other 4xx | `FAILED_PRECONDITION` |
| other 5xx | `INTERNAL` |

The client also gets the message of the error. The message of a 5xx error shows only when `APP_ENV` is `development` or `local`.

## Metadata

**Metadata** is the gRPC name for headers. `call.clientMetadata` has the headers of the client, with no `grpc-*` headers. Set `call.headers` before the first reply, and `call.trailers` for the end of the call:

```dart
@override
Future<HelloReply> sayHello(ServiceCall call, HelloRequest request) async {
  String? language = call.clientMetadata!['accept-language'];
  call.headers!['x-served-by'] = 'greeter';
  call.trailers!['x-done'] = 'yes';
  return HelloReply(message: 'Hello ${request.name} ($language)');
}
```

The maps are nullable in the `ServiceCall` type, so use `!`.

### Binary metadata

A value with a name that ends in `-bin` is base64 text. `GrpcWire.decodeBinary` gives its bytes, and `GrpcWire.encodeBinary` makes a value from bytes:

```dart
Uint8List bytes = GrpcWire.decodeBinary(call.clientMetadata!['trace-bin']!);
call.trailers!['trace-bin'] = GrpcWire.encodeBinary(bytes);
```

## Deadlines and cancelled calls

When the deadline of the client passes, Dox stops the call with `DEADLINE_EXCEEDED`. Your method can still run, so a long method must check `call.isCanceled` and `call.isTimedOut`:

```dart
@override
Stream<HelloReply> sayHelloMany(
    ServiceCall call, HelloRequest request) async* {
  while (!call.isCanceled && !call.isTimedOut) {
    yield HelloReply(message: 'Hello ${request.name}');
    await Future<void>.delayed(Duration(seconds: 1));
  }
}
```

`call.deadline` is the time of the deadline, or null. gRPC routes skip the `RequestTimeout` middleware, so a long stream does not stop.

## Changing the options

Give a `GrpcOptions` to `Grpc.register`. All options are in [Options](#options):

```dart
Grpc.register(
  GreeterService(),
  options: GrpcOptions(
    maxReceiveMessageSize: 16 * 1024 * 1024,
    maxSendMessageSize: 16 * 1024 * 1024,
    gzipResponses: true,
    idleTimeout: Duration(minutes: 30),
  ),
);
```

Set `idleTimeout` longer than your slowest method, because the time also counts while your method sends no message. A quiet `Watch` stream also stops, so send a message from time to time. Dox always reads gzip requests.

## Health check

`HealthService` is the standard `grpc.health.v1.Health` service, with `Check` and `Watch`. Load balancers and Kubernetes use it. Do not put it behind auth middleware, because a load balancer has no token.

### Set the status of a service

The full server has the empty name `''`, and it starts as `SERVING`. Keep the `HealthService` object to set the status of one service in all isolates:

```dart
HealthService health = HealthService();
Grpc.register(health);

health.setStatus('greeter.Greeter', ServingStatus.SERVING);
health.setStatus('greeter.Greeter', ServingStatus.NOT_SERVING);
```

`statusOf(name)` gives the status, or null. `clearStatus(name)` removes it, and a `Check` for that name then gets `NOT_FOUND`.

## Services and isolates

Each [isolate](isolate.md) gets its own copy of your service. A database connection or a socket can not be copied, so make it on the first call:

```dart
class GreeterService extends GreeterServiceBase {
  HttpClient? _client;

  // made on the first call, in the isolate that runs the call
  HttpClient get client => _client ??= HttpClient();
}
```

## Deployment

Build your app with `dox build`. See [Deployment](deployment.md#build).

gRPC clients on the internet use TLS. There are two ways:

- Dox does the TLS. Set `tls` together with `http2: true` in `AppConfig`. Then `grpcurl` works without `-plaintext`. See [Deployment: HTTPS without a proxy](deployment.md#https-without-a-proxy).
- A proxy does the TLS and sends h2c to Dox. With nginx, use `grpc_pass`. With Caddy, use `h2c://` in `reverse_proxy`. See [Deployment: HTTP/2 and gRPC](deployment.md#http2-and-grpc).

## Benchmark

On one core, `dox_grpc` does the most small calls. Small calls are the most usual type of gRPC call.

With large messages and with streaming, grpc-go is faster on one core. `dox_grpc` is faster than `package:grpc` in all three tests.

Calls a second on one core:

| Test                                   | `dox_grpc` | `package:grpc` | grpc-go |
| -------------------------------------- | ---------: | -------------: | ------: |
| Unary, small message                   | 48,700     | 35,300         | 44,000  |
| Unary, 100 KB reply                    | 14,600     | 11,400         | 17,200  |
| Server streaming, 100 messages of 1 KB | 4,390      | 2,010          | 6,240   |

On four cores, Dox runs four isolates. Then the two servers are almost equal:

| Test                                   | `dox_grpc` | grpc-go |
| -------------------------------------- | ---------: | ------: |
| Unary, small message                   | 56,500     | 56,800  |
| Unary, 100 KB reply                    | 19,300     | 21,000  |
| Server streaming, 100 messages of 1 KB | 7,550      | 7,650   |

For small calls, both servers stop at approximately 57,000 calls a second. This number is near the limit of the client on 4 cores.

### Test setup

- All servers run the same service: the gRPC interop `TestService`.
- The Dart servers are AOT builds. The build command is `dart build cli`.
- `package:grpc` runs on `dart:io` and has one isolate. For this reason, it is only in the one-core table.
- All tests ran in Linux containers on one machine with 8 cores. The server used 4 cores. The client, [ghz](https://ghz.sh), used the other 4 cores.
- The client used 16 connections. For small calls, it kept 128 calls open at the same time. For the other two tests, it kept 32 calls open.
- Each number is the median of 3 runs. Each run took 10 seconds, after a warm up of 3 seconds.

# Scheduler

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/scheduler/

# Scheduler

`dox_scheduler` runs your tasks on a schedule, so you do not need a cron line for each task.

You write the full schedule in Dart, in one file, and each task is a plain function. A task runs one time for each tick, also when many isolates or servers run the schedule.

## Setup

A new app already has the scheduler. In an older app, run this command:

```bash
dox add scheduler
```

It adds the package and writes these files. It never overwrites a file:

- `lib/config/schedule.dart`: your tasks and the `ScheduleConfig`. See [Defining tasks](#defining-tasks).
- `bin/schedule.dart`: the program that runs the schedule. See [Running the scheduler](#running-the-scheduler).
- `lib/providers/schedule_provider.dart`: runs the schedule inside the server. See [Run inside the server](#run-inside-the-server).

## Defining tasks

Add a task with `s.call(name, function)` in `lib/config/schedule.dart`, then add a frequency:

```dart title="lib/config/schedule.dart"
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';

ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig();

void schedule(Schedule s) {
  s.call('cleanup', cleanup).dailyAt('02:00');
  s.call('report', sendReport).hourly();
  s.call('ping', ping).cron('*/5 * * * *').timezone('Asia/Yangon');
}

Future<void> cleanup() async {
  // delete old rows, files, ...
}
```

The name must be unique, because the logs and the locks use it. A task with no frequency runs every minute. `s.find(name)` gives the task with that name, or null.

### Scheduling queued jobs

For a slow task, put a [queue](queue.md) job on the queue. A queue worker then runs it:

```dart
s.call('report', () => SendReport().dispatch()).hourly();
s.call('prune', () => PruneFiles().dispatch(connection: 'redis')).hourly();
```

### Scheduling shell commands

Use `exec` to run a program. An exit code that is not 0 fails the task:

```dart
s.exec('pg_dump', args: <String>['-f', 'backup.sql', 'mydb']).daily();
```

No shell is used, so `|`, `>` and `*` are plain text. To use a shell, run it yourself:

```dart
s.exec('sh', args: <String>['-c', 'pg_dump mydb | gzip > backup.sql.gz'])
    .daily();
```

### Scheduling dox commands

Use `command` to run `dox <command> <args>`:

```dart
s.command('queue:prune', args: <String>['--hours=48']).hourly();
```

The task name is the command line, and the logs show it. If `args` has a secret, give your own name:

```dart
s.command('sync', args: <String>['--token=$token'], name: 'sync');
```

If `dox` is not on the PATH, set `Schedule.doxExecutable = '/usr/local/bin/dox';`.

## Frequency options

Add one of these methods to set how often a task runs:

| Method | Runs |
| --- | --- |
| `everySecond()` | every second. Also `everyTwoSeconds`, `everyFiveSeconds`, `everyTenSeconds`, `everyFifteenSeconds`, `everyTwentySeconds`, `everyThirtySeconds` |
| `everyMinute()` | every minute (the default) |
| `everyTwoMinutes()` | every 2 minutes. Also `everyThreeMinutes`, `everyFourMinutes`, `everyFiveMinutes`, `everyTenMinutes`, `everyFifteenMinutes` |
| `everyThirtyMinutes()` | at minute 0 and 30 |
| `hourly()` | at minute 0 of every hour |
| `hourlyAt(17)` | at minute 17 of every hour |
| `everyTwoHours()` | every 2 hours at minute 0. Also `everyThreeHours`, `everyFourHours`, `everySixHours`. Give a minute: `everyTwoHours(15)` |
| `everyOddHour()` | at 01:00, 03:00 ... 23:00. Give a minute: `everyOddHour(30)` |
| `daily()` | every day at 00:00 |
| `dailyAt('13:00')` | every day at 13:00. `at('13:00')` is the same |
| `twiceDaily(1, 13)` | every day at 01:00 and 13:00 |
| `twiceDailyAt(1, 13, 15)` | every day at 01:15 and 13:15 |
| `weekly()` | every Sunday at 00:00 |
| `weeklyOn(DateTime.monday, '08:00')` | every Monday at 08:00 |
| `monthly()` | the 1st of every month at 00:00 |
| `monthlyOn(15, '12:00')` | the 15th of every month at 12:00 |
| `twiceMonthly(1, 16, '13:00')` | the 1st and 16th of every month at 13:00 |
| `lastDayOfMonth('15:00')` | the last day of every month at 15:00 |
| `quarterly()` | January, April, July and October 1st at 00:00 |
| `quarterlyOn(4, '14:00')` | January, April, July and October 4th at 14:00 |
| `yearly()` | January 1st at 00:00 |
| `yearlyOn(6, 1, '17:00')` | June 1st at 17:00 |
| `cron('*/5 9-17 * * 1-5')` | any 5 field cron expression |

The last method that sets a field wins. So `.dailyAt('09:00').weekly()` runs at 00:00, but `.weekly().dailyAt('09:00')` runs at 09:00.

### Day constraints

Add a day method to run a task only on some days:

| Method | Runs |
| --- | --- |
| `weekdays()` | Monday to Friday |
| `weekends()` | Saturday and Sunday |
| `mondays()` ... `sundays()` | only on that day of the week |
| `days(<int>[DateTime.monday, DateTime.friday])` | only on these days |

```dart
s.call('standup', remind).weekdays().dailyAt('09:00');
```

A day of the month and a day of the week join with OR, like in cron. So `monthlyOn(15).fridays()` runs on the 15th and on every Friday.

### Sub-minute tasks

A seconds method, like `everyFiveSeconds()`, repeats the task in each due minute. Call it first, because it also sets the task to every minute:

```dart
s.call('poll', poll).everyFiveSeconds().between('09:00', '17:00');
```

### Cron expressions

`cron()` takes the 5 standard fields: `minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week`.

| Field | Values |
| --- | --- |
| minute | 0-59 |
| hour | 0-23 |
| day of month | 1-31 |
| month | 1-12 or `JAN`-`DEC` |
| day of week | 0-7 or `SUN`-`SAT` (0 and 7 are Sunday) |

Each field takes `*`, a number `5`, a range `1-5`, a list `1,15`, and a step `*/15` or `0-30/10`.

## Time zones

The schedule uses UTC by default. Use `timezone()` to read the time of a task in another zone:

```dart
s.call('report', sendReport).dailyAt('08:00').timezone('Asia/Yangon');
```

The name is an IANA name, like `Europe/London`. To use one zone for all tasks, set it in the config:

```dart
ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig =
    const ScheduleConfig(timezone: 'Asia/Yangon');
```

On a summer time change, a time that does not exist that day does not run. A time that occurs two times runs one time.

## Limiting when a task runs

### Between times

Use `between` to run a task only in a time of day, and `unlessBetween` to skip a time of day. A range can cross midnight:

```dart
s.call('sync', sync).everyFiveMinutes().between('09:00', '17:00');
s.call('night', night).hourly().between('22:00', '06:00');
s.call('quiet', quiet).hourly().unlessBetween('23:00', '04:00');
```

### Truth tests

`when` runs the task when the function gives true. `skip` skips the task when the function gives true:

```dart
s.call('promo', promo).daily().when(isPromoOn);
s.call('backup', backup).daily().skip(isHoliday);
```

### Environments

Run a task only when `APP_ENV` is one of the names:

```dart
s.call('emails', sendEmails).daily()
    .environments(<String>['production']);
```

When `APP_ENV` is not set, the task does not run.

## Preventing task overlaps

Skip a run while the last run of the task still runs:

```dart
s.call('report', sendReport).everyFiveMinutes().withoutOverlapping();
```

The lock expires after 24 hours. Give another time with `withoutOverlapping(Duration(hours: 1))`. After a crash, remove the lock with [`clear-cache`](#clearing-overlap-locks).

## Running tasks on one server

A task runs one time for each tick on all isolates and servers. This is `onOneServer()`, the default. The locks are in a [cache](cache.md) store, so use a shared store like Redis for many servers:

```dart
ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig(store: 'redis');
```

To run a task on every process, use `onEveryServer()`:

```dart
s.call('clear-tmp', clearTmp).hourly().onEveryServer();
```

## Background tasks

Tasks of the same minute run one after the other. Use `runInBackground` so a long task does not stop the next one:

```dart
s.call('export', export).daily().runInBackground();
```

## Timeouts

Count a run as failed when it takes too long. The failure hooks then run:

```dart
s.exec('pg_dump', args: <String>['mydb']).daily()
    .timeout(Duration(minutes: 5));
```

An `exec()` or `command()` process gets SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after `Schedule.processGrace` (5 seconds). A Dart function cannot be stopped, so its work can continue.

## Running the scheduler

`bin/schedule.dart` runs your schedule. With `app`, it starts your app providers first, like the database:

```dart title="bin/schedule.dart"
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/schedule.dart';
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await SchedulerRunner(
    schedule: schedule,
    app: appConfig,
    config: scheduleConfig,
  ).run(args);
}
```

The `dox` CLI runs the same file: `dox schedule:work` is `dart run bin/schedule.dart work`.

### Running the worker

Start a process that runs the due tasks at each full minute. Run it next to your server:

```bash
dox schedule:work
```

On Ctrl+C or SIGTERM, it waits for the running tasks. A second signal stops it at once.

### Running from cron

`run` runs the tasks of this minute one time, then exits. Add one line to the crontab:

```bash
* * * * * cd /path/to/app/build/bundle && ./bin/schedule run
```

`./bin/schedule` is the binary that `dox build` makes. The exit code is 1 when a task failed.

### Listing tasks

Show each task, its schedule and its next run:

```bash
dox schedule:list
```

```
Task     Schedule                   Next run
cleanup  0 2 * * *                  2026-10-26 02:00 UTC
report   0 * * * *                  2026-10-25 14:00 UTC
ping     */5 * * * * Asia/Yangon    2026-10-25 20:35 Asia/Yangon
```

The next run does not check `when()`, `skip()` and `environments()`.

### Running one task now

Run one task now, with its hooks. The schedule, the filters and the locks are not checked:

```bash
dox schedule:test cleanup
```

### Clearing overlap locks

Remove the `withoutOverlapping()` locks that a crash left in the store:

```bash
dox schedule:clear-cache
```

Run it only when the task does not run on another process. If it does, the task can start a second time.

## Run inside the server

For a small app, run the schedule inside the Dox server. Add a provider that extends `SchedulerProvider`:

```dart title="lib/providers/schedule_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/schedule.dart';

class ScheduleProvider extends SchedulerProvider {
  ScheduleProvider() : super(schedule: schedule, config: scheduleConfig);
}
```

Then turn it on, and run `dart run build_runner build`:

```dart title="lib/config/schedule.dart"
ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig(inProcess: true);
```

Only the first isolate of the web server runs the tasks, so heavy tasks can slow its requests. Use `work` for heavy tasks. In a test of the in-process schedule, set `Dox().isWebServer = true;` first.

## Logging the schedule

Send the `[schedule]` lines through the app `Logger`:

```dart title="lib/config/schedule.dart"
ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig(
  flags: SchedulerFlags(loggerLines: true),
);
```

The lines then get the tag `[scheduler]`, like `[scheduler] ran cleanup in 12ms`. `SchedulerFlags.all()` turns on every flag.

## Task output

These hooks keep the output of an `exec()` or `command()` task. Without them, the output is lost.

Write the output to a file. Each run replaces the file:

```dart
s.exec('pg_dump', args: <String>['mydb']).daily()
    .sendOutputTo('storage/logs/backup.log');
```

Add the output to the end of the file:

```dart
s.exec('pg_dump', args: <String>['mydb']).daily()
    .appendOutputTo('storage/logs/backup.log');
```

Get the output in code after the process ends:

```dart
s.exec('pg_dump', args: <String>['mydb']).daily()
    .onOutput((String output) {...});
```

`onOutput` keeps the full output in memory, so do not use it for very large output.

## Task hooks

Run code around a task, for example to tell your team when it fails:

```dart
s
    .call('report', sendReport)
    .daily()
    .before(logStart)
    .onSuccess(logDone)
    .onFailure(alertTeam)
    .after(cleanUp);

Future<void> alertTeam(Object error, StackTrace stack) async {
  await notifyTeam('report failed: $error');
}
```

| Hook | Runs |
| --- | --- |
| `before` | before the task. If it throws, the task does not run and fails |
| `onSuccess` | after the task worked |
| `onFailure` | after the task threw or timed out. It gets the error and the stack trace |
| `after` | after the task, always |

An error in a task is logged, and the next task still runs.

### Pinging URLs

Send a GET request to a URL around a task, for example to a health check service:

```dart
s
    .call('backup', backup)
    .daily()
    .pingBefore('https://health.example.com/backup/start')
    .pingOnSuccess('https://health.example.com/backup')
    .pingOnFailure('https://health.example.com/backup/fail');
```

`thenPing(url)` pings after the task, always. Each ping method has an `If` form, like `pingOnFailureIf(isProduction, url)`. A failed ping is logged, and the task does not fail. A ping stops after `ScheduledTask.pingTimeout` (10 seconds).

## Testing

Give `Scheduler` a fake clock to test a schedule with no wait:

```dart
import 'package:dox_cache/dox_cache.dart';
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/schedule.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

class FakeClock extends ScheduleClock {
  FakeClock(this.time);

  DateTime time;

  @override
  DateTime now() {
    return time;
  }
}

test('cleanup runs at 02:00', () async {
  Schedule s = Schedule(timezone: scheduleConfig.timezone);
  schedule(s);
  Scheduler scheduler = Scheduler(
    tasks: s.tasks,
    store: CacheStore(MemoryDriver()),
    clock: FakeClock(DateTime.utc(2026, 10, 25, 2)),
  );
  Map<String, TaskOutcome> outcomes = await scheduler.runDue();
  expect(outcomes['cleanup'], TaskOutcome.ran);
});
```

To run one task, use `scheduler.runTask(task, time)`. To check a schedule with no run, use `task.isDue(time)` and `task.nextRun(time)`. To replace the ping request, set `ScheduledTask.sendPing = (Uri url) async {...};`.

## Without Dox

`dox_scheduler` also works in a plain Dart app. Leave out `app`:

```dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';

void schedule(Schedule s) {
  s.call('cleanup', cleanup).dailyAt('02:00');
}

Future<void> cleanup() async {
  // delete old files, ...
}

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await SchedulerRunner(schedule: schedule).run(args);
}
```

With no `app`, the locks use a memory store. For many servers, give a shared `CacheStore` from `dox_cache`: `SchedulerRunner(schedule: schedule, store: myRedisStore)`.

## Next steps

- [Queue](queue.md): jobs that must not get lost.
- [Background work](../guides/background-work.md): pick the right tool for work after the response.
- [CLI](../reference/cli.md): the `schedule:*` commands.

# File Storage

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/file-storage/

# File Storage

`Storage()` saves and reads files on a disk: a local folder, AWS S3 (and R2, MinIO, Spaces), Azure Blob Storage, or memory.

All disks have the same methods. So you can use a local folder in development and S3 or Azure in production, with the same code. Storage is in the `dox_storage` package. You can also use it [without Dox](#without-dox).

```dart
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';

Route.post('/avatar', (DoxRequest req) async {
  RequestFile file = req.input('avatar');
  String path = await Storage().putFile('avatars', file);
  return <String, String>{'path': path}; // /avatars/<uuid>.png
});
```

## Setup

A new project already has storage. In an older project, run this command:

```bash
dox add storage
```

It writes `lib/config/storage.dart`, the provider, the `storage` folder and the `STORAGE_DISK=local` key. It never overwrites a file.

Add `--disk=s3` to also add an `s3` disk and the `AWS_*` keys. `STORAGE_DISK` stays `local`, so fill in the keys first, then set `STORAGE_DISK=s3`.

Add `--disk=azure` to also add an `azure` disk and the `AZURE_STORAGE_*` keys. See [Azure Blob Storage](#azure-blob-storage).

### Configuration

The disks are in `lib/config/storage.dart`. `STORAGE_DISK` in `.env` picks the default disk. This example adds a `url` to the local disk, an `s3` disk and a `memory` disk:

```dart title="lib/config/storage.dart"
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

StorageConfig storageConfig = StorageConfig(
  defaultDisk: env.storageDisk,
  disks: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
    'local': <String, dynamic>{
      'driver': 'local',
      'root': 'storage',
      // for signedUrl(). Without it, url() gives /storage/<path>
      'url': 'https://app.test/files',
    },

    /// only when AWS_BUCKET is set
    if (env.awsBucket != null)
      's3': <String, dynamic>{
        'driver': 's3',
        'bucket': env.awsBucket,
        'region': env.awsDefaultRegion,
        'key': env.awsAccessKeyId,
        'secret': env.awsSecretAccessKey,
        'endpoint': env.awsEndpoint, // R2, MinIO, Spaces
      },
    'memory': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'memory'},
  },
);
```

| Driver | Use for | Options |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `local` | a folder on the server | `root` (default `storage`), `url`, `app_key` (default: your APP_KEY), `visibility`, `atomic_writes`, `permissions` |
| `s3` | AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, MinIO, DigitalOcean Spaces, GCS | `bucket`, `region`, `key`, `secret`, `token`, `endpoint`, `path_style` (MinIO), `url` (CDN), `visibility`, `acl`, `batch_delete`, `unsigned_payload` |
| `azure` | Azure Blob Storage, Azurite | `account`, `key`, `container`, `endpoint` (Azurite), `url` (CDN) |
| `memory` | tests | none |

Signed upload URLs work only on S3 and Azure.

The provider in `lib/providers/` sets up these disks in every isolate:

```dart title="lib/providers/storage_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/storage.dart';

class AppStorageProvider extends StorageProvider {
  AppStorageProvider() : super(storageConfig);
}
```

## Drivers

### Local disk

The local disk saves files in the `root` folder on the server.

#### Atomic writes

A local disk writes a file in place. With `atomic_writes`, it writes a temp file and renames it, so a failed upload never leaves a partial file:

```dart
'local': <String, dynamic>{
  'driver': 'local',
  'root': 'storage',
  'atomic_writes': true,
},
```

The rename makes a new file, so the file gets the default mode and owner.

#### Visibility on a local disk

Add `'permissions': true` to use file modes. Then `setVisibility` runs `chmod`, and `getVisibility` reads the mode:

```dart
'local': <String, dynamic>{
  'driver': 'local',
  'root': 'storage',
  'permissions': true,
},
```

The modes are: public file `0644`, private file `0600`, public folder `0755`, private folder `0700`. On Windows, `permissions` does nothing.

#### Custom file modes

Give `permissions` a map with a `file` and a `dir` key. Dart has no octal numbers, so write the modes in hex: `0x1a0` is `0640`:

```dart
'private': <String, dynamic>{
  'driver': 'local',
  'root': 'storage-private',
  'visibility': 'private',
  'permissions': <String, dynamic>{
    'file': <String, int>{'public': 0x1a4, 'private': 0x1a0},
    'dir': <String, int>{'public': 0x1ed, 'private': 0x1e8},
  },
},
```

A mode you leave out keeps its default. A mode that is not an int from 0 to 0x1ff throws an ArgumentError.

### S3

Add the S3 keys to `lib/config/env.dart`, then run `dart run build_runner build`. The `s3` disk is added only when `AWS_BUCKET` is set:

```dart title="lib/config/env.dart"
  String? get awsBucket;

  String get awsDefaultRegion => 'us-east-1';

  String? get awsAccessKeyId;

  String? get awsSecretAccessKey;

  /// R2, MinIO or Spaces. Null for AWS.
  String? get awsEndpoint;
```

Without `bucket`, `key` or `secret`, the app stops at start with an ArgumentError. To save CPU on big uploads, set `'unsigned_payload': true`. The signature then does not cover the body, so use it only over HTTPS.

These examples use `S3DriverConfig`, the class behind an `s3` disk. In a Dox config, the same settings are the disk keys `endpoint`, `path_style`, `acl` and `batch_delete`. See [Configuration](#configuration).

#### Cloudflare R2

R2 does not take ACL headers, so set `supportsAcl: false`:

```dart
S3DriverConfig(
  bucket: 'my-bucket',
  region: 'auto',
  endpoint: 'https://<account-id>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com',
  accessKeyId: '...',
  secretAccessKey: '...',
  supportsAcl: false,
);
```

#### MinIO

MinIO needs path style URLs:

```dart
S3DriverConfig(
  bucket: 'my-bucket',
  region: 'us-east-1',
  endpoint: 'http://localhost:9000',
  forcePathStyle: true,
  accessKeyId: 'minioadmin',
  secretAccessKey: 'minioadmin',
);
```

#### DigitalOcean Spaces

Put the region of your space in `region` and in the endpoint:

```dart
S3DriverConfig(
  bucket: 'my-space',
  region: 'nyc3',
  endpoint: 'https://nyc3.digitaloceanspaces.com',
  accessKeyId: '...',
  secretAccessKey: '...',
);
```

#### Google Cloud Storage

GCS does not take ACL headers or the S3 batch delete call:

```dart
S3DriverConfig(
  bucket: 'my-bucket',
  region: 'auto',
  endpoint: 'https://storage.googleapis.com',
  accessKeyId: 'GOOG...',
  secretAccessKey: '...',
  supportsAcl: false,
  supportsBatchDelete: false,
);
```

### Azure Blob Storage

Use the `azure` disk when your files are in an Azure storage account. The driver stores each file as a block blob in one container.

Run `dox add storage --disk=azure` to add the `azure` disk, the `AppEnv` getters and the `AZURE_STORAGE_*` keys. `STORAGE_DISK` stays `local`, so fill in the keys first, then set `STORAGE_DISK=azure`.

To add the disk by hand, add the Azure keys to `lib/config/env.dart`, then run `dart run build_runner build`:

```dart title="lib/config/env.dart"
  String? get azureStorageAccount;

  String? get azureStorageKey;

  String? get azureStorageContainer;

  /// Azurite or a custom domain. Null for Azure.
  String? get azureStorageEndpoint;

  String? get azureStorageUrl;
```

Then add the disk to `lib/config/storage.dart`. The `azure` disk is added only when `AZURE_STORAGE_CONTAINER` is set:

```dart title="lib/config/storage.dart"
    /// only when AZURE_STORAGE_CONTAINER is set
    if (env.azureStorageContainer != null)
      'azure': <String, dynamic>{
        'driver': 'azure',
        'account': env.azureStorageAccount,
        'key': env.azureStorageKey,
        'container': env.azureStorageContainer,
        'endpoint': env.azureStorageEndpoint, // Azurite, custom domain
        'url': env.azureStorageUrl,
      },
```

| `.env` key | Disk option | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AZURE_STORAGE_ACCOUNT` | `account` | The name of the storage account. Required. |
| `AZURE_STORAGE_KEY` | `key` | The base64 account key from the Azure portal. Required. |
| `AZURE_STORAGE_CONTAINER` | `container` | The blob container. Required. |
| `AZURE_STORAGE_ENDPOINT` | `endpoint` | The URL of the blob service, without the container. The default is `https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net`. |
| `AZURE_STORAGE_URL` | `url` | The base of the URLs that `url` returns, for example a CDN. The default is the container URL. |

The driver does not create the container. Create the container before you use the disk. Without `account`, `key` or `container`, the app stops with an ArgumentError.

#### Azurite

Azurite is the Azure Storage emulator. Use it for local development, so you do not need an Azure account. Start it with Docker:

```bash
docker run -d --rm --name dox-storage-azurite -p 10000:10000 \
  mcr.microsoft.com/azure-storage/azurite:3.38.0 \
  azurite-blob --blobHost 0.0.0.0 --skipApiVersionCheck --loose
```

Then point the `azure` disk to Azurite. `devstoreaccount1` is the default account of Azurite. Its key is in the Azurite documentation:

```ini title=".env"
STORAGE_DISK=azure
AZURE_STORAGE_ACCOUNT=devstoreaccount1
AZURE_STORAGE_KEY=<the Azurite account key>
AZURE_STORAGE_CONTAINER=files
AZURE_STORAGE_ENDPOINT=http://127.0.0.1:10000/devstoreaccount1
```

Azurite starts with no containers. Create the `files` container before you use the disk, for example with Azure Storage Explorer or the Azure CLI.

### Memory disk

Use the memory disk in tests. It gives fake URLs. See [Testing](#testing).

## Using another disk

`Storage()` uses the default disk. Use `disk` to pick another one:

```dart
await Storage().disk('s3').put('reports/2026.pdf', bytes, exact: true);
```

## Storing files

`putFile` saves a file in a folder with a new uuid name, and returns the path. It takes a `RequestFile` or bytes. For bytes, give `extension:`, or Dox finds it from the bytes:

```dart
// returns '/images/<uuid>.png'
String path = await Storage().putFile('images', file); // a RequestFile
Uint8List bytes = Uint8List.fromList(<int>[1, 2, 3]);
String path2 =
    await Storage().putFile('images', bytes, extension: 'png');
String path3 =
    await Storage().put('images', bytes, extension: 'png'); // like putFile
```

When the bytes are a known format, like png, the extension of the bytes wins over the file name. So a png sent as `a.html` is saved as `.png`.

### Storing with your own name

`putFileAs` uses your file name. It replaces an old file with that name:

```dart
String path4 = await Storage().putFileAs('avatars', file, 'user-1.png');
```

Do not use the file name from the client, because the name is used as it is.

### Storing at an exact path

`put` with `exact: true` writes to an exact path. It takes a string, a `List<int>` or a `Stream<List<int>>`:

```dart
await Storage().put('notes/a.txt', 'hello', exact: true);
```

### Storing uploaded files

An uploaded file can store itself. `store` works like `putFile`, and `storeAs` works like `putFileAs`:

```dart
RequestFile file = req.input('image');
String path = await file.store('images');
String onS3 = await file.store('images', disk: 's3');
String avatar = await file.storeAs('avatars', 'user-1.png');
```

`putRequestFile` and `putRequestFileAs` on `Storage()` do the same:

```dart
String path = await Storage().putRequestFile('images', file);
String avatar =
    await Storage().putRequestFileAs('avatars', 'user-1.png', file);
```

On a local disk, the upload temp file is moved, not read into memory.

### Prepending and appending

Add text to the end or the start of a file. A missing file is made:

```dart
await Storage().append('logs/app.log', 'new line');
await Storage().prepend('logs/app.log', 'first line');
```

A new line goes between the old and the new text. Change it with `separator`. Two writers at the same time can lose a write.

## Retrieving files

`get` gives the bytes of a file, or null when the file is missing:

```dart
Uint8List? found = await Storage().get(path);
```

### Checking if a file exists

`exists` checks for a file. `missing` is the opposite:

```dart
bool exists = await Storage().exists(path);
bool gone = await Storage().missing(path);
```

### File metadata

`size` gives the size in bytes, and `lastModified` gives the time of the last change. Both throw `FileNotFoundException` when the file is missing:

```dart
int size = await Storage().size(path);
DateTime changed = await Storage().lastModified(path);
```

## Downloading files

`stream` shows a file in the browser, and `download` makes the browser save it. Both stream the file, and a missing file answers 404:

```dart
Route.get('/photo', (DoxRequest req) {
  return Storage().stream(req.input('path'));
});

Route.get('/report', (DoxRequest req) {
  return Storage().disk('s3').download('reports/2024.pdf');
});
```

`download` uses the last part of the path as the file name. Give `name:` to use another name:

```dart
Route.get('/invoice', (DoxRequest req) {
  return Storage().download('invoices/42.pdf', name: 'Invoice 42.pdf');
});
```

To add headers, put the download in a `response()`:

```dart
Route.get('/invoice', (DoxRequest req) async {
  DownloadableFile file = await Storage().download('invoices/42.pdf');
  return response(file).header('Cache-Control', 'no-store');
});
```

## File URLs

`url` gives the URL of a file. On a local disk with no `url` option, it gives `/storage/<path>`:

```dart
String url = await Storage().url(path);
```

Dox serves that URL only with `Storage.route('storage', signed: false)`. See [Serving local files](#serving-local-files).

### Signed URLs

A signed URL opens a file for a short time, like a private invoice. `temporaryUrl` is the same as `signedUrl`:

```dart
String signed =
    await Storage().signedUrl(path, expiresIn: Duration(minutes: 10));
String same = await Storage().temporaryUrl(path);
```

On a local disk, `signedUrl` needs the disk `url` option: the full URL of the route, like `https://app.test/files`.

### Serving local files

`Storage.route` adds a route that serves the files of a disk:

```dart title="lib/routes/web.dart"
Storage.route('files');                  // GET /files/{key*}, signed only
Storage.route('public', signed: false);  // any file of the disk
Storage.route('docs', disk: 'memory', signed: false); // another disk
Storage.route('uploads', download: true); // every file is a download
```

A signed URL of the `files` route looks like this:

```dart
String url = await Storage().signedUrl('invoices/1.pdf');
// https://app.test/files/invoices/1.pdf?expires=...&signature=...
```

A missing, wrong or expired signature answers 403. Signed routes work only on a `local` disk. An html, svg, xml or javascript file is always sent as a download in a sandbox, so its script cannot run on your site.

## Copying and moving files

`copy` and `move` replace an old file at the new path:

```dart
await Storage().copy('notes/a.txt', 'backup/a.txt');
await Storage().move('backup/a.txt', 'old/a.txt');
```

On S3, the copy runs inside S3. A missing source file answers 404.

On Azure, the copy runs inside the storage account. The copy keeps the content type of the source, unless you set `contentType` in `WriteOptions`. Azure can leave a copy pending. Then the driver waits up to 5 minutes, stops the copy and throws `DriverException`.

## Deleting files

Delete a file with `delete`. A missing file is not an error:

```dart
await Storage().delete(path);
```

On Azure, `delete` also deletes the snapshots of the blob.

## Directories

`files` gives the files in a folder, `allFiles` also gives the files in sub-folders, and `directories` gives the sub-folders. Each path starts with `/`:

```dart
List<String> files = await Storage().files('images');
List<String> all = await Storage().allFiles('images');
List<String> folders = await Storage().directories('images');
```

`directoryExists` checks for a folder. On S3 and memory disks, a folder exists when a file is in it:

```dart
bool folder = await Storage().directoryExists('images');
```

On Azure, a folder exists when a blob name starts with the folder name and `/`. A folder marker blob, like `images/`, also counts.

`makeDirectory` makes a folder. It works only on a local disk:

```dart
await Storage().makeDirectory('reports');
```

`deleteDirectory` deletes a folder and all files in it:

```dart
await Storage().deleteDirectory('old');
```

The root (`''` or `/`) throws `InvalidKeyException`. To empty a full disk, use `Storage().use().deleteAll()`.

## File visibility

A file is public or private. Use `setVisibility` and `getVisibility`:

```dart
await Storage().setVisibility(path, Visibility.private);
Visibility visibility = await Storage().getVisibility(path);
```

On S3, `setVisibility` sets the ACL. With `'acl': false` (R2 and similar), it does nothing, and `getVisibility` gives the disk `visibility`. On a local disk it is the same, unless you turn on `permissions`. See [Visibility on a local disk](#visibility-on-a-local-disk).

Azure sets public access for each container, not for each file. So on Azure, `getVisibility` gives the level of the container, the same for all files. `setVisibility` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. The driver ignores the `visibility` of `WriteOptions`. Set the access level on the container in Azure.

## The disk API

`Storage()` has short methods for common work. For more control, get a `Disk` with `use`. With no name, you get the default disk:

```dart
Disk disk = Storage().use('s3');
```

A `Disk` also has `get`, `exists`, `missing`, `delete`, `copy`, `move`, `size`, `lastModified`, `append`, `prepend`, `files`, `allFiles`, `directories`, `directoryExists`, `makeDirectory`, `deleteDirectory`, `getVisibility` and `setVisibility`. Its `get` throws `FileNotFoundException` when the file is missing.

### Write options

`put` on a `Disk` writes to the exact key. `WriteOptions` sets the content type and the visibility. `copy` and `move` also take `options:`:

```dart
await disk.put('a.json', '{}',
    options: WriteOptions(
        contentType: 'application/json', visibility: Visibility.public));
```

### Storing big files

`putStream` writes a stream, so the file is not loaded into memory:

```dart
await disk.putStream('videos/big.mp4', File('big.mp4').openRead());
```

On S3, `put` has a limit of 5 GiB. `putStream` uses a multipart upload with parts of `multipartPartSize` (8 MiB, a field of `S3DriverConfig`), up to about 78 GiB.

On Azure, a stream smaller than `blockSize` goes up as one Put Blob request. A stream of `blockSize` bytes or more goes up as blocks, then one Put Block List request. `blockSize` is a field of `AzureBlobDriverConfig`, 8 MiB by default. Only one block is in memory at a time. If an upload fails, Azure removes the blocks after 7 days.

### Reading text and streams

`getString` reads a file as text. For a big file, use `getStream`. Both throw `FileNotFoundException` when the file is missing:

```dart
String text = await disk.getString('notes/a.txt');

Stream<List<int>> stream = await disk.getStream('videos/big.mp4');
```

`getStreamWithMetaData` gives the stream and the metadata together. On S3 it is one request. On Azure it is two requests:

```dart
ObjectStream file = await disk.getStreamWithMetaData('videos/big.mp4');
// file.stream, file.metaData
```

### All metadata in one call

`getMetaData` gives the size, content type, last change time and etag:

```dart
ObjectMetaData meta = await disk.getMetaData('avatars/1.png');
```

### Public URLs

`getUrl` gives the public URL of a file:

```dart
String url = await disk.getUrl('avatars/1.png');
```

### Deleting many files

`deleteAll` removes all files under a prefix. With `''` or no argument, it empties the disk:

```dart
await disk.deleteAll('avatars');
```

### Listing page by page

For a big folder, read one page at a time with `listAll`:

```dart
ListResult page = await disk.listAll('avatars',
    ListOptions(recursive: true, limit: 100));
// next page: ListOptions(paginationToken: page.paginationToken)
```

### Signed URL options

`getSignedUrl` takes `SignedUrlOptions`. `expiresIn` is 30 minutes by default, and on S3 the maximum is 7 days. Azure has no such limit, but the expiry must be in the future. `contentDisposition` sets the header of the download:

```dart
String signed = await disk.getSignedUrl('avatars/1.png',
    options: SignedUrlOptions(expiresIn: Duration(minutes: 10)));
```

### Signed upload URLs

On S3 and Azure, the browser can upload a file directly to the bucket or container with a signed upload URL:

```dart
String upload = await disk.getSignedUploadUrl('avatars/2.png',
    options: SignedUrlOptions(contentType: 'image/png'));
```

On Azure, the client must send the header `x-ms-blob-type: BlockBlob` with the PUT. Azure does not enforce the `contentType` of `SignedUrlOptions`. A successful upload answers 201:

```bash
curl -X PUT -H 'x-ms-blob-type: BlockBlob' \
  --data-binary @2.png "$UPLOAD_URL"
```

## Custom drivers

Implement `DriverContract`, and register it in a [provider](providers.md) so every isolate has it:

```dart
Storage.manager.register('dropbox', DropboxDriver());
await Storage().disk('dropbox').put('notes/a.txt', 'hello', exact: true);
```

## Errors

All errors extend `StorageException` and have the `key`:

| Error | When |
| --- | --- |
| `FileNotFoundException` | the file does not exist |
| `PermissionDeniedException` | a file system permission error, or a 403 from S3 or Azure |
| `InvalidKeyException` | an unsafe key |
| `UnsupportedOperationException` | the driver cannot do this, like `setVisibility` on Azure |
| `DriverException` | any other error. The first error is in `cause`. On Azure, a missing container and a copy that stays pending also give it |

A key with `..`, an absolute path like `/etc/passwd`, or a null byte throws `InvalidKeyException`. So a user cannot get files outside the disk.

## Testing

To replace a disk with a memory disk in tests, see [Testing](testing.md#test-file-storage). A disk also has `assertExists` and `assertMissing`. They throw a StateError when the check fails:

```dart
Disk fake = Storage.manager.fake('s3');
await fake.assertExists('avatars/1.png');
await fake.assertMissing('avatars/old.png');
```

`Storage.manager.restore('s3')` removes one fake, and `Storage.manager.restoreAll()` removes all fakes.

## Without Dox

`dox_storage` also works on its own:

```bash
dart pub add dox_storage
```

Make a `DriveManager` with your disks:

```dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';

Map<String, String> env = Platform.environment;

DriveManager drive = DriveManager(
  defaultDisk: 'local',
  disks: <String, DriverContract>{
    'local': LocalDriver(LocalDriverConfig(
      root: 'storage',
      urlBase: 'https://app.test/uploads',
      atomicWrites: true, // off by default
      appKey: env['APP_KEY'], // signs local URLs
    )),
    's3': S3Driver(S3DriverConfig(
      bucket: 'my-bucket',
      region: 'us-east-1',
      accessKeyId: env['AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID']!,
      secretAccessKey: env['AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY']!,
    )),
    'azure': AzureBlobDriver(AzureBlobDriverConfig(
      accountName: env['AZURE_STORAGE_ACCOUNT']!,
      accountKey: env['AZURE_STORAGE_KEY']!,
      container: 'files',
    )),
  },
);

Disk disk = drive.use('s3'); // or drive.use() for the default disk
```

To add your own driver, call `drive.register('dropbox', DropboxDriver())`. For file modes, give `LocalDriverConfig(permissions: LocalPermissions())`.

`AzureBlobDriverConfig` also has `endpoint`, `urlBase`, `blockSize` (8 MiB by default) and `copyTimeout` (5 minutes by default). `blockSize` must be from 1 byte to 4000 MiB, or the driver throws an ArgumentError. In a Dox config, only `endpoint` and `url` are disk options.

### Checking a local signed URL

Check a local signed URL in the route that serves the file:

```dart
LocalDriver local = LocalDriver(localConfig);
bool ok = local.verifySignedUrl(keyFromPath, req.uri.queryParameters);
if (!ok) {
  return response('Forbidden').statusCode(403);
}
```

- [Static files and SPA](../guides/static-files.md): serve a folder.

# Environment Variables

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/env/

# Environment Variables

Declare your env keys one time, in a typed class, and read them as normal Dart values.

Each machine needs different settings, like the database password. Keep these values in environment variables or in a `.env` file, not in your code. Dox reads them through a typed class, so a missing key stops the app at startup.

## Defining env keys

A new project already has `lib/config/env.dart`. Its keys are in the [Env reference](../reference/env.md#read-by-a-new-project). Each getter is one env key:

```dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'env.g.dart';

enum LogLevel { debug, info, error }

@DoxEnv()
abstract class AppEnv {
  static AppEnv load([EnvReader? reader]) {
    return _$AppEnv.load(reader);
  }

  String get appName;                       // APP_NAME, required
  String get appKey;                        // APP_KEY, required
  int get dbPort => 5432;                   // DB_PORT, default 5432
  bool get appDebug => false;               // APP_DEBUG, default false
  LogLevel get logLevel => LogLevel.info;   // LOG_LEVEL=debug
  Duration get cacheTtl =>
      const Duration(minutes: 5);           // CACHE_TTL=5m
  List<String> get corsOrigins =>
      <String>[];                           // CORS_ORIGINS=a.com,b.com

  @EnvKey('AWS_BUCKET')
  String? get s3Bucket;                     // optional, null when not set
}

/// The env of the app. Read and checked one time, on first use.
final AppEnv env = AppEnv.load();
```

Run `dart run build_runner build` after each change to the class. It writes `env.g.dart`. The builder reads only the getters of the class itself, not getters of a superclass or a mixin.

### Key names

The key is the getter name in UPPER_SNAKE case. So `appName` reads `APP_NAME`, and `dbURL` reads `DB_URL`. To use another name, add `@EnvKey('X')`.

### Default values

The getter body is the default. It runs only when the key is missing. A default can use another getter. Write the getter directly, not `env.appPort`, or the app stops with a StateError:

```dart
String get appUrl => 'http://localhost:$appPort';
```

### Required and optional keys

- A getter with no body is required. A missing key stops the app.
- A nullable getter with no body, like `String? get s3Bucket;`, is optional. It is null when the key is missing.
- An empty value, or the text null, counts as missing.

### Types

| Type | Value in `.env` |
|------|-----------------|
| `String` | any text |
| `int`, `double`, `num` | `3000`, `0.5` |
| `bool` | `true`/`false`, `1`/`0`, `yes`/`no`, `on`/`off` (any case) |
| `Uri` | `https://dox.dev` |
| `Duration` | a number and a unit: `500ms`, `30s`, `5m`, `2h`, `1d`. A plain number is seconds. |
| an enum | the name of a value, any case: `debug` |
| `List<String>` | comma separated: `a, b, c`. Empty items are removed. |

Any other type is a build error.

### Missing or bad keys

At startup, `AppEnv.load()` checks every key. It throws one `EnvException` with all missing or bad keys:

```
EnvException: the env is not valid
  - APP_KEY is missing
  - DB_PORT must be an int
```

The error shows the key name, never the value.

## Reading env values

Import the config file and use `env`:

```dart
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: 'postgres',
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'postgres': ConnectionConfig(port: env.dbPort /* int */, ...),
  },
);
```

Keep only plain keys in the env class. For a computed value, use the app config, like `appConfig.isDevelopment`.

## Where values come from

Dox reads values from these places. The first one that has the key wins:

1. Real environment variables (from the shell, Docker or systemd).
2. In tests only: the `.env.testing` file. See [Testing: a test database](testing.md#use-a-test-database-with-envtesting).
3. The `.env` file in the folder where you start the app. It is optional.

### The `.env` file

The `.env` file has one `KEY=value` on each line:

```ini title=".env"
APP_NAME=dox
APP_KEY=<output of dox key:generate>
DB_PORT=5432
```

- Quotes around a value are removed: `APP_NAME="My app"` gives `My app`.
- A line that starts with `#` is a comment. A `#` after a space also starts a comment: `APP_PORT=3000 # dev` gives `3000`.
- `COLOR=#fff` gives `#fff`, because no space comes before the `#`.
- `KEY=` gives the default value.
- `export KEY=value` also works.
- A value is on one line only. For a PEM key, put the file path in the env, or use `\n` with `envExpand`.

## Use one value in another

Turn on `CoreFlags.envExpand` to build a value from other values:

```ini title=".env"
HOST=localhost
PORT=3000
APP_URL=http://${HOST}:${PORT}
GREETING="Hello\nWorld"
```

`${OTHER}` works in an unquoted value and in a `"..."` value. A name that Dox cannot find stays as `${OTHER}`. In a `"..."` value, `\n`, `\t`, `\"`, `\\` and `\$` are escapes.

### Turning on envExpand

The `.env` file is read before `AppConfig` exists. So set the flags in `AppConfig` and in `Env.flags`, at the top of `main()`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

const CoreFlags flags = CoreFlags(envExpand: true);

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  appKey: Env.get('APP_KEY', ''),
  flags: flags,
  // ...
);
```

```dart title="bin/server.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';

void main() async {
  Env.flags = flags;
  Dox().initialize(appConfig);
  await Dox().startServer();
}
```

A test does not run `bin/server.dart`. So also set `Env.flags = flags;` at the top of `main()` in each test file:

```dart title="test/http_test.dart"
void main() {
  Env.flags = flags;
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
  });
  // ...
}
```

If you forget it, `${OTHER}` stays as it is, and Dox prints a warning.

## Generating the env class

Make `lib/config/env.dart` from your `.env.example`:

```bash
dox env:generate
```

Digits become an `int` default, and true or false become a `bool` default. An empty value becomes an optional `String?`. Any other value becomes a required `String`, so a secret in the example never goes into the code. The command does not overwrite an existing file.

## Checking the env

Print every missing or bad key. The command exits with code 1 when a key is wrong, so you can use it in CI:

```bash
dox env:check
```

## The app key

Dox uses `APP_KEY` to encrypt and sign data. Make one with `dox key:generate`. A missing, short or sample key stops `Dox().startServer()`. In development and test environments, it only logs a warning.

## Reading a key by name

Use `Env.get()` when you know the key name only at run time:

```dart
Env.get<String>('APP_KEY');               // '' when missing
Env.get('APP_KEY', 'default_value');
Env.get<int>('APP_PORT', 3000);
Env.get<bool>('SOCKETIO_ENABLED', false); // true, 1, yes, on
Env.get<String?>('AWS_BUCKET');           // null when not set
```

A missing or empty key gives the default. With no default, `int`, `num`, `double` and `bool` throw an ArgumentError. `Env.get()` reads the value again on each call, so do not use it on a hot path.

### The environment name

`Env.appEnv` gives `APP_ENV` in lower case. `Env.isTesting` is true under `dart test`, or when `APP_ENV=testing` is a real environment variable:

```dart
if (Env.appEnv == 'staging') {
  // ...
}
```

An empty `Env.appEnv` means production.

## Testing

To give your own values in a test, see [Testing](testing.md#test-the-env).

## Next steps

- [Environment variables](../reference/env.md): every env var that Dox reads.
- [Environments](../guides/environments.md): dev, staging and production config.

# Isolate

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/isolate/

# Isolate

Dox runs your app on many isolates (threads) at once, so it can use every CPU core.

Each isolate runs its own [native server](native-server.md) on the same port, and the operating system spreads the connections between them:

<div class="dox-fan" role="group" aria-label="One port, one native server and one isolate per CPU">
  <div class="dox-fan__top"><strong>Port 3000</strong><span>the OS spreads the connections</span></div>
  <div class="dox-fan__cols">
    <ol>
      <li><strong>Rust acceptor</strong></li>
      <li><strong>Isolate 1, main</strong><span>own memory cache</span></li>
      <li data-via="crash: the process exits"><strong>Supervisor</strong><span>restarts the process: Docker, systemd</span></li>
    </ol>
    <ol>
      <li><strong>Rust acceptor</strong></li>
      <li><strong>Isolate 2</strong><span>own memory cache</span><em>crash: started again after 1 second</em></li>
    </ol>
    <ol>
      <li><strong>Rust acceptor</strong></li>
      <li><strong>Isolate N</strong><span>own memory cache</span><em>crash: started again after 1 second</em></li>
    </ol>
  </div>
</div>

## Setup

Dox starts one isolate per CPU the process may use. In a container, it uses the CPU limit, and a quota rounds up: 1.5 CPUs gives 2 isolates. On Windows only one isolate serves HTTP.

To change the number, set `totalIsolate` in the app config. A new app reads it from `APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  totalIsolate: env.appTotalIsolate,
);
```

## Setting the number in code

Call `Dox().totalIsolate()` before `startServer()`. It wins over the config:

```dart title="bin/server.dart"
Dox().initialize(appConfig);
Dox().totalIsolate(2);
await Dox().startServer();
```

## Each isolate has its own memory

A static value, a singleton and the `memory` cache store exist one time per isolate. To share data between isolates or servers, use a database, Redis or files.

To give each isolate its own heap and garbage collector too, see [Give each isolate its own memory](deployment.md#give-each-isolate-its-own-memory).

## Finding the current isolate

`Dox().isolateId` is the id of the isolate that runs your code. The first isolate is 1. `Dox().isolateCount` is the number of running isolates:

```dart
int id = Dox().isolateId;
int count = Dox().isolateCount;
```

`Dox().isPrimary` is true in the first isolate only:

```dart
if (Dox().isPrimary) {
  // runs one time, not in each isolate
}
```

## Sending a message to the other isolates

`IsolateBus` sends a message from one isolate to all the other isolates in the same process. Listen in the `setup()` of a provider, and publish from anywhere:

```dart
IsolateBus.instance.on('users').listen(onMessage);
IsolateBus.instance.publish('users', <Object>['changed', 42]);
```

An isolate never gets its own message, and a listener gets only the messages sent after it started to listen. A message must be a value a `SendPort` can send, or `publish` throws an `ArgumentError`.

`IsolateBus.instance.size` is the number of isolates that listen, this one included. For many servers, use Redis. [Socket.IO](../packages/socketio.md#many-isolates) uses the bus to share broadcasts.

## What each isolate does at start

Dox copies the `AppConfig`, the providers and the routes to each new isolate. Then every isolate:

1. runs `setup()` of each provider,
2. registers the routes of your routers,
3. reads the parameter types of each controller one time,
4. runs `boot()` of each provider,
5. starts its HTTP server.

So the config and the providers must not hold open sockets or database pools. Open them in `setup()`. See [Providers](providers.md).

## Heavy CPU work

Heavy CPU work in a request blocks every other request on the same isolate. Run it on a worker isolate with `Dox().compute`:

```dart
Future<List<int>> renderPdf(Map<String, dynamic> data) {
  return Dox().compute(() => buildPdf(data));
}
```

The task can use only values that can go between isolates: numbers, strings, lists, maps and plain objects. It can not use the container, a database connection or a cache store, so read the data first and pass it in. Make the task in a small top-level or static function.

The tasks run on a pool of 4 workers, and more tasks wait in line. Set `computeWorkers` to change the number:

```dart
AppConfig(
  // ...
  computeWorkers: 8,
);
```

An error of the task is thrown at the `await`. `compute` also works with no server, like in a command, a test or a queue job.

## When an isolate crashes

An error in a request gives a 500, and an async error outside a request goes to the [exception handler](../the-basic/errors.md). If a worker isolate dies, Dox starts a new one after 1 second.

If the first isolate dies, the process exits with a non-zero code. Let a supervisor start it again, like Docker `restart:` or systemd `Restart=always`. See [Deployment](deployment.md#keep-it-running).

## Next steps

- [Providers](providers.md): code that runs in each isolate at start.
- [Native server](native-server.md): the HTTP server in each isolate.
- [Deployment](deployment.md): run the app on a server.

# Providers

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/providers/

# Providers

A provider is a class that sets up one part of your app in every isolate when it starts, like the database, auth or a Redis connection.

Dox runs your app on many [isolates](isolate.md), and they do not share memory. So code in `bin/server.dart` sets up only the first isolate. Each isolate runs every provider itself.

## Setup

Make a provider with the CLI. It writes `lib/providers/cache_provider.dart`:

```bash
dox make:provider Cache
```

Dox finds every class that extends `DoxProvider` after `dart run build_runner build`. You do not register it. Its constructor can ask for other classes of the container. See [Dependency injection](../the-basic/dependency-injection.md#routers-and-providers).

## Setting up a part of the app

Put the code in `setup()`. It runs in each isolate before the routes are registered, and Dox waits for it:

```dart title="lib/providers/orm_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';

class ORMProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig);
  }
}
```

Open connections in `setup()`, not in the constructor. Dox copies a provider to each isolate, and an open socket can not be copied.

A package with no `dox_core` dependency imports `DoxProvider` from `package:dox_annotation/provider.dart`.

## Running code after all providers

`boot()` runs after `setup()` of every provider is done. Use it for work that needs the other providers, like a background worker:

```dart
class ReportProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {}

  @override
  Future<void> boot() async {
    // every provider has run setup() here
  }
}
```

The web server and the queue worker (`bin/queue.dart`) run `boot()`. The scheduler (`bin/schedule.dart`) and `dox openapi:generate` run only `setup()`.

## Clean up on shutdown

`shutdown()` runs in every isolate when the server stops, after the open requests are done. See [Graceful shutdown](deployment.md#graceful-shutdown):

```dart title="lib/providers/redis_provider.dart"
class RedisProvider extends DoxProvider {
  late RedisConnection redis;

  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    redis = await RedisConnection.open();
  }

  @override
  Future<void> shutdown() async {
    await redis.close();
  }
}
```

Dox closes the cache stores by itself. An error in `shutdown()` goes to the [exception handler](../the-basic/errors.md), and the other providers still run.

## Choosing the order

Providers run in the order of their file path. List a provider in `AppConfig` to run it first:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  container: registerContainer,
  providers: <DoxProvider>[ORMProvider()], // runs before the others
);
```

No provider runs twice.

## Adding a provider in code

Call `Dox().addProvider()` or `Dox().addProviders()` before `startServer()`:

```dart title="bin/server.dart"
Dox().initialize(appConfig);
Dox().addProvider(MyProvider());
Dox().addProviders(<DoxProvider>[OtherProvider()]);
await Dox().startServer();
```

## Adding global middleware

A provider can add a global middleware in `setup()`. It runs before the middleware of the app. See [Middleware](../the-basic/middleware.md#global-middleware):

```dart
@override
void setup() {
  Dox().addGlobalMiddleware(AuditMiddleware());
}
```

## Work only in the web server

`Dox().isWebServer` is true only in the web server process. It is false in the queue worker, the scheduler and tests:

```dart
@override
void boot() {
  if (Dox().isWebServer) startMetrics();
}
```

## Example: auth

This provider sets up [authentication](../security/authentication.md). Its name is `AppAuthProvider`, because `dox_auth` already has an `AuthProvider` class:

```dart title="lib/providers/auth_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

class AppAuthProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Auth.initialize(AuthConfig(
      defaultGuard: 'web',
      guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
        'web': AuthGuard(
          driver: JwtAuthDriver(secret: SecretKey(env.appKey)),
          provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
        ),
      },
    ));
  }
}
```

- [Isolate](isolate.md#what-each-isolate-does-at-start): what each isolate does at start.
- [Dependency injection](../the-basic/dependency-injection.md): the container.
- [Package commands](package-commands.md): add CLI commands from a package.

# Dox CLI

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/dox-cli/

# Dox CLI

The `dox` CLI creates projects and files, runs the dev server, builds for production and runs migrations.

Run `dox help` to see all commands, or `dox help <command>` for one command. The [CLI reference](../reference/cli.md) has every command and option.

## Setup

Install the CLI with `dart pub`:

```bash
dart pub global activate dox
```

If your shell can not find `dox`, add the pub bin folder to your `PATH` in `~/.bashrc` or `~/.zshrc`:

```bash
export PATH="$PATH":"$HOME/.pub-cache/bin"
```

### Updating the CLI

`dox update` installs the newest version with the same major version as your CLI:

```bash
dox update
```

To remove the CLI, run `dart pub global deactivate dox`.

## Creating a project

`dox create` copies the [dox-sample](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-sample) template and makes `.env` with a new `APP_KEY`:

```bash
dox create new_blog
cd new_blog
dart pub get
dox serve
```

To pick a template release, pass `--version <release tag>`.

## Running the dev server

`dox serve` (or `dox s`) starts your app and runs `build_runner watch`:

```bash
dox serve
```

A change in `lib/app/` hot reloads into the running server. A change in routes, providers, config, `bin/`, `db/` or generated files restarts the server. Hot reload keeps the old value of a changed static or global value until a restart.

The server prints the VM service link. Open it in a browser to get DevTools, the debugger and the profiler.

Turn off hot reload or `build_runner watch` with these options:

```bash
dox s --no-reload             # restart on every change
dox s --ignore-build-runner   # do not run build_runner watch
```

See [`dox serve`](../reference/cli.md#dox-serve).

## Building for production

`dox build` builds a native (AOT) bundle into `build/bundle`. Run the server from there:

```bash
dox build
cd build/bundle
./bin/server
```

See [Deployment](deployment.md#build).

## Creating files

The `make:*` commands write new files with the right names and folders. So `BlogPost` makes `blog_post.controller.dart` with the class `BlogPostController`.

After `make:controller` or `make:dto`, run `dox build_runner:build`, or keep `dox serve` running.

### Controllers

`make:controller` writes a controller in `lib/app/http/controllers`. Add `-r` for all resource methods, `--api` for the resource methods with no `create` and `edit`, and `--model` to use a model:

```bash
dox make:controller Blog
dox make:controller Blog -r
dox make:controller Blog --api
dox make:controller Blog --model=Post
```

### Models

`make:model` writes a model. The options also make the files that belong to it:

```bash
dox make:model Blog -m      # model and a create_blogs_table migration
dox make:model Blog -mcr    # model, migration, resource controller
dox make:model Blog -a      # all of the files
```

The options are `-m` migration, `-c` controller, `-r` resource controller, `--api` API controller, `-f` factory, `-s` seeder and `-a` all. You can join them, like `-mfs`. The table is the name in plural snake case, so `BlogPost` gets `blog_posts`.

### Migrations

`make:migration` writes a Dart migration. Add `--sql` for a `.sql` file:

```bash
dox make:migration create_blogs_table
dox make:migration create_blogs_table --sql
```

### Mail and views

`make:mail` writes a mailable in `lib/app/mail` and its view. Add `--no-view` for a plain text body. `make:view` writes a `.dox.html` view:

```bash
dox make:mail Welcome
dox make:mail Invoice --no-view
dox make:view pages/about       # resources/views/pages/about.dox.html
```

### Tests

`make:test` writes a test that starts the app with `DoxTestClient`. Add `--unit` for a plain test:

```bash
dox make:test Ping              # test/ping_test.dart
dox make:test Math --unit       # test/math_test.dart
```

### Other files

```bash
dox make:middleware Auth     # lib/app/http/middleware/auth.middleware.dart
dox make:dto CreateBlog      # lib/app/dtos/create_blog/create_blog.dto.dart
dox make:serializer Blog     # lib/app/serializers/blog.serializer.dart
dox make:provider Cache      # lib/providers/cache_provider.dart
dox make:command send_report # run it with dox app:send-report
```

## Listing routes

`dox route:list` prints every route of the app. Add `--json` for JSON output:

```bash
dox route:list
```

See [`dox route:list`](../reference/cli.md#dox-routelist).

## Running migrations

The migration commands read the database settings from `.env` and the real environment. A real environment variable wins:

```ini title=".env"
# postgres, mysql or sqlite
DB_CONNECTION=postgres
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432
# for sqlite: the file path
DB_NAME=postgres
DB_USERNAME=admin
DB_PASSWORD=password
```

`DB_CONNECTION` is `sqlite` by default. A `DATABASE_URL` wins over all the `DB_*` keys. See the [Env reference](../reference/env.md#read-by-the-framework).

Run new migrations with `migration:run` (or `migrate`). `migration:status` shows which ones ran:

```bash
dox migration:run
dox migration:status
```

A failed migration stops the run with exit code 1. On MySQL, a `CREATE`, `ALTER` or `DROP` statement saves at once, so a migration that fails half way keeps these changes.

### Rolling back migrations

`migration:rollback` undoes the last batch. `--step` undoes the last N migrations, and `--batch` undoes one batch:

```bash
dox migration:rollback
dox migration:rollback --step=2
dox migration:rollback --batch=3
```

### Resetting the database

`migration:reset` undoes all migrations. `migration:refresh` undoes all, then runs them again. `migration:fresh` drops all tables, then runs all migrations:

```bash
dox migration:reset
dox migration:refresh
dox migration:fresh
```

Add `--seed` to `migration:run`, `migration:refresh` or `migration:fresh` to also run the seeders. The `migrate:*` names also work, like `migrate:fresh`.

- [CLI reference](../reference/cli.md): every command and option.
- [Add a package](../getting-started/add-a-package.md): `dox add`.
- [Package commands](package-commands.md): commands that come from a package.
