# Package commands

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/package-commands/

# Package commands

A package or an app can add its own `dox` commands, and the `dox` CLI finds them by itself.

## Setup

Add the package and run its command. For example, `dox queue:table` comes from the `dox_queue_database` package:

```bash
dart pub add dox_queue_database
dox queue:table
```

`dox help` lists the commands of each package, under the package name.

## Add a command to your package

A package command needs three things: the command class, a list of commands and a key in `pubspec.yaml`.

### 1. Write the command

A command extends `Command` from `package:dox_core/command.dart`. The `run` method gets the words after the command name:

```dart title="lib/src/commands/hello_command.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/command.dart';

class HelloCommand extends Command {
  @override
  String get name => 'hello:say';

  @override
  String get description => 'Say hello';

  /// optional, shown by `dox help`. The default is the name.
  @override
  String get usage => 'hello:say <name>';

  @override
  Future<void> run(List<String> args) async {
    print('Hello ${args.join(' ')}');
  }
}
```

So `dox hello:say Ann` calls `run(['Ann'])`. A package with no `dox_core` dependency imports `package:dox_annotation/command.dart`.

### 2. List the commands

Make one library with a top-level `commands` list:

```dart title="lib/commands.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/command.dart';

import 'src/commands/hello_command.dart';

final List<Command> commands = <Command>[HelloCommand()];
```

### 3. Name the library in pubspec.yaml

Add the `dox: commands:` key. Its value must be a library of the package itself:

```yaml title="pubspec.yaml"
dox:
  commands: package:my_package/commands.dart
```

An app that depends on your package now has `dox hello:say`.

## Add a command to your app

`dox make:command` writes the command, adds it to `lib/app/commands/commands.dart` and sets the `dox: commands:` key:

```bash
dox make:command send_report
```

The command name is `app:send-report`. See [`dox make:command`](../reference/cli.md#dox-makecommand).

## Name clashes

A built-in command always wins over a package command with the same name. When two packages have a command with the same name, `dox <name>` prints an error with both package names.

## Failing a command

Set `exitCode` from `dart:io`, or throw. The exit code of the command is the exit code of `dox`:

```dart
exitCode = 1;
```

A thrown error prints its stack trace and gives exit code 1.

## Writing a migration

`MigrationFile().create` writes a migration with the same file name format as `dox make:migration`. It returns null and writes nothing when a migration with this name is already there:

```dart
String? path = MigrationFile().create('create_queue_tables', source);
if (path == null) {
  print('A create_queue_tables migration is already in db/migration.');
  exitCode = 1;
}
```

`MigrationFile().exists(name)` only tells you if the migration is there. The next `dox migrate` runs the new file.

## Ship an install command

`dox add <x>` adds the package `dox_x`, then runs its `<x>:install` command. If your package needs config files, env keys or a provider, ship an `<x>:install` command.

`Installer` from `package:dox_annotation/install.dart` does the steps. A step never overwrites a file and never adds a key twice, so it is safe to run twice:

```dart title="lib/src/commands/hello_install_command.dart"
import 'package:dox_annotation/command.dart';
import 'package:dox_annotation/install.dart';

class HelloInstallCommand extends Command {
  @override
  String get name => 'hello:install';

  @override
  String get description => 'Set up dox_hello in this app';

  @override
  Future<void> run(List<String> args) async {
    Installer installer = Installer();
    String app = installer.appName;
    installer.writeFile(
      'lib/config/hello.dart',
      "import 'package:$app/config/env.dart';\n",
    );
    installer.addEnvGetter("String get helloName => 'world';");
    installer.addEnv('HELLO_NAME', 'world');
    await installer.buildRunner();
    installer.printSummary(<String>['Restart the server.']);
  }
}
```

| Member | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `Installer(root: dir)` | Works in the folder `dir`. The default is the current folder. |
| `appName` | The `name` of the app `pubspec.yaml`, for `package:<app>/...` imports. |
| `writeFile(path, content)` | Writes the file only when it is not there. Returns true when it wrote it. |
| `makeFolder(path)` | Makes the folder when it is not there. |
| `addEnv(key, value)` | Adds `KEY=value` to `.env.example` and `.env` when the key is missing. |
| `addEnvGetter(getter)` | Adds a getter to `AppEnv` in `lib/config/env.dart` when the class has no member with that name. |
| `hasDependency(package)` | True when the app `pubspec.yaml` has the package. |
| `addDependency(package, dev: false)` | Runs `dart pub add` when the app does not have the package. |
| `buildRunner()` | Runs `dart run build_runner build`. |
| `note(line)` | Adds your own line to the summary, like `added    hooks to pubspec.yaml`. |
| `lines` | The lines of the summary. |
| `ok` | False when a step failed. |
| `printSummary(nextSteps)` | Prints what was done and the next steps. Sets exit code 1 when a step failed. |

Read the options from `args`, like `--driver=postgres`, and give a good default, so `dox add <x>` works with no options. `dox_orm` has an example: `orm:install`.

## Next steps

- [Dox CLI](dox-cli.md): the commands of the CLI.
- [Add a package](../getting-started/add-a-package.md): `dox add` runs the install command of a package.
- [Providers](providers.md): set up a package when the app starts.

# Deployment

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/deployment/

# Deployment

This page shows how to build a Dox app for production and run it safely.

You build the app into a native binary, copy it to a server or a Docker image, and put a proxy in front of it for HTTPS.

!!! danger "Never run production with `dart run`"
    `dart run` and `dox serve` use the JIT compiler, which is for
    development. It uses about 25x more memory at start (around 390 MB
    instead of 16 MB) and starts slower. Always build an AOT binary for
    production.

## Build

`dox build` builds your app for production into `build/bundle/`:

```bash
dox build
```

| File                        | What it is                                       |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `build/bundle/bin/server`   | the native binary. It needs no Dart SDK          |
| `build/bundle/bin/queue`    | the queue worker, when `bin/queue.dart` exists   |
| `build/bundle/bin/schedule` | the scheduler, when `bin/schedule.dart` exists   |
| `build/bundle/lib/`         | native libraries from build hooks (like SQLite)  |
| `build/bundle/db/`          | your `db/` folder, with no SQLite database files |
| `build/bundle/.env.example` | copy it to `build/bundle/.env`, or use env variables |

Keep `bin/` and `lib/` together, because the binary loads the native libraries from `../lib`. Do not use `dart compile exe`: it does not run build hooks, so the app has no native libraries.

### Starting the server

Start the binary from the bundle folder. It reads `.env` and `db/` from the folder you start it in:

```bash
cd build/bundle
./bin/server
```

A real environment variable wins over the `.env` file. A new Dox app runs the migrations in `bin/server.dart`, before the server starts.

## Docker

A new Dox app has this multi-stage `Dockerfile`. The final image is `FROM scratch`: only the Dart AOT runtime, the bundle and an empty `/tmp`.

```dockerfile
FROM dart:stable AS build

# Resolve dependencies first, so this layer is cached.
WORKDIR /app
COPY pubspec.* ./
RUN dart pub get

COPY . .
RUN dart pub get --offline

# `dox build` runs build_runner, then builds bin/server.dart,
# bin/queue.dart and bin/schedule.dart into build/bundle.
RUN dart pub global activate dox
RUN /root/.pub-cache/bin/dox build

# The final file tree: /app/bin, /app/lib, /app/db, /app/storage and
# a writable /tmp (uploads bigger than 1 MB go to a temp file).
RUN mkdir -p /out/app/storage /out/tmp \
  && chmod 1777 /out/tmp \
  && cp -r build/bundle/. /out/app/

# The AOT runtime files of the dart image plus the bundle.
FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /runtime/ /
COPY --from=build /out/ /
WORKDIR /app

# Config comes from env variables. The image has no .env file.
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["/app/bin/server"]
```

The image has no `.env` file, so secrets stay out of it. Pass the config as environment variables:

```bash
docker build -t my-app .
docker run -p 3000:3000 --env-file .env -e DB_HOST=... my-app
```

### Docker compose

A new app also has a `docker-compose.yml`. It runs the app, a queue worker and Postgres:

```bash
docker compose up -d --build
```

- The compose services set `DB_CONNECTION=postgres` and `DB_NAME=dox`. To use this Postgres with `dox s`, set the same two values in `.env`.
- A new app skips the Postgres driver in `pubspec.yaml`. Remove the `dox_postgres_native` skip lines first. See [Skip unused drivers](../database/index.md#skip-unused-drivers).

See [Docker](../guides/docker.md) for a health check in the image.

## Running the queue worker and scheduler

One build has three binaries. Run each one as its own process:

| Process | Command |
| --- | --- |
| web server | `/app/bin/server` (the default `CMD`) |
| queue worker | `/app/bin/queue work` |
| scheduler | `/app/bin/schedule work` |

The image has no shell, so start the other binaries with `--entrypoint`:

```bash
docker run -d -p 3000:3000 --env-file .env my-app
docker run -d --env-file .env --entrypoint /app/bin/queue my-app work
docker run -d --env-file .env --entrypoint /app/bin/schedule my-app work
```

In compose, use `command: ["/app/bin/queue", "work"]`. With no Docker, run `./bin/queue work` and `./bin/schedule work` in `build/bundle`. Only the server runs the migrations, so start the server first.

A small app can run the jobs and the schedule inside the server, with `QueueConfig(inProcess: true)` and `ScheduleConfig(inProcess: true)`. See [Running jobs in the web server](queue.md#running-jobs-in-the-web-server).

## HTTPS without a proxy

Dox can serve HTTPS itself, so a small server needs no proxy for TLS. The TLS work is in Rust (rustls), in the [native server](native-server.md). TLS is off by default.

Use a proxy when you also want gzip, automatic certificates or more than one app on a server. See [HTTPS: put a proxy in front](#https-put-a-proxy-in-front).

### Turn on TLS

Set `tls` in the app config. Give the certificate file and the key file:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  serverPort: 443,
  tls: TlsOptions(
    certificatePath: '/etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem',
    keyPath: '/etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem',
  ),
  // ...
);
```

| Option | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `certificatePath` | A PEM file. The certificate is first, then the intermediate certificates. An example is `fullchain.pem` of certbot. |
| `keyPath` | A PEM file with the private key of the certificate (PKCS #8, PKCS #1 or SEC1). An example is `privkey.pem` of certbot. |

- Dox reads the two files when the server starts. A bad file, or a key of a different certificate, throws a `TlsException`, and the server does not start.
- The user of the app must have permission to read the two files.
- The server uses TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3. There are no cipher options.
- The TLS handshake must end in `idleTimeout`.
- Your routes stay the same. WebSocket (`wss://`) and streamed responses work on the TLS port.
- `req.scheme()` is `https` and `req.isSecure()` is true. Thus the session cookie and other cookies get `Secure`, and `SecurityHeaders` sends HSTS.
- Set `APP_URL` to the `https://` address, because signed URLs and absolute URLs use it.
- gzip is off by default. With no proxy, set `compress: true` if you want gzip.

On Linux, a port below 1024 needs a permission. With systemd, add `AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE` to the `[Service]` part of the unit file.

### Read the files from the env

Keep the file paths out of the code, so each machine can use its own files. Add two optional getters to your `AppEnv`, then run `dart run build_runner build`:

```dart title="lib/config/env.dart"
/// the certificate file (PEM). Not set: plain HTTP.
String? get tlsCert;

/// the private key file (PEM) of the certificate
String? get tlsKey;
```

The getters hold only the keys. The config file makes the `TlsOptions`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
TlsOptions? tlsOptions() {
  String? cert = env.tlsCert;
  String? key = env.tlsKey;
  if (cert == null || key == null) {
    return null;
  }
  return TlsOptions(certificatePath: cert, keyPath: key);
}

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  tls: tlsOptions(),
  // ...
);
```

```bash title=".env"
TLS_CERT=/etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem
TLS_KEY=/etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem
```

An empty value (`TLS_CERT=`) is the same as no key, so TLS stays off. Keep the two keys empty on your own machine, where you have no certificate.

### One port, one mode

A port with `tls` accepts only TLS. A plain HTTP client gets no answer, and the connection closes. A port without `tls` accepts only plain HTTP.

Dox does not send `http://` visitors to `https://`. See [Not included](#not-included).

### HTTP/2 and gRPC over TLS

Browsers use HTTP/2 only with TLS. Set `http2: true` together with `tls`, and browsers and gRPC clients use HTTP/2 with no proxy:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  http2: true,
  tls: TlsOptions(certificatePath: 'fullchain.pem', keyPath: 'privkey.pem'),
  // ...
);
```

The client selects the protocol in the TLS handshake (ALPN):

| `http2` | The server offers |
| --- | --- |
| `true` | `h2` and `http/1.1` |
| `false` | `http/1.1` only |

A client with no ALPN gets HTTP/1.1. `grpcurl` works without `-plaintext`. See [HTTP/2](http2.md) and [gRPC](grpc.md).

### reloadCertificate

A certificate has an end date, and a tool such as certbot writes a new one before that date. Call `reloadCertificate()` to use the new certificate without a restart:

```dart
await Dox().server.reloadCertificate();
```

- The method reads the same two files again.
- New connections get the new certificate. Open connections keep the old certificate until they close.
- One call is sufficient. All isolates of the process get the new certificate.
- If a file is bad, the method throws a `TlsException`. The server keeps the old certificate.
- If `tls` is off, the method throws a `StateError`.

Dox does not watch the files and has no signal for this. Your app decides when to call the method. This example calls it on `SIGHUP`:

```dart title="bin/server.dart"
Future<void> main() async {
  // ...
  await Dox().startServer();
  ProcessSignal.sighup.watch().listen(reloadCertificate);
}

Future<void> reloadCertificate(ProcessSignal signal) async {
  try {
    await Dox().server.reloadCertificate();
    Logger.info('The server has the new certificate');
  } on TlsException catch (error) {
    Logger.danger('The server keeps the old certificate: $error');
  }
}
```

Then let certbot send the signal after each renewal. With the systemd unit of [Keep it running](#keep-it-running):

```bash
certbot renew --deploy-hook "systemctl kill --signal=HUP dox"
```

Windows has no `SIGHUP`. There, call the method from a scheduled task or a timer in the server process, for example one time each day.

### Not included

- ACME: Dox does not get or renew a certificate (for example from Let's Encrypt). Use certbot or a similar tool, then call `reloadCertificate()`.
- Redirect from port 80: Dox does not send `http://` visitors to `https://`. Use a proxy for this.
- mTLS: Dox does not ask the client for a certificate.
- SNI: one port has one certificate. Dox does not select a certificate for each domain.

## HTTPS: put a proxy in front

A proxy gets and renews the certificate, does gzip and sends `http://` visitors to `https://`. Run Dox on a private port with plain HTTP, and put [Caddy](https://caddyserver.com) or nginx in front of it. When the proxy is on the same machine, set `APP_HOST=127.0.0.1`:

<ol class="dox-flow dox-flow--labels dox-flow--plain" aria-label="A proxy in front of Dox">
  <li><strong>Client</strong></li>
  <li data-via="HTTPS"><strong>Caddy or nginx</strong><span>TLS and gzip</span></li>
  <li data-via="HTTP" class="dox-flow__end"><strong>Dox</strong><span>a private port</span></li>
  <li><strong>Database</strong></li>
</ol>

### Trusting the proxy

Tell Dox to trust the proxy, so `req.ip()` and `req.scheme()` show the real client:

```dart
AppConfig(
  // the IP of the proxy, or a range like '10.0.0.0/8'
  trustedProxies: <String>['127.0.0.1', '::1'],
);
```

`req.ip()` then reads `X-Forwarded-For`, and `req.scheme()` reads `X-Forwarded-Proto`. The list is empty by default, so Dox ignores these headers. `['*']` trusts any direct client, so use it only when the app port can not be reached from outside.

### Caddy

Caddy gets a certificate for you and sets the forwarded headers. WebSockets work with no extra config:

```
example.com {
  encode gzip
  reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:3000
}
```

### Nginx

```nginx
upstream dox {
  server 127.0.0.1:3000;
  keepalive 64;
}

map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
  default upgrade;
  ''      '';
}

server {
  listen 443 ssl http2;
  server_name example.com;

  ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem;
  ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem;

  # match maxMultipartSize in AppConfig
  client_max_body_size 100m;

  gzip on;
  gzip_types application/json text/plain text/css application/javascript;

  location / {
    proxy_pass http://dox;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;

    # websocket upgrade
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;

    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

    # stream uploads to Dox, do not buffer them in nginx first
    proxy_request_buffering off;
  }
}

server {
  listen 80;
  server_name example.com;
  return 301 https://$host$request_uri;
}
```

### HTTP/2 and gRPC

gRPC needs HTTP/2 between the proxy and Dox. Set `http2: true` in `AppConfig` (see [HTTP/2](http2.md)). Without `tls`, Dox speaks h2c, so the proxy keeps the TLS. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 use the same port.

With Caddy, `h2c://` sends HTTP/2 with no TLS to the app:

```
example.com {
  reverse_proxy h2c://127.0.0.1:3000
}
```

With nginx, use `grpc_pass` for the gRPC paths and `proxy_pass` for the other routes:

```nginx
server {
  listen 443 ssl;
  http2 on;
  server_name example.com;

  ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem;
  ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem;

  # Normal routes: HTTP/1.1 to the app
  location / {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
  }

  # gRPC service paths only
  location /greeter.Greeter/ {
    grpc_pass grpc://127.0.0.1:3000;
  }
}
```

The nginx `grpc_read_timeout` and `grpc_send_timeout` are 60 seconds by default, and a quiet stream stops after that time. Raise them for long streams.

### Pass the real `Host` header

The proxy must pass the real `Host` header, like `proxy_set_header Host $host;` above. If it sends its own host, the WebSocket origin check gives 403, and `back()` goes to the fallback.

## Behind a load balancer

Dox closes an idle connection after 30 seconds. Set `idleTimeout` longer than the idle timeout of the balancer, or clients can get 502. AWS ALB keeps idle connections for 60 seconds, so use 65 seconds:

```dart
AppConfig(
  // ...
  idleTimeout: Duration(seconds: 65),
)
```

## Keep it running

When the main isolate dies, the process exits with a non-zero code. See [Isolate](isolate.md#when-an-isolate-crashes). Let a supervisor restart it, like `restart: unless-stopped` in Docker compose or `Restart=always` in systemd:

```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/dox.service
[Service]
WorkingDirectory=/srv/app/build/bundle
ExecStart=/srv/app/build/bundle/bin/server
EnvironmentFile=/srv/app/build/bundle/.env
Restart=always

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

## Graceful shutdown

On SIGTERM (docker stop, Kubernetes, Cloud Run, systemd) and SIGINT (Ctrl+C), Dox lets open requests finish. In every isolate it:

1. stops taking new connections,
2. lets open requests finish, for `shutdownTimeout` at most (8 seconds by default),
3. runs `shutdown()` of every provider (see [Providers](providers.md#clean-up-on-shutdown)),
4. closes the cache stores of `Cache()`,
5. exits with code 0.

A second signal stops the process at once. Set the timeout in `lib/config/app.dart`:

```dart
AppConfig(
  shutdownTimeout: Duration(seconds: 20),
  // ...
)
```

Keep it shorter than the time your platform waits before it kills the process:

| Platform | Waits | Change it with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `docker stop` | 10 seconds | `docker stop -t 30`, or `stop_grace_period` in compose |
| Kubernetes | 30 seconds | `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` |
| Cloud Run | 10 seconds | can not be changed |
| Fly.io | 5 seconds | `kill_timeout` in `fly.toml` |
| systemd | 90 seconds | `TimeoutStopSec` |

### Stopping in code

`Dox().stop()` does steps 1 to 4, and the process keeps running:

```dart
await Dox().stop();
```

## Give each isolate its own memory

By default, all isolates share one heap and one garbage collector, and the Dart VM runs only 8 of them at the same time. Turn on `isolateGroups` to give each isolate its own heap, with no such limit:

```dart
AppConfig(
  appKey: env.appKey,
  flags: CoreFlags(isolateGroups: env.appEnv == 'production'),
);
```

Turn it on only in production. In development the app starts slower and uses more memory with this flag, and one group is sufficient there.

Each isolate then runs `main()` of `bin/server.dart` from the start. The migrations in `main()` need no change: the first isolate runs them before the other isolates start, and the other isolates find none to run.

For other work that must run only one time, use `Dox().isPrimary`:

```dart
if (Dox().isPrimary) {
  await warmUpReports();
}
```

Each isolate builds the config again, so read your settings and the app key from the env, not from command line arguments.

### Build

On Linux, the bundle of `dox build` works with no change. On macOS, also make a snapshot file with the name of the executable and `.aot`:

```bash
dart compile aot-snapshot bin/server.dart -o build/bundle/bin/server.aot
```

If Dox finds no file to start, it prints a warning and the isolates share memory.

### Memory for each isolate

The Dart VM keeps free memory pages for one isolate only. To keep them for all isolates, set 32 MB for each isolate:

```dockerfile
# 4 isolates: 4 x 32 = 128
ENV DART_VM_OPTIONS=--new_gen_semi_max_size=128,--new_gen_semi_initial_size=32,--new_gen_garbage_threshold=0
```

The app is faster and uses more memory, approximately 30 MB for each isolate.

## Many processes or machines

One Dox process uses every core. Run more processes only for more machines, or to restart one process with no downtime. List them in the proxy:

```nginx
upstream dox {
  server 10.0.0.11:3000;
  server 10.0.0.12:3000;
  keepalive 64;
}
```

Socket.IO rooms then need a shared adapter, like Redis.

- [Deploy to a Linux server](../guides/deploy-vps.md): your own server with systemd and Caddy.
- [Deploy to Fly.io](../guides/deploy-fly.md): Fly.io.
- [Deploy to Google Cloud Run](../guides/deploy-cloud-run.md): Google Cloud Run.

# Native server

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/native-server/

# Native server

Dox runs on a native HTTP server from the package `dox_http_native`: Rust owns the sockets and parses HTTP, and all your code stays in Dart.

## Setup

Every Dox app uses the native server, and you do not need Rust. The package gets a ready-built library for your system when you build the app. See [Performance](performance.md) for the numbers.

Build with `dox build` or `dart build cli`. `dart compile exe` does not run build hooks, so the app has no library. See [Deployment](deployment.md).

### Limits

| Limit | Value | Answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Request line and headers | 16 KB | 431 |
| Body | `maxBodySize` (10 MB) | 413 |
| Multipart form | `maxMultipartSize` (100 MB) | 413 |
| No body bytes for | `bodyTimeout` (120 seconds) | 408 |
| Request head arrives in | `idleTimeout` (30 seconds) | connection closed |
| Keep-alive connection with no request | `idleTimeout` (30 seconds) | connection closed |
| Both `Content-Length` and chunked | - | 400 |
| Transfer encoding other than chunked | - | 501 |

These are the defaults of `AppConfig`, where you can change them. See [App config](../reference/app-config.md).

## Writing handlers

The server has the same API as the `dart:io` `HttpServer`, so code for `dart:io` keeps working. Each isolate runs the server on its own thread, so a slow synchronous handler blocks all the sockets of its isolate. An `await` gives the isolate back.

## When the library does not load

Dox stops at start and the error says why and how to fix it:

```
Unsupported operation: dox_http_native did not load: <reason>.
Fix: install Rust (cargo, see https://rustup.rs), then run the app again ...
```

A reason like `native library ABI 8, expected 9` means the library on disk is from another version of the package. See [Troubleshooting](../reference/troubleshooting.md#the-native-http-library-did-not-load).

## HTTP/2

The native server also speaks HTTP/2 (h2c) on the same port, with `http2: true`. See [HTTP/2](http2.md).

## WebSocket

`NativeWebSocket.upgrade(request)` gives a `dart:io` `WebSocket`. Your route, middleware and the `Origin` check run first, and a normal answer (like 403) refuses the upgrade:

```dart
if (NativeWebSocket.isUpgradeRequest(request)) {
  WebSocket socket = await NativeWebSocket.upgrade(request,
      protocol: 'chat', maxMessageSize: 64 * 1024);
}
```

A message over `maxMessageSize` (16 MB by default) closes the socket with code 1009. On a graceful stop, every open socket gets code 1001.

### Finding lost clients

Set `pingInterval` to find clients that vanished with no close, like a phone that lost its network. When the client stays quiet for two intervals, the socket closes with 1001:

```dart
socket.pingInterval = Duration(seconds: 30);
```

## Streaming a response

Write with `add()` and call `flush()`. The first `flush()` sends the status, the headers and the bytes so far:

```dart
import 'dart:convert';
import 'dart:io';

server.listen((HttpRequest req) async {
  req.response.headers.contentType = ContentType('text', 'event-stream');
  req.response.add(utf8.encode('data: hello\n\n'));
  await req.response.flush();
});
```

A streamed response with a `contentLength` must send exactly that many bytes, or `add()` or `close()` fails.

### Checking the response state

Cast `req.response` to `NativeResponse` to read its state. `headSent` is true when the status and headers went out, so no error page can go out after it. `isGone` is true when the client left, and `gone` completes when it leaves:

```dart
NativeResponse res = req.response as NativeResponse;
bool sent = res.headSent;
bool left = res.isGone;
await Future.any(<Future<void>>[res.gone, res.done]);
```

`gone` never completes for a response that ends normally, so always race it against `done` or a timeout.

## Security notes

- On the internet, run the app behind a reverse proxy like Caddy or nginx. The proxy does HTTPS and buffers slow clients. Without a proxy, turn on [TLS](deployment.md#https-without-a-proxy).
- Set `maxConnections` when the app port is open to the internet.
- Another process of the same OS user can bind the same port. Do not run untrusted code as the user of the app.
- `req.uri` resolves `..` in the path. Never build a file path from the raw path. Use the storage helpers.

## Where the library comes from

The build hook of `dox_http_native` uses the first one that works:

1. A path in the root `pubspec.yaml` of your app:

    ```yaml
    hooks:
      user_defines:
        dox_http_native:
          lib_path: /path/to/libdox_http_native.so
    ```

2. A local build in `native/target/release` of the package.
3. The ready-built library from the GitHub release, checked with sha256. There are builds for macOS (arm64, x64), Linux (x64, arm64) and Windows (x64).
4. A build from source with `cargo`, when Rust is installed.

For a git or path dependency, step 4 comes before step 3. When none works, the app stops at start with the error above.

## How it works

The server runs on the thread of the isolate, in a loop:

1. Dart calls Rust (one FFI call).
2. Rust writes the answers of the last batch, reads the sockets and parses the new requests. It gives them back to Dart as one batch.
3. Dart runs your handlers and calls Rust again with their answers.

When the isolate has nothing to do, a small helper thread watches the sockets and wakes it. The OS spreads connections, not requests, between the [isolates](isolate.md). So a few busy connections (like from one proxy) can keep some isolates idle. Use more connections than isolates.

## Without Dox

`dox_http_native` also works on its own, in any Dart app:

```bash
dart pub add dox_http_native
```

Bind a server and listen for requests, like with the `dart:io` `HttpServer`:

```dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_http_native/dox_http_native.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  NativeHttpServer server = await NativeHttpServer.bind(3000);
  server.listen((HttpRequest req) async {
    req.response.write('Hello World');
    await req.response.close();
  });
}
```

With no address, the server listens on all interfaces. These are the options of `bind`:

```dart
NativeHttpServer.bind(
  3000,
  address: '127.0.0.1',
  maxConnections: 10000, // no limit by default
  maxBodySize: 10 * 1024 * 1024,
  maxMultipartSize: 50 * 1024 * 1024,
  bodyTimeout: Duration(seconds: 120),
  idleTimeout: Duration(seconds: 30),
  http2: true, // see HTTP/2
);
```

At `maxConnections`, the server stops accepting until a connection closes. Behind a load balancer, set `idleTimeout` longer than the idle timeout of the balancer, or clients can get 502.

### Checking the library

`NativeHttpServer.isAvailable` is true when the native library loads. `loadError` says why it did not, and `ensureAvailable()` throws that error:

```dart
if (!NativeHttpServer.isAvailable) print(NativeHttpServer.loadError);
```

### Stopping the server

`close()` waits for open requests. `close(force: true)` closes every connection at once. `isOpen` is false after the close:

```dart
await server.close();
```

### Encrypting with AES-GCM

`AesGcm` does AES-256-GCM in Rust. Dox uses it for encrypted cookies. The key is 32 bytes, and `open` gives null when the data or the `aad` is wrong:

```dart
Uint8List sealed = AesGcm.seal(key, plain, aad);
Uint8List? plain2 = AesGcm.open(key, sealed, aad);
```

## Working on the native code

`dox_http_native` lives in its own repo: [dartondox/dox-http-native](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-http-native). The Rust code is in its `native` folder:

```bash
cd dox-http-native/native
cargo build --release   # the hook uses this build from now on
cargo test
cd .. && dart test --concurrency=1
```

To use your local copy in the Dox repo, see [Contribute](../community/contribute.md#native-packages).

## Next steps

- [HTTP/2](http2.md): turn on HTTP/2.
- [Performance](performance.md): the benchmark numbers.
- [Isolate](isolate.md): one server per CPU core.

# Performance

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/performance/

# Performance

This page shows how fast Dox is, and how to keep your app fast in production.

## Setup

Dox is fast by default. In production, follow these rules:

1. Build with `dox build` and run the AOT binary. See [Deployment](deployment.md#build).
2. Put Caddy or nginx in front, for HTTPS and gzip.
3. Keep the default isolates, one per CPU core.
4. Keep the body limits on.

For the code mistakes that slow an app down, see [Performance mistakes](performance-mistakes.md).

## Bodies, uploads and big responses

Dox keeps big requests and responses out of the memory by default:

- A body over `maxBodySize` or `maxMultipartSize` gets 413 before Dart reads it. Set the same limit in the proxy. See [Size limits](../the-basic/request.md#size-limits).
- An upload over 1 MB streams to a temp file. See [Request](../the-basic/request.md#requestfile).
- A `File` or `Stream` response streams. See [Files and big responses](../the-basic/response.md#files-and-big-responses).

## gzip

A proxy does gzip better than Dart, so gzip in Dart is off by default. With no proxy, turn it on:

```dart
AppConfig(compress: true);
```

Dox gzips only a body over 256 bytes, for a client that accepts gzip. A streamed response is not compressed.

## Logging

`LogMiddleware` logs one line per request. A new project turns it off when `APP_ENV` is `production` or not set, because the proxy writes access logs.

`Logger` writes its lines every 20 ms in one write. If the process is killed hard, the last 20 ms of logs can be lost.

## Response handler

Leave `responseHandler` unset if you do not need it. With no handler, Dox sends a plain value (text, map, list) with no `DoxResponse`.

## Benchmark

This benchmark uses the rules of [the-benchmarker/web-frameworks](https://github.com/the-benchmarker/web-frameworks). Each server answers `GET /` (empty body), `GET /user/:id` (the id) and `POST /user` (empty body). "Dox server only" is `dox_http_native` with no framework.

It measures only the HTTP stack. A real app spends most of its time on the database and your own code. See [App benchmark](#app-benchmark).

### Why it is fast

The server runs on the thread of the isolate, so a request never waits for another thread to wake up. See [Native server](native-server.md#how-it-works). A profile with `perf` (4 server cores, 64 connections):

| | Dox | Bun |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| CPU time per request | 4.85 µs | 5.5 µs |
| Context switches per request | 0.08 | 0.035 |

### How it was run

- Docker on an Apple M2 (8 CPUs in the Docker VM), `linux/arm64`.
- One server at a time. The server and wrk run in two containers on
  different CPUs: the server on 2 CPUs, wrk on the other 6. Host
  network, keep-alive.
- wrk 4.1, 64, 256 and 512 connections, 5 seconds warm-up, then 15 seconds
  per route.
- 3 rounds on 2026-11-22. In each round, every server runs one time. The
  tables show the median of the 3 rounds.
- Every server has as many workers as server CPUs.
- Peak memory is the peak of the container (all workers).
- Dart 3.13.7, AOT build with `dart build cli` (this is what `dox build`
  does). `dox_core` and `dox_http_native` are the releases of 2026-11-22. Node 26.13, Bun 1.4.5, Go 1.26, Rust 1.99 with hyper 1.
- Relic is `relic` 2.0.0 with `relic_native` 2.0.0, started with `serveNative()`.

The server gets 2 CPUs, the database gets 2 CPUs and wrk gets the other 4.
Each server has 4 database connections per core, 8 in total. One run of 15
seconds per route. The Postgres Dox row was measured again on 2026-11-16 (same Mac, a new Docker VM). The other servers and the MySQL table are from the run before.

## Database drivers

One find-by-id query, AOT build (`dart build cli`), database on the same machine (Apple M-series), one isolate:

| Database | One query at a time | Many queries in flight | App CPU time per query |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Postgres 14<br>4 connections | 60 µs | 12.5 µs each<br>64 in flight | |
| MySQL 8.4<br>10 connections | 67 µs | 11 µs each<br>32 in flight | 13.5 µs |
| MariaDB 11<br>10 connections | 63 µs | 9.7 µs each<br>32 in flight | 12.4 µs |

The CPU time counts the Dart thread and the Rust thread. For MySQL, it is about 75,000 queries per second on one core. Many requests at the same time, like in a web server, get the most out of the driver.

## Dart VM flags

A bigger young generation (`DART_VM_OPTIONS=--new_gen_semi_max_size=64` or `128`) did not give a better p99 in 5 runs, so Dox sets no VM flags. The AOT binary of `dox build` reads `DART_VM_OPTIONS`, so you can try your own.

## Next steps

- [Performance mistakes](performance-mistakes.md): the code that makes an app slow.
- [Isolate](isolate.md): how Dox uses the CPU cores.

# Performance mistakes

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/performance-mistakes/

# Performance mistakes

These are the mistakes that make a Dox app slow, with the fix for each one, and a strict mode that warns you about the worst of them.

Dart runs one thing at a time in each isolate. When one request does slow work with no `await`, every other request on that isolate waits. For server settings, see [Performance](performance.md).

## Heavy CPU work in a request

A PDF, an image or a huge JSON file keeps the CPU busy. Run the work on a worker isolate with `Dox().compute`:

```dart title="Wrong"
Future<List<int>> invoice(DoxRequest req) async {
  Order order = await Order().findOrFail(req.param['id']);
  return buildPdf(order.toJson()); // blocks the isolate
}
```

```dart title="Right"
Future<List<int>> invoice(DoxRequest req) async {
  Order order = await Order().findOrFail(req.param['id']);
  return renderPdf(order.toJson());
}

Future<List<int>> renderPdf(Map<String, dynamic> data) {
  return Dox().compute(() => buildPdf(data));
}
```

Pass only plain values to the task, like numbers, strings, lists and maps. See [Heavy CPU work](isolate.md#heavy-cpu-work).

## Sync password hashing

`Hash.make` and `Hash.verify` run bcrypt on the isolate, and bcrypt is slow on purpose. In a handler, use the async methods:

```dart title="Wrong"
bool ok = Hash.verify(password, user.password);
```

```dart title="Right"
bool ok = await Hash.verifyAsync(password, user.password);
String hashed = await Hash.makeAsync(password);
```

## Sync file calls

A sync file call stops the isolate until the disk answers. Use the async call:

```dart title="Wrong"
String text = File('data/terms.txt').readAsStringSync();
```

```dart title="Right"
String text = await File('data/terms.txt').readAsString();
```

## Loading a whole table

`all()` and `get()` read every row into memory. On a big table, read one page:

```dart title="Wrong"
List<Order> orders = await Order().all();
```

```dart title="Right"
Pagination<Order> page =
    await Order().orderBy('id').paginate(currentPage: 1, perPage: 50);
```

To work on all rows, use `chunk()`, `lazy()` or `cursor()`:

```dart
await for (Order order in Order().orderBy('id').cursor(chunkSize: 500)) {
  // one row at a time
}
```

See [Paginating results](../database/query-builder.md#paginating-results), [Chunking results](../database/query-builder.md#chunking-results) and [Streaming results](../database/query-builder.md#streaming-results).

## A query inside a loop

This is the **N+1 problem**: 100 posts make 101 queries. `preload()` loads the relation for all rows in one extra query:

```dart title="Wrong"
List<Post> posts = await Post().all();
for (Post post in posts) {
  await post.$getRelation('author'); // one query per post
  User? author = post.author;
}
```

```dart title="Right"
List<Post> posts = await Post().preload('author').get();
for (Post post in posts) {
  User? author = post.author; // already loaded
}
```

## Awaiting independent work one by one

Start two calls that do not need each other at the same time. The total time is then the slowest call:

```dart title="Wrong"
int users = await User().count();
int orders = await Order().count();
```

```dart title="Right"
(int, int) counts = await (User().count(), Order().count()).wait;
```

For a list of futures, use `Future.wait(futures)`.

## A static Map as a cache

A static map that you never clean grows until the memory is full, and each isolate has its own copy. Use the [cache](cache.md) with a time to live:

```dart title="Wrong"
static final Map<String, Object> _settings = <String, Object>{};
```

```dart title="Right"
Map<String, dynamic> settings = await Cache().remember(
  'settings',
  Duration(minutes: 10),
  loadSettings,
);
```

With the `redis` or `database` store, all isolates and servers share the same values.

## Forgetting await

An async call with no `await` loses its error, and it can end after the response is sent:

```dart title="Wrong"
mailer.sendWelcome(user);
```

```dart title="Right"
await mailer.sendWelcome(user);
```

The `unawaited_futures` lint in `analysis_options.yaml` finds these. To answer the client first, use a [queue job with `dispatchAfterResponse`](queue.md).

## A new client for every request

A new HTTP or Redis client in each request opens and closes a connection every time. Make one client and share it:

```dart title="Wrong"
Future<String> rate(DoxRequest req) async {
  HttpClient client = HttpClient();
  // ...
}
```

```dart title="Right"
class RateService {
  RateService(this._client);

  final HttpClient _client;

  Future<String> rate() async {
    // use _client
  }
}
```

Register the client one time in the [container](../the-basic/dependency-injection.md) and inject it.

## A long transaction

A transaction holds one database connection until it ends, so a slow API call inside it can empty the pool. Do the slow call before or after the transaction:

```dart title="Wrong"
await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  await order.save();
  await paymentApi.charge(order); // the connection waits here
});
```

```dart title="Right"
await paymentApi.charge(order);
await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  await order.save();
});
```

## Reading a big file into memory

`bytes` loads the whole upload into memory. Stream it. See [Request](../the-basic/request.md#requestfile) and [Files and big responses](../the-basic/response.md#files-and-big-responses):

```dart title="Wrong"
List<int> data = await file.bytes;
```

```dart title="Right"
Stream<List<int>> data = file.stream();
```

## Timers and listeners that never stop

On a long connection, like a WebSocket, a `Timer.periodic` or a stream listener keeps running after the client leaves. Cancel it when the connection closes:

```dart
StreamSubscription<Event> subscription = events.listen(send);
// when the client disconnects
await subscription.cancel();
```

## Let Dox warn you

**Strict mode** writes a warning for the worst mistakes while you develop. It is off by default.

### Strict mode in Dox

Set `strict` in `AppConfig`, only in development:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  strict: StrictConfig(enabled: Env.appEnv == 'development'),
  // ...
);
```

Warnings go to stderr with a `[strict]` tag. `blockLimit` is how long code may block the isolate, 50 ms by default:

```dart
StrictConfig(enabled: true, blockLimit: Duration(milliseconds: 100))
```

A route that blocks the isolate for too long warns one time:

```text
[strict] GET /invoices/{id} blocked the isolate for 180 ms (limit 50 ms). Other requests on this isolate had to wait. Move heavy CPU work (like bcrypt, PDF or image work) to await Dox().compute(...), and use Hash.makeAsync or Hash.verifyAsync for passwords.
```

Code that blocks the event loop after an `await` warns at most one time in 10 seconds, with no name of the code:

```text
[strict] The event loop of isolate 1 was blocked for about 120 ms (limit 50 ms). Some code ran that long without an await, so other requests had to wait. Move heavy CPU work to await Dox().compute(...).
```

`Hash.make`, `Hash.verify` and `Hash.check` in the web server warn one time for each place in your code:

```text
[strict] Hash.make ran in the web server at AuthController.register (package:my_app/app/http/controllers/auth_controller.dart:21:18). It blocks the isolate while bcrypt runs, so other requests wait. Use await Hash.makeAsync(...) instead.
```

### Strict mode in the ORM

Set `strict` in `DatabaseConfig`:

```dart title="lib/config/database.dart"
DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  // ...
  strict: OrmStrict(enabled: appConfig.isDevelopment),
);
```

`nPlusOneCount` (default 5) is how many row by row loads of one relation in about one second give a warning. `maxRows` (default 1000) is how many rows `get()` or `all()` may read. The warnings have a `[db]` tag:

```text
[db] Strict mode: possible N+1 query. The relation "author" of Post was loaded row by row 5 times in a short time. Load it for all rows in one query with preload('author').
```

```text
[db] Strict mode: table "orders" read 25000 rows into memory (the limit is 1000). Use paginate(), chunk(), lazy() or cursor() for big results.
```

## Next steps

- [Performance](performance.md): the benchmark numbers.
- [Isolate](isolate.md): how Dox uses the CPU cores.
- [Cache](cache.md): keep slow results.

# Testing

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/testing/

# Testing

This page shows how to test a Dox app with the `test` package: HTTP routes, cache, storage, env and the database.

## Setup

A new app from `dox create` already has the `test` package. In another app, add it as a dev dependency:

```bash
dart pub add dev:test
```

Put your tests in the `test/` folder and run them:

```bash
dart test
```

### Creating a test

`dox make:test` writes `test/ping_test.dart`, which starts the app with a `DoxTestClient`. Add `--unit` for a plain test with no app:

```bash
dox make:test Ping
```

See [`dox make:test`](../reference/cli.md#dox-maketest).

## Test HTTP routes

`DoxTestClient` from `package:dox_core/testing.dart` starts your app inside the test and sends requests to it. Start it in `setUpAll` and close it in `tearDownAll`:

```dart title="test/http_test.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
  });

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('GET /api/ping', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.get('/api/ping');
    res.expectStatus(200).expectBody('pong');
  });
}
```

`start` runs your providers and adds your routes, like a real start. It uses one isolate on `127.0.0.1` and a free port. `close` stops the server and runs `shutdown()` of every provider.

### Making requests

The client has `get`, `post`, `put`, `patch` and `delete`. Use `send` for any other method:

```dart
await client.get('/api/users?page=2');
await client.post('/api/posts',
    body: <String, dynamic>{'title': 'Hello'});
await client.send('OPTIONS', '/api/users');
```

A map or list body goes as JSON. A string or byte list body goes as it is. The client does not follow redirects, so you can check a 302 and its `Location` header.

### Sending headers

Pass `headers` for one request. `withHeaders` gives a copy of the client that sends the headers with each request:

```dart
await client.get('/api/me',
    headers: <String, String>{'Accept-Language': 'de'});

DoxTestClient german =
    client.withHeaders(<String, String>{'Accept-Language': 'de'});
```

### Log in as a user

`withToken` gives a copy of the client that sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>`:

```dart
TestResponse login = await client.post(
  '/api/auth/login',
  body: <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com', 'password': 'secret'},
);
DoxTestClient ann = client.withToken(login.json['token'] as String);
(await ann.get('/api/auth/me')).expectStatus(200);
```

### Keep a session (cookies and CSRF)

`withSession` gives a client that works like a browser. It keeps the cookies of each response and sends the CSRF token on POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE:

```dart
test('log in with a form', () async {
  DoxTestClient browser = client.withSession();

  // the first page gives the session and XSRF-TOKEN cookies
  (await browser.get('/login')).expectStatus(200);

  (await browser.post(
    '/login',
    body: <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com', 'password': 's3'},
  )).expectStatus(303).expectHeader('location', '/dashboard');

  (await browser.get('/dashboard')).expectStatus(200);
});
```

`browser.cookies` has the kept cookies, and you can change them. The normal client keeps no cookies. To send the cookies of one response, use `withCookies(res.cookies)`.

### Testing a server that runs

Give the URL of a running server to the constructor. `baseUri` and `headers` show the URL and the headers of a client:

```dart
DoxTestClient client = DoxTestClient(Uri.parse('http://127.0.0.1:3000'));
```

## Checking the response

A `TestResponse` has the status, the body, the headers and the cookies:

```dart
int status = res.status;
String body = res.body;
List<int> bytes = res.bodyBytes;
dynamic json = res.json; // the body read as JSON
String? type = res.header('content-type'); // any case
Map<String, String> cookies = res.cookies;
```

`res.headers` has all headers, with lower case names.

### Expect methods

Each `expect` method fails the test when the response is not right. It returns the response, so you can chain them:

```dart
res
    .expectStatus(422)
    .expectHeader('content-type', contains('application/json'))
    .expectJson(<String, dynamic>{'title': 'The title is required'});
```

- `expectStatus(code)`: the failure message shows the body.
- `expectJson(value)`: a value or a matcher, like `containsPair('id', 1)`.
- `expectBody(value)`: the body as text.
- `expectHeader(name, value)`: use `isNull` for a header that must be missing.

## Test the cache

Replace `Dox().cache` with a memory store in `setUp`. `Cache()` then uses it, and each test starts with an empty cache:

```dart
setUp(() {
  Dox().cache = CacheManager(CacheConfig(
    defaultStore: 'memory',
    stores: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
      'memory': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'memory'},
    },
  ));
});

test('caches the posts', () async {
  await Cache().put('posts', <String>['a', 'b']);
  expect(await Cache().get('posts'), <dynamic>['a', 'b']);
});
```

See [Cache](cache.md).

## Test file storage

`Storage.manager.fake(name)` from `dox_storage` puts an empty memory disk in place of one disk. `restore(name)` puts the real disk back:

```dart
setUpAll(() {
  Dox().initialize(appConfig);
});

test('saves the report', () async {
  Disk fake = Storage.manager.fake('s3');

  String path = await Storage()
      .disk('s3')
      .putFile('reports', <int>[1, 2, 3], extension: 'pdf');

  expect(await fake.exists(path.substring(1)), isTrue);
  Storage.manager.restore('s3');
});
```

Call `Dox().initialize()` first, or `Storage.manager` has only the `local` disk. A `Storage()` path starts with `/` and a `Disk` key does not, so remove the first `/`.

`assertExists(key)` and `assertMissing(key)` of a disk throw a `StateError` when the check fails:

```dart
await fake.assertExists('reports/a.pdf');
```

See [File Storage](file-storage.md).

## Use a test database with `.env.testing`

Put the values for tests in a `.env.testing` file, next to `.env`:

```ini title=".env.testing"
DB_NAME=my_app_test
CACHE_STORE=memory
```

In tests (`dart test`, or `APP_ENV=testing`), Dox reads `.env` and then `.env.testing`. A key in `.env.testing` wins, and a real environment variable wins over both files.

## Test the database

Run the migrations one time in `setUpAll`. `refreshDatabase()` from `package:dox_orm/testing.dart` empties the tables before each test:

```dart title="test/user_test.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    await Migrator(
      migrations: migrations,
      config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig(),
    ).migrate();
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig); // runs the ORM provider
  });

  // every test starts with empty tables
  setUp(refreshDatabase);

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('register makes a user', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.post(
      '/api/auth/register',
      body: <String, dynamic>{
        'name': 'Ann',
        'email': 'ann@example.com',
        'password': 'secret123',
      },
    );
    res.expectStatus(201);
  });
}
```

`refreshDatabase()` empties every table and starts the ids at 1 again. It keeps the tables and the rows of the `dox_db_migration` table.

!!! warning
    `refreshDatabase()` deletes all rows. Use a separate test database, set in [`.env.testing`](#use-a-test-database-with-envtesting).

### Keeping some tables

Pass the tables that every test needs in `keep`:

```dart
refreshDatabase(keep: <String>['dox_db_migration', 'countries']);
```

See [Testing with a database](../guides/testing-with-database.md) for a full example with SQLite.

### Running test files one by one

`dart test` runs test files at the same time. When two files use the same tables, run them one by one:

```bash
dart test --concurrency=1
```

## Test the env

Give your own values to `AppEnv.load()`. Then it reads nothing from the shell or the `.env` file:

```dart
AppEnv env = AppEnv.load(
  EnvReader(
    environment: <String, String>{'APP_KEY': 'test'},
    dotEnv: <String, String>{'DB_PORT': '5433'},
  ),
);
expect(env.dbPort, 5433);
```

A missing or bad key throws an `EnvException`. A getter default that calls `Env.get()` reads the real env, so use other getters in a default. See [Environment Variables](env.md).

## Next steps

- [Testing with a database](../guides/testing-with-database.md): a full example with SQLite.
- [Cache](cache.md): the cache stores.
- [File Storage](file-storage.md): the disks.

# Health check

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/health-check/

# Health check

A health route tells a load balancer, Docker or Kubernetes if the app can serve requests.

## Setup

Add `Route.health` in a router. Use a router with no auth middleware, or the check gets 401:

```dart title="lib/routes/web.dart"
@override
void register() {
  Route.health('/health');
}
```

A GET request to `/health` gets 200 with `{"status": "ok"}`.

## Checking the database and the cache

Give named checks. A check fails when it throws, returns false or takes longer than the timeout:

```dart title="lib/routes/web.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

Route.health(
  '/health',
  checks: <String, HealthCheckFunction>{
    'database': () => QueryBuilder.query('select 1'),
    'cache': HealthCheck.cache(),
  },
);
```

When all checks pass, the answer is 200:

```json
{"status": "ok", "checks": {"database": "ok", "cache": "ok"}}
```

When one check fails, the answer is 503:

```json
{"status": "fail", "checks": {"database": "fail", "cache": "ok"}}
```

`HealthCheck.cache()` writes a key to the default cache store and reads it back. `HealthCheck.cache('redis')` checks the store with that name.

## Changing the timeout

A check fails after 5 seconds by default. Set `timeout` to change it:

```dart
Route.health(
  '/health',
  timeout: Duration(seconds: 2),
  checks: <String, HealthCheckFunction>{
    'database': () => QueryBuilder.query('select 1'),
  },
);
```

## Seeing why a check failed

The error of a failed check goes to `exceptionHandler.report()`, so it is in your logs. The answer shows the error text in `errors` only when `APP_ENV` is `development` or `local`.

## Next steps

- [Docker](../guides/docker.md): a health check in the image.
- [Deployment](deployment.md): run the app on a server.

# Database

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/database/

# Database

Connect Dox to Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB or SQLite with the `dox_orm` package.

Dox gives you two ways to work with the data:

- The [query builder](query-builder.md) builds SQL with methods, like `QueryBuilder.table('blog').where('id', 1).get()`.
- [Models](model/index.md) give you one class per table, with relations and events.

You can also run [transactions](transactions.md), and make tables with [migrations](migration.md) and the [schema builder](schema.md).

## Setup

A new app already has `dox_orm`. To add it to an app, run:

```bash
dox add orm --driver=sqlite
```

The driver is sqlite (the default), postgres or mysql. The command adds `dox_orm` and `dox_migration`, the config, the ORM provider, `bin/migrate.dart`, `db/migration/` and the `DB_*` keys in `.env`. It never overwrites a file. See [Add a package](../getting-started/add-a-package.md).

### Supported databases

| Database | `Driver` | Package | Pool | Good for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Postgres | `Driver.postgres` | [`dox_postgres_native`](postgres-native.md) | yes | production |
| MySQL 8+ and MariaDB | `Driver.mysql` | [`dox_mysql_native`](mysql-native.md) | yes | production |
| SQLite | `Driver.sqlite` | `sqlite3` | no, one connection per isolate | development, tests, small apps |

Postgres and MySQL use a native (Rust) driver. If the native library can not load, the app stops with an error. See [Postgres](postgres-native.md#when-the-library-does-not-load) and [MySQL](mysql-native.md#when-the-library-does-not-load).

## Configuration

Put your connections in `lib/config/database.dart`. `connection` is the name of the default connection:

```dart title="lib/config/database.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: env.dbConnection,
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'postgres': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.postgres,
      host: env.dbHost,
      port: env.dbPort ?? 5432,
      user: env.dbUsername,
      password: env.dbPassword,
      database: env.dbName,
      extra: <String, dynamic>{'maxConnectionCount': 10},
      debug: appConfig.isDevelopment,
    ),
    'mysql': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.mysql, // also for MariaDB
      host: env.dbHost,
      port: env.dbPort ?? 3306,
      user: env.dbUsername,
      password: env.dbPassword,
      database: env.dbName,
      extra: <String, dynamic>{'maxConnectionCount': 10},
      debug: appConfig.isDevelopment,
    ),
    'sqlite': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.sqlite,
      database: env.dbName, // file path, like db/dox.sqlite, or ':memory:'
      debug: appConfig.isDevelopment,
    ),
  },
);
```

Change `my_app` to the name of your app. With `debug` on, each query prints with its values put in:

```
▌ [db:default] SELECT * FROM "users" WHERE "email" = 'a@b.com' LIMIT 1;
```

### Connection options

| Option | What it does |
|---|---|
| `driver` | `Driver.postgres`, `Driver.mysql` or `Driver.sqlite`. |
| `host`, `port`, `user`, `password` | The server. SQLite does not use them. |
| `database` | The database name. For SQLite, the file path or `:memory:`. |
| `useSSL` | Turn on TLS. See [Postgres TLS](postgres-native.md#tls) and [MySQL](mysql-native.md). |
| `debug` | Print each query. |
| `printer` | The query printer: `PrettyQueryPrinter` (default), `ConsoleQueryPrinter`, `FileQueryPrinter` or your own `QueryPrinter`. |
| `logRedact` | Names of values to show as `***` in the log, like `['password', 'token']`. A key that ends with a name matches. |
| `slowQueryMs` | Log queries slower than this. See [Slow query log](#slow-query-log). |
| `extra` | Driver options. See [All extra options](#all-extra-options). |
| `read`, `write`, `sticky` | Read replicas. See [Read replicas](replicas.md). |
| `driverFactory` | A function that makes your own `DBDriver` from the config. |

`DatabaseConfig` also takes `url` ([`DATABASE_URL`](#database_url)), `flags` ([ORM flags](#orm-flags)) and `strict`. For `strict`, see [Strict mode in the ORM](../digging-deeper/performance-mistakes.md#strict-mode-in-the-orm).

### Environment values

The app config and the [migration](migration.md) commands read these keys from `.env`:

```py title=".env"
DB_CONNECTION=postgres # postgres, mysql or sqlite
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432           # 3306 for mysql
DB_NAME=dox            # for sqlite: the file path, like db/dox.sqlite
DB_USERNAME=postgres
DB_PASSWORD=postgres
```

### Starting the ORM

The ORM starts in a provider. The app template already has this file:

```dart title="lib/providers/orm_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';

class ORMProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig);
  }

  @override
  Future<void> shutdown() async {
    await SqlQueryBuilder.close();
  }
}
```

After you add a provider, run `dart run build_runner build`. Isolates with the same settings share one pool, so `maxConnectionCount` is for the whole process.

### `DATABASE_URL`

Many hosts give you one database url. Dox reads it from the `DATABASE_URL` key, in `.env` or in the shell. The shell wins:

```bash
DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:s%40cret@db.example.com:5432/blog?sslmode=require
```

| Form | Database |
|---|---|
| `postgres://user:pass@host:5432/db` or `postgresql://...` | Postgres |
| `mysql://user:pass@host:3306/db` or `mariadb://...` | MySQL, MariaDB |
| `sqlite:///abs/path.db`, `sqlite://db/dox.sqlite`, `sqlite::memory:`, `file:db/dox.sqlite` | SQLite |

The url replaces the config of the default connection. That config still gives `debug`, `printer`, `logRedact`, `slowQueryMs`, `extra` and the read hosts. Pass the url through the env class, so the app and `dox migrate` read the same url:

```dart title="lib/config/database.dart"
DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  url: env.databaseUrl, // String? get databaseUrl; in env.dart
  connection: env.dbConnection,
  connections: {...},
);
```

Without the `url` line, Dox reads `DATABASE_URL` only from the shell. An empty url turns it off.

- The user, password and database name are url-decoded. Write `@` in a password as `%40`.
- For Postgres, `sslmode` works like libpq. `require` does not check the certificate, so use `verify-full` when you can. See [Postgres TLS](postgres-native.md#tls).
- For MySQL, `ssl=true` turns on TLS and checks the certificate. `verifyCertificate=false` skips the check, for development only.
- Other options go to `extra`, like `?maxConnectionCount=20`.

To make one `ConnectionConfig` from a url, use `ConnectionConfig.fromUrl(url)`.

### Unix socket

A host that starts with `/` is a Unix socket:

```bash
DB_HOST=/cloudsql/my-project:europe-west1:blog
# or
DATABASE_URL=postgres://blog:secret@/blog?host=/cloudsql/my-project:europe-west1:blog
```

For Postgres, the host is the socket folder, like in libpq. For MySQL and MariaDB, the host is the socket file, like `/var/run/mysqld/mysqld.sock`. In the url, `?socket=` and `?host=` do the same.

### Pool settings

Set the pool of Postgres and MySQL in the `extra` map. A time is a `Duration` or a number of seconds:

```dart
extra: <String, dynamic>{
  'maxConnectionCount': 10,
  'requestTimeout': const Duration(seconds: 30),
  'maxConnectionAge': const Duration(minutes: 30),
  'idleTimeout': const Duration(minutes: 5),
  'serverKill': false, // MySQL only
},
```

A request is a wait for a connection, the connect and the query. A transaction with no request for the `requestTimeout` is rolled back. Set `serverKill` to false behind a proxy like ProxySQL, because the kill can reach another server.

### All extra options

| Key | Database | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `maxConnectionCount` | Postgres, MySQL | 10 | Most connections in the pool. |
| `requestTimeout` | Postgres, MySQL | 300 s | The longest time for one request. |
| `maxConnectionAge` | Postgres, MySQL | no limit on Postgres, 12 hours on MySQL | Close a connection older than this, when it has no query. |
| `idleTimeout` | Postgres, MySQL | no limit on Postgres, 12 hours on MySQL | Close a connection not used for this long. |
| `serverKill` | MySQL | true | Stop a cancelled or timed out query on the server with `KILL QUERY`. |
| `preparedStatementCacheSize` | MySQL, SQLite | 100 | Prepared statements kept per connection. |
| `sslMode` | Postgres | disable | TLS mode: disable, prefer, require, verify-ca or verify-full. |
| `sslRootCert` | Postgres | none | PEM file with the CA certificates for verify-ca and verify-full. |
| `verifyCertificate` | MySQL | true | false skips the TLS certificate check. Development only. |
| `timeZone` | Postgres | UTC | Time zone of the session. |
| `applicationName` | Postgres | none | Name of the app in `pg_stat_activity`. |
| `busyTimeout` | SQLite | 5000 | Milliseconds a query waits for a lock. |
| `background` | SQLite | false | Run the queries in a [helper isolate](#run-queries-in-a-helper-isolate). |

To stop one query, see [Cancelling a query](query-builder.md#cancelling-a-query).

## Skip unused drivers

`dox_orm` brings all three drivers, and the build downloads a native library for each. To skip the ones you do not use, add a `hooks: user_defines:` block to the root `pubspec.yaml`. A new app uses SQLite and already has this block:

```yaml title="pubspec.yaml"
hooks:
  user_defines:
    dox_postgres_native:
      skip: true
    dox_mysql_native:
      skip: true
```

For a Postgres app:

```yaml title="pubspec.yaml"
hooks:
  user_defines:
    dox_mysql_native:
      skip: true
    sqlite3:
      source: system
```

For a MySQL app:

```yaml title="pubspec.yaml"
hooks:
  user_defines:
    dox_postgres_native:
      skip: true
    sqlite3:
      source: system
```

Only the bool true skips. With `sqlite3: source: system`, the app loads the `libsqlite3` of the system. If your app opens SQLite, remove these lines, because an image without `libsqlite3` fails.

When you change the database, remove the skip line of the new driver and run `dart pub get`.

## Running raw queries

`QueryBuilder.query()` runs your own SQL. Use `@name` for values, so they are bound:

```dart
List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.query(
  'select * from blog where id = @id',
  substitutionValues: <String, dynamic>{'id': 1},
);

await QueryBuilder.query('select 1', connection: 'mysql');
```

## Using other connections

`withConnection()` runs a query on another connection from the config:

```dart
List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.table('blog')
    .withConnection('mysql')
    .get();
```

A model keeps its connection, so `save()` and `delete()` use it:

```dart
Blog blog = Blog()..withConnection('mysql');
blog.title = 'Hello';
await blog.save(); // saved on 'mysql'
```

## Listen to queries

`SqlQueryBuilder().listen()` runs your function after each query, on every connection:

```dart
void onQuery(QueryEvent e) {
  print('${e.connection} ${e.time.inMilliseconds} ms: ${e.sql}');
}

SqlQueryBuilder().listen(onQuery);
```

A `QueryEvent` has `sql`, `bindings` (with `logRedact` values as `***`), `time` and `connection`. A failed query is not sent. `SqlQueryBuilder().removeListener(onQuery)` stops it.

### Slow query log

Set `slowQueryMs` on a connection to log each query slower than that many milliseconds. It works with `debug` off:

```dart
'postgres': ConnectionConfig(
  driver: Driver.postgres,
  // ...
  debug: appConfig.isDevelopment,
  slowQueryMs: 500,
),
```

The line goes to the query printer:

```
▌ [db:postgres SLOW 812ms] SELECT * FROM "orders" WHERE "user_id" = 42;
```

Set it to 0 to log every query.

## ORM flags

`OrmFlags` turns on opt-in ORM behaviors. Each flag is off by default. Pass them as `flags` in `DatabaseConfig`:

```dart title="lib/config/database.dart"
DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: env.dbConnection,
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{ /* ... */ },
  flags: OrmFlags.all(), // every flag on
);
```

To turn on only some flags, name them:

```dart
flags: const OrmFlags(pluralTableNames: true, sumReturnsZero: true),
```

| Flag | Off (default) | On |
|---|---|---|
| `skipCleanUpdateEvents` | `save()` with no changes fires `saving`, `updating`, `updated` and `saved`. | It fires only `saving` and `saved`. A model with a `Map` or `List` field always counts as changed. |
| `belongsToKeyFromRelation` | The `belongsTo` foreign key comes from the class name: `@BelongsTo(User) User? author` uses user_id. | It comes from the relation name: author_id. |
| `pluralTableNames` | The table name is singular: `User` uses user. | It is plural: users, blog_posts, categories. A name in `@DoxModel(table: ...)` does not change. |
| `createWritesNull` | `create()` does not send a null key, so the column default is used. | It writes NULL for a null key. |
| `sumReturnsZero` | `sum()` gives null when no row matches. | It gives 0. |
| `selectRawAdds` | `selectRaw()` replaces the select list. | It adds to it. |
| `groupByAdds` | A second `groupBy()` replaces the first. | It adds to the first. `groupByRaw()` too. |
| `lastPageAtLeastOne` | `paginate()` gives `lastPage` 0 when there are no rows. | It gives 1. |
| `updateSetsUpdatedAt` | A model query `update()` does not set updated_at. | It sets updated_at, unless the data has it. |
| `incrementFiresEvents` | `increment()` and `decrement()` on a model fire no events and do not set updated_at. | They fire `saving`, `updating`, `updated` and `saved`, and set updated_at. |
| `preloadUnknownThrows` | `preload('typo')` loads nothing, with no error. | It throws an `ArgumentError`. |
| `toJsonLoadedRelations` | `toJson()` has only the relations named in `preload()`. | It also has the relations loaded with `$getRelation()`. |
| `laravelPostgresTypes` | On Postgres, `timestamps()` and `softDeletes()` make TIMESTAMPTZ, and `json()` makes JSONB. | A new table gets TIMESTAMP and JSON. |

`bin/migrate.dart` does not start the ORM, so give the flags to the migrator too: `Migrator(migrations: migrations, flags: databaseConfig.flags)`. See [Migration](migration.md#database-settings).

## SQLite

SQLite is good for development, tests and small apps. The `sqlite3` package brings SQLite with a build hook, so you do not install it.

For the AOT binary, use `dox build`. It puts the library in `build/bundle/lib/`, so keep it next to `build/bundle/bin/`. See [Deployment](../digging-deeper/deployment.md).

SQLite has no bool, JSON or date type, so Dox converts them:

- `boolean()` is saved as 0 or 1 and read back as a bool.
- `json()` is saved as text and read back as a map or a list.
- Dates are saved as ISO text in UTC and read back as a `DateTime`.

This works for columns with these type names: BOOLEAN, JSON, TIMESTAMP, DATE and DATETIME. Schema limits are in [SQLite notes](schema.md#sqlite-notes).

### Run queries in a helper isolate

A SQLite query blocks its isolate. Set `background` to true to run the queries in a helper isolate, so your isolate keeps serving requests:

```dart
'sqlite': ConnectionConfig(
  driver: Driver.sqlite,
  database: 'db/dox.sqlite',
  debug: false,
  extra: {'background': true},
),
```

With `DATABASE_URL`, add `?background=true`. Each query costs two messages, so turn it on for slow queries and leave it off for many tiny queries.

## MySQL and MariaDB

The driver is [`dox_mysql_native`](mysql-native.md). On MySQL and MariaDB, a transaction can not undo CREATE, ALTER and DROP.

## Without Dox

`dox_orm` also works on its own:

```bash
dart pub add dox_orm
```

Start it with a `DatabaseConfig`, or with your own database object: a `PgNativePool`, a `MysqlNativePool` or a SQLite `Database`:

```dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig);
// or
SqlQueryBuilder.initialize(database: db, driver: Driver.sqlite);
```

`initialize` also takes `debug`, `printer`, `flags` and `strict`. Call `await SqlQueryBuilder.close()` to close the connections.

## Next steps

- [Query Builder](query-builder.md): write queries.
- [Model](model/index.md): work with rows as objects.
- [Migration](migration.md): create and change tables.
