# GraphQL

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/packages/graphql/

# GraphQL

GraphQL makes an API for your app from your models. You add annotations to a model, run the builder, and the API is ready.

A GraphQL API has one URL. The client writes the fields that it wants, and it gets JSON with only those fields. To learn GraphQL, read [graphql.org/learn](https://graphql.org/learn/).

## Setup

Run the setup command in your app:

```bash
dox add graphql
```

The command adds the packages, `lib/config/graphql.dart` and `lib/providers/graphql_provider.dart`. It does not overwrite a file. For an app with no models, see [Without the ORM](#without-the-orm).

### Configuration

All settings are fields of `GraphQLConfig` in `lib/config/graphql.dart`. Set only the settings that you want to change:

```dart title="lib/config/graphql.dart"
GraphQLConfig graphqlConfig = GraphQLConfig(
  schema: graphqlSchema,
  path: '/api/graphql',
);
```

| Setting | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `path` | `/graphql` | The URL of the API. |
| `middleware` | none | Route middleware, like `AuthMiddleware()`. |
| `graphiql` | on in development | The GraphiQL page. |
| `introspection` | on in development | Lets tools like GraphiQL read the list of your types and fields. |
| `showInternalErrors` | on in development | Sends the real text of an error to the client. |
| `rules` | none | More validation rules, run after the rules of the GraphQL spec. |
| `maxDepth` | `64` | How deep a query can nest fields. |
| `maxQueryLength` | `1000000` | The most characters in the text of one query. |
| `maxFields` | `20000` | The most fields one query can ask for. |
| `maxNodes` | `100000` | The most values one request can load. |
| `maxRootFields` | `50` | The most top-level fields in one request. Each alias counts. |
| `maxRelationRows` | `50000` | The most rows that one list relation can load for all parent rows together. |
| `maxErrors` | `100` | The most errors in one result. After it, the fields that start give null. |

"On in development" means on when `APP_ENV` is `development`. A request that is larger than a `max` setting gets an error.

## Add a model to the API

Put `@GraphQL()` on a model. Then add one annotation for each operation that a client can use:

```dart title="lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart"
@DoxModel()
@GraphQL()
@GraphQLAll()
@GraphQLFind()
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  @Column()
  int? userId;

  @BelongsTo(User)
  User? user;
}
```

`@GraphQLAll()` adds the `posts` query, and `@GraphQLFind()` adds the `post` query. An operation with no annotation does not exist.

The `id`, the columns and the relations of the model are fields that a client can ask for. `Post` has a relation to `User`, so put `@GraphQL()` on `User` also.

Run the builder, and start the app again. Do these two steps after each change to an annotation:

```bash
dart run build_runner build
```

## Run a query

A query is a request that reads data. In development, open `http://localhost:3000/graphql` in a browser. This URL shows GraphiQL, a page where you write and run queries:

```graphql
{
  posts(limit: 10) {
    title
    user { name }
  }
}
```

The result has the same shape as the query:

```json
{ "data": { "posts": [{ "title": "Hello GraphQL", "user": { "name": "Ada" } }] } }
```

Dox loads the users of all ten posts with one database query.

Your client sends the same query as a POST request to `/graphql`. The JSON body is `{"query": "..."}`. A query can also come as a GET request, with `query` in the URL. A mutation needs POST.

## All operations

Each annotation adds one query or one mutation. A mutation is a request that changes data.

| Annotation | GraphQL field | Function |
|---|---|---|
| `@GraphQLAll()` | `posts(limit, offset)` | Reads a list. |
| `@GraphQLPaginate()` | `posts(first, page)` | Reads a page of a list, with the total number of rows. |
| `@GraphQLFind()` | `post(id)` | Reads one row. |
| `@GraphQLCreate(dto:)` | `createPost(input)` | Adds a row. |
| `@GraphQLUpdate(dto:)` | `updatePost(id, input)` | Changes a row. |
| `@GraphQLDelete()` | `deletePost(id)` | Removes a row. |

Create and update use a [DTO](../the-basic/dto.md), so the input gets the same validation as your HTTP routes. For each annotation, see [Model annotations](#model-annotations).

## Write your own query

Write your own query when the annotations are not sufficient, for example for a search. Put `@GraphQLQuery()` on a method of a class in `lib/`:

```dart title="lib/app/graphql/post.resolver.dart"
class PostResolver {
  @GraphQLQuery()
  Future<List<Post>> latestPosts({int limit = 10}) {
    return Post().orderBy('id', 'desc').limit(limit).get();
  }
}
```

The method name is the query name, and the parameters are the values that a client can send:

```graphql
{ latestPosts(limit: 3) { title } }
```

For more, see [Your own resolvers](#your-own-resolvers).

## Protect the API

By default, all clients can use all operations. Set `guard: true` on an operation that a guest must not use. Give an ability with `can:`, and Dox asks the [policy](../security/authorization.md#writing-policies) of the model before the operation runs:

```dart title="lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart"
@DoxModel()
@GraphQL(filter: Ability.view)
@GraphQLAll(can: Ability.viewAny)
@GraphQLFind(can: Ability.view)
@GraphQLCreate(
    dto: PostInput, can: Ability.create, guard: true, owner: 'userId')
@GraphQLUpdate(dto: PostInput, can: Ability.update, guard: true)
@GraphQLDelete(can: Ability.delete, guard: true)
class Post extends PostGenerator {}
```

- `guard: true` makes the operation need a login.
- `can:` asks the policy if the user can do the operation.
- `filter:` hides the rows that the user cannot read.
- `owner: 'userId'` sets the owner of a new row to the logged-in user.

A guest that Dox refuses gets the error `UNAUTHENTICATED`. A user that Dox refuses gets the error `FORBIDDEN`. The other fields of the request still give their data.

To set this up, see [Authentication](#authentication) and [Authorization](#authorization).

## Production defaults and limits

In production, GraphiQL and introspection are off, and error details stay on the server. You do not set anything for this.

Limits stop a very large query before it causes much work on your server. For example, a query can nest 64 levels, and a list gives a maximum of 100 rows. Set lower limits when your API is open to the public:

```dart title="lib/config/graphql.dart"
GraphQLConfig graphqlConfig = GraphQLConfig(
  schema: graphqlSchema,
  maxDepth: 10,
  maxNodes: 10000,
);
```

For all settings, see [Configuration](#configuration).

## Model annotations

Each annotation can have these options:

| Option | Function |
|---|---|
| `name:` | A different name for the type or the field. |
| `description:` | The text that GraphiQL shows. |
| `guard: true` | A client must log in. See [Authentication](#authentication). |
| `can:` | The policy must allow the user. `@GraphQL` does not have this option. See [Authorization](#authorization). |

### @GraphQL

Use it to make the model a type of the API. All other model annotations need it.

```dart
@GraphQL()
```

A model with only `@GraphQL()` has no queries and no mutations. A client gets it only through a relation, for example `post.user`.

Dox does not show the fields in the `hidden` list of the model, so a password stays on the server. To hide a different field, put `@GraphQLIgnore()` above its `@Column()`.

A field can be a `String`, `int`, `double`, `bool`, `DateTime`, an enum, a `@GraphQL` class, or a `List` of them. A different type stops the build, so put `@GraphQLIgnore()` on a field that the API does not need.

To make a getter a field, put `@GraphQLField()` on it. It has `name:`, `description:`, `deprecationReason:` and `guard: true`:

```dart
@GraphQLField()
String get fullName => '$firstName $lastName';
```

`@GraphQL` also has `filter:`. See [Hide rows](#hide-rows).

### @GraphQLAll

Use it when a client must read a list with `limit` and `offset`:

```dart
@GraphQLAll()
```

```graphql
{ posts(limit: 10, offset: 20) { title } }
```

The default `limit` is `20`. A `limit` of more than `100` gives an error.

### @GraphQLPaginate

Use it when a client shows pages and needs the total number of rows. The client sends `first`, which is the number of rows on a page, and `page`:

```dart
@GraphQLPaginate()
```

```graphql
{
  posts(first: 10, page: 2) {
    data { title }
    paginatorInfo { total currentPage lastPage hasMorePages }
  }
}
```

```json
{
  "data": {
    "posts": {
      "data": [{ "title": "Hello GraphQL" }],
      "paginatorInfo": { "total": 11, "currentPage": 2, "lastPage": 2, "hasMorePages": false }
    }
  }
}
```

The default `first` is `20`, and the default `page` is `1`. A `first` of more than `100` gives an error.

`data` has the rows of the page. `paginatorInfo` has these fields:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| `total` | The number of rows on all pages. |
| `count` | The number of rows on this page. |
| `perPage` | The value of `first`. |
| `currentPage` | The number of this page. |
| `lastPage` | The number of the last page. |
| `hasMorePages` | `true` if there is a page after this page. |
| `firstItem` | The number of the first row of this page. The first row of page 1 is `1`. `null` on an empty page. |
| `lastItem` | The number of the last row of this page. `null` on an empty page. |

If the model also has `@GraphQLAll()`, the list is `posts` and the paged list is `postsPaginate`. To set a different name, use `name:`:

```dart
@GraphQLPaginate(name: 'postPages')
```

### @GraphQLFind

Use it when a client must read one row by its id:

```dart
@GraphQLFind()
```

```graphql
{ post(id: 1) { title } }
```

The result is `null` if no row has that id.

### @GraphQLCreate

Use it to let a client add a row. First, write a [DTO](../the-basic/dto.md) with the fields that the client can set:

```dart title="lib/app/dtos/post_input/post_input.dto.dart"
@Dto()
class PostInput {
  PostInput({required this.title});

  @MinLength(3, message: 'The title is too short')
  final String title;
}
```

Then give the DTO to the annotation:

```dart
@GraphQLCreate(dto: PostInput)
```

```graphql
mutation {
  createPost(input: { title: "My second post" }) { id title }
}
```

A client can set only the fields of the DTO. Thus, a client cannot set a different column, for example `userId`.

Dox applies the rules of the DTO before it saves the row. If the input is not correct, Dox saves nothing. The client gets the error `VALIDATION_FAILED`, with the message for each field in `extensions.fields`.

### Set the owner of a new row

Use `owner:` when each row belongs to the user that made it. Dox sets that column to the id of the logged-in user:

```dart
@GraphQLCreate(dto: PostInput, owner: 'userId')
```

With `owner:`, the client must log in to create a row. The owner column must not be a field of the DTO. An update never changes the owner column.

### @GraphQLUpdate

Use it to let a client change a row. It can use the same DTO as `@GraphQLCreate`:

```dart
@GraphQLUpdate(dto: PostInput, can: Ability.update, guard: true)
```

```graphql
mutation { updatePost(id: 1, input: { title: "A better title" }) { title } }
```

`updatePost` changes only the fields that the client sends, and Dox applies only the rules of those fields. The result is `null` if no row has that id.

!!! warning

    Without `can:`, each client that can call `updatePost` or `deletePost` can change or delete each row. Add `can:` to `@GraphQLUpdate` and `@GraphQLDelete`. The builder shows a warning if one of them has no `can:` and no `guard:`.

### @GraphQLDelete

Use it to let a client remove a row. It needs no DTO:

```dart
@GraphQLDelete(can: Ability.delete, guard: true)
```

```graphql
mutation { deletePost(id: 1) }
```

The result is `true`, or `false` if no row has that id.

## Authentication

Use `guard: true` when a client must log in. If your app does not have a login, set it up first with [`dox add auth`](../security/authentication.md).

Add `AuthMiddleware()` to the config. Dox uses it to read the user:

```dart title="lib/config/graphql.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_graphql/dox_graphql.dart';
import 'package:my_app/generated/schema.g.dart';

GraphQLConfig graphqlConfig = GraphQLConfig(
  schema: graphqlSchema,
  middleware: <Object>[AuthMiddleware()],
);
```

The middleware does not stop a request. All fields stay public until you add `guard: true`. The client sends its token in the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header, as usual.

If you use a subclass of `AuthMiddleware`, override `asOptional()` to return your subclass. Else your changes do not run.

### Make a query or mutation need a login

Set `guard: true` on each operation that a guest must not use:

```dart title="lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart"
@DoxModel()
@GraphQL()
@GraphQLAll()
@GraphQLFind()
@GraphQLCreate(dto: PostInput, guard: true)
@GraphQLUpdate(dto: PostInput, guard: true)
@GraphQLDelete(guard: true)
class Post extends PostGenerator {}
```

Here, a guest can read posts, but only a logged-in user can change them.

If a guest asks for a guarded field, the guest gets the error `UNAUTHENTICATED` for that field. The other fields in the same request still give their data.

`guard: true` needs `AuthMiddleware()` in the config. Without it, the app stops at start and shows the name of the type or field.

### Protect a model everywhere

Write `@GraphQL(guard: true)` on a model that a guest must never see, for example `User`:

```dart title="lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart"
@DoxModel()
@GraphQL(guard: true)
@GraphQLFind()
class User extends UserGenerator {}
```

Then each field that gives a user needs a login. This includes its queries, its mutations, each relation such as `post.user`, and your own resolvers.

### Read the logged-in user

Add a `DoxGraphQLContext` parameter to a resolver method. The client does not send this value. Dox puts the current request in it:

```dart title="lib/app/graphql/user.resolver.dart"
@GraphQLQuery()
Future<User?> me(DoxGraphQLContext context) {
  return context.user<User>();
}
```

`context.user<User>()` gives null for a guest. The context also has these members:

- `context.auth()` gives the `IAuth` of the login, or null.
- `context.make<T>()` gives a service from the container.
- `context.request` is the `DoxRequest`.
- `context.loader` gives a `DataLoader` of the request, see [Without the ORM](#without-the-orm).

## Authorization

`guard: true` is only a login check. Use a [policy](../security/authorization.md#writing-policies) when the answer is different for each user or each row.

### Write a policy

A policy is a class with one method for each rule. The `abilities` map gives a name to each method. This name is the ability. `Ability` has the usual names: `viewAny`, `view`, `create`, `update` and `delete`.

```dart title="lib/app/policies/post_policy.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/post/post.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

class PostPolicy extends Policy<User, Post> {
  bool update(User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id;

  @override
  Map<String, Function> get abilities => <String, Function>{
    Ability.update: update,
  };
}
```

Each ability section below adds one method to this policy. Add each new method to `abilities` also.

### Register the policy

Register the policy in the `setup()` of a provider. `dox add graphql` made the GraphQL provider, so you can use it. Keep the `super.setup()` call:

```dart title="lib/providers/graphql_provider.dart"
class AppGraphQLProvider extends GraphQLProvider {
  AppGraphQLProvider() : super(graphqlConfig);

  @override
  void setup() {
    Gate.policy<Post>(PostPolicy());
    super.setup();
  }
}
```

The config must have `AuthMiddleware()`. Without it, Dox cannot read the user, and each client is a guest.

When the app starts, Dox makes sure that the policy has each ability of `can:` and `filter:`. If one is missing, the app stops with an error that shows the available abilities:

```text
@GraphQLDelete(can: 'delete') on Post: PostPolicy has no ability 'delete'. Available: update.
```

### Use it on a model

Give an ability to an operation with `can:`. Dox asks the policy before the operation runs. An operation with no `can:` does not ask the policy.

```dart title="lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart"
@DoxModel()
@GraphQL(filter: Ability.view)
@GraphQLAll(can: Ability.viewAny)
@GraphQLPaginate(can: Ability.viewAny)
@GraphQLFind(can: Ability.view)
@GraphQLCreate(
    dto: PostInput, can: Ability.create, guard: true, owner: 'userId')
@GraphQLUpdate(dto: PostInput, can: Ability.update, guard: true)
@GraphQLDelete(can: Ability.delete, guard: true)
class Post extends PostGenerator {}
```

Some policy methods get a row, and some do not:

| Annotation | The policy method gets | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `@GraphQLAll(can:)`, `@GraphQLPaginate(can:)` | The user. | `Ability.viewAny` |
| `@GraphQLCreate(can:)` | The user. | `Ability.create` |
| `@GraphQLFind(can:)` | The user and the row. | `Ability.view` |
| `@GraphQLUpdate(can:)` | The user and the row. | `Ability.update` |
| `@GraphQLDelete(can:)` | The user and the row. | `Ability.delete` |
| `@GraphQL(filter:)` | The user and each row. | `Ability.view` |

Do not use an ability that needs a row, like `Ability.view`, on `@GraphQLAll`, `@GraphQLPaginate` or `@GraphQLCreate`.

When the policy refuses a user, the field is `null`. The other fields keep their data:

```json
{ "data": { "posts": null, "me": { "name": "Ada" } } }
```

The `errors` list of the result has one error for `posts`. Its code is `FORBIDDEN`, in `extensions.code`.

For an id that does not exist, Dox asks the policy about an empty row, so a refused user gets `FORBIDDEN` for each id. If your policy method allows an empty row, a client can find which ids exist.

### viewAny

Use `viewAny` when some users must not get lists of the model:

```dart
@GraphQLAll(can: Ability.viewAny)
```

```dart
bool viewAny(User user) => user.banned != true;
```

### view

Use `view` when a user can read some rows and not others. Here, a user can read a published post and their own posts:

```dart
@GraphQLFind(can: Ability.view)
```

```dart
bool view(User user, Post post) {
  return post.status == 'published' || post.userId == user.id;
}
```

A refused user gets `FORBIDDEN` from `post(id)`.

### Hide rows

Use `filter:` on `@GraphQL` when a client must get only the rows that the user can read:

```dart
@GraphQL(filter: Ability.view)
```

Dox hides each row that the ability refuses, and gives no error. This applies to each field that gives the model:

- A list, a paged list, or a list relation such as `user.posts` does not include the row. Thus, a list can have fewer rows than `limit`.
- `post(id)` or a single relation such as `comment.post` gives `null`.
- Your own queries, mutations and fields that return the model do the same.

!!! warning

    `filter:` does not decide who can change a row. `updatePost` and `deletePost` ask only their `can:`. Give them a `can:`.

To get null and no error from `post(id)`, use `filter:` and no `can:` on `@GraphQLFind`.

- In a paged list, `data` and `count` do not include the hidden rows, but `total` and `lastPage` include them.
- `createPost` always gives the new row. `updatePost` saves a hidden row, but its result is null.
- A field can give a filtered model as `Post`, `Post?`, `List<Post>` or `List<Post>?`. A different shape stops the build.

### create

Use `create` when only some users can add a row. The method gets only the user, because no row exists yet:

```dart
@GraphQLCreate(dto: PostInput, can: Ability.create)
```

```dart
bool create(User user) => user.verified == true;
```

Dox asks the policy first. It applies the rules of the DTO only for a user that the policy allows. For a refused user, Dox saves nothing.

### update

Use `update` to decide who can change a row:

```dart
@GraphQLUpdate(dto: PostInput, can: Ability.update)
```

```dart
bool update(User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id;
```

For a refused user, Dox writes nothing.

### delete

Use `delete` to decide who can remove a row:

```dart
@GraphQLDelete(can: Ability.delete)
```

```dart
bool delete(User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id;
```

For a refused user, the row stays in the database.

### Add your own ability

Use your own ability when the five names of `Ability` are not sufficient. Write the name as a constant on the policy:

```dart title="lib/app/policies/post_policy.dart"
class PostPolicy extends Policy<User, Post> {
  static const String publish = 'publish';

  bool canPublish(User user, Post post) => user.editor == true;

  @override
  Map<String, Function> get abilities => <String, Function>{
    publish: canPublish,
  };
}
```

```dart
@GraphQLUpdate(dto: PostInput, can: PostPolicy.publish)
```

### Let guests in

A guest is a client that is not logged in. With `Policy<User, Post>`, Dox refuses each guest with the error `UNAUTHENTICATED`.

Use `Policy<User?, Post>` when a guest can read some rows. Then a guest gets to your methods, and `user` is `null`:

```dart
class PostPolicy extends Policy<User?, Post> {
  bool view(User? user, Post post) {
    if (post.status == 'published') return true;
    return user != null && post.userId == user.id;
  }

  @override
  Map<String, Function> get abilities =>
      <String, Function>{Ability.view: view};
}
```

Now a guest can read the published posts, and a user can also read their own drafts. To refuse guests on one operation of this model, add `guard: true` to that operation.

## Your own resolvers

A resolver is a method that gives the result of a query or a mutation. Write one when the model annotations are not sufficient. The builder finds each class in `lib/` that has a resolver method.

```dart title="lib/app/graphql/post.resolver.dart"
import 'package:dox_graphql/dox_graphql.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/post/post.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/services/post.service.dart';

class PostResolver {
  PostResolver(this.postService);

  final PostService postService;

  @GraphQLQuery()
  Future<List<Post>> trendingPosts({int limit = 10}) {
    return postService.trending(limit);
  }
}
```

Dox gets the data of the query from the method:

- The method name is the query name: `trendingPosts`.
- The parameters are the values that a client can send. A parameter with a default value is optional.
- The return type is the type that the client gets.
- Dox gets the constructor parameters from the [container](../the-basic/dependency-injection.md).

A resolver annotation has `name:`, `description:` and `guard: true`, the same as a model annotation. It also has `deprecationReason:`, which marks the field as deprecated.

### Write your own mutation

Write your own mutation when one saved row is not sufficient. Put `@GraphQLMutation()` on a resolver method, and use a DTO for the input:

```dart title="lib/app/graphql/post.resolver.dart"
@GraphQLMutation()
Future<Post> importPost(PostInput input) {
  return postService.import(input);
}
```

Dox applies the rules of the DTO before your method runs.

### Send an error to the client

To send your own message, throw a `GraphQLError`:

```dart
throw GraphQLError('This post is not published yet',
    extensions: <String, Object?>{'code': 'NOT_PUBLISHED'});
```

`extensions` is optional. For all other errors, the client sees "Internal server error" in production. Dox sends the real error to the `ExceptionHandler` of your app.

### Check a policy in a resolver

`can:` works only on the model annotations. To refuse a user in your own resolver, call [`Gate`](../security/authorization.md#checking-a-gate) yourself:

```dart title="lib/app/graphql/post.resolver.dart"
@GraphQLQuery()
Future<Post?> latestPost(DoxGraphQLContext context) async {
  Post? post = await postService.latest();
  User? user = await context.user<User>();
  if (post != null && await Gate.denies(user, Ability.view, post)) {
    throw GraphQLAuth.forbidden();
  }
  return post;
}
```

`GraphQLAuth.forbidden()` gives the same `FORBIDDEN` error as `can:`. `filter:` also hides rows in the result of your own resolvers.

## Without the ORM

If your app does not use models, install with `dox add graphql --no-orm`. Put `@GraphQL()` on a plain Dart class. Its public fields are the fields that a client can ask for. You write all the queries yourself:

```dart title="lib/app/graphql/product.resolver.dart"
@GraphQL()
class Product {
  Product({required this.id, required this.name, required this.shopId});

  final int id;
  final String name;

  @GraphQLIgnore()
  final int shopId;
}

class ProductResolver {
  ProductResolver(this.productRepository, this.shopRepository);

  final ProductRepository productRepository;
  final ShopRepository shopRepository;

  @GraphQLQuery()
  Future<List<Product>> products({int limit = 20}) {
    return productRepository.latest(limit);
  }

  @GraphQLResolveField()
  Future<Shop?> shop(Product product, DoxGraphQLContext context) {
    DataLoader<int, Shop> shops = context.loader<int, Shop>(
      'shops',
      () => DataLoader<int, Shop>(shopRepository.findByIds),
    );
    return shops.load(product.shopId);
  }
}
```

`@GraphQLResolveField()` adds a field to the class of its first parameter. Thus, `Product` gets a `shop` field, and `Shop` also needs `@GraphQL()`.

The `DataLoader` collects the shop ids of the full request. Thus, fifty products cause one shop query, not fifty queries. `findByIds` takes a `List<int>` and returns a `Future<List<Shop?>>`, in the same order as the ids.

A `DataLoader` also has these methods:

- `loadMany(ids)` loads a list of keys in the same batch.
- `prime(id, value)` puts a value in the loader, if the key is not there. Use it when you already have the row.
- `clear(id)` and `clearAll()` remove values, for example after a change.

When some keys can fail on their own, use `DataLoader.withResults`. The batch function gives one `LoadValue(value)` or `LoadError(error)` for each key:

```dart
DataLoader<int, Shop> shops = DataLoader<int, Shop>.withResults(
    (List<int> ids) async => <LoadResult<Shop>>[
          for (int id in ids) LoadValue<Shop>(await findShop(id)),
        ]);
```

`DataLoader.of(loader)` takes a class that implements `BatchLoader`.

## Performance

The same GraphQL API in Dox and in Go, on Postgres. The Dox app uses the ORM with `@GraphQLAll` and `@GraphQLFind`. The Go apps use gqlgen, one with pgx and one with GORM, and a dataloader for the relation.

All three queries at 256 connections, requests per second:

| Server               | One row by id | 20 rows | 20 rows with a relation | peak MB |
| -------------------- | ------------: | ------: | ----------------------: | ------: |
| Dox (ORM)            | 88,330        | 7,837   | 5,990                   | 223     |
| Go (gqlgen + pgx)    | 27,870        | 7,618   | 3,918                   | 132     |
| Go (gqlgen + GORM)   | 24,675        | 7,436   | 3,683                   | 105     |

- On one row by id, Dox is 3.2 times as fast as Go with pgx.
- On a list of 20 rows, all three are about the same. Postgres is the limit here.
- On a list with a relation, Dox is 1.5 times as fast.
- Dox uses more memory at the peak. After the load, its memory goes down again.

How it was run: the same rig as the [benchmark](../digging-deeper/performance.md#how-it-was-run) of the server. The server gets 2 CPUs, the database gets 2 CPUs and wrk gets the other 4. Each server has 8 database connections. Each query runs for 15 seconds, three times. The numbers are the median.

| [Custom errors](custom-errors.md) | Your own exception classes, one JSON shape for every error, logging. |
| [Background work](background-work.md) | Run work after the response, on another thread, in a queue job, or on a schedule. |

# File upload

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/guides/file-upload/

# File upload

Accept an image from a form, check its size and type, save it to a disk, and return its URL.

An uploaded file can be too big, or of a different type than its name says. So this guide checks the file in a [DTO](../the-basic/dto.md) first, and then saves it.

## What you need

- A Dox app (`dox create my_app`). A new app has the `dox_storage` package, `lib/config/storage.dart` and `lib/providers/storage_provider.dart`.

## 1. Set up the disk

Give the `local` disk a `url`. `Storage().url()` uses it to make the public URL of a file:

```dart title="lib/config/storage.dart"
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

StorageConfig storageConfig = StorageConfig(
  defaultDisk: env.storageDisk,
  disks: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
    /// uploads go to the `storage` folder.
    /// `url` is the public address of `Storage.route('files', ...)`.
    'local': <String, dynamic>{
      'driver': 'local',
      'root': 'storage',
      'url': '${env.appUrl}/files',
    },
  },
);
```

Add a getter for the new `APP_URL` key to the `AppEnv` class:

```dart title="lib/config/env.dart"
  /// the public URL of this app, used in file links
  String get appUrl => 'http://localhost:3000';
```

Run `dart run build_runner build`. Then add `APP_URL=http://localhost:3000` to your `.env`.

The provider of a new app sets up the disks. Keep it as it is:

```dart title="lib/providers/storage_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/storage.dart';

class AppStorageProvider extends StorageProvider {
  AppStorageProvider() : super(storageConfig);
}
```

## 2. Write the DTO

The DTO checks the file before the controller runs. A failed check answers 422:

```dart title="lib/app/dtos/upload_image/upload_image.dto.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'upload_image.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class UploadImage {
  /// jpg, jpeg, png, gif, webp or bmp. Dox reads the first bytes of the
  /// file to find the real type. The file name is not trusted.
  @Image()
  @MaxSize('5MB')
  final RequestFile image;

  const UploadImage({required this.image});

  static const DtoSchema<UploadImage> schema = $UploadImageDto;
}
```

For other file types, use `@Mimes(<String>['pdf', 'docx'])` in place of `@Image()`.

## 3. Write the controller

Save the file with `putFile`, and return its path and URL. `putFile` gives the file a new UUID name:

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/upload.controller.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/upload_image/upload_image.dto.dart';

@Inject()
class UploadController {
  /// POST /api/upload (multipart/form-data, field `image`)
  Future<Map<String, String>> store(UploadImage body) async {
    // saves the file as /images/<uuid>.<ext> on the default disk
    String path = await Storage().putFile('images', body.image);
    String url = await Storage().url(path);
    return <String, String>{'path': path, 'url': url};
  }
}
```

!!! warning "Save the file before you return"
    Dox deletes the uploaded temp file when it sends the response.
    So call `putFile`, `store` or `moveTo` in the controller, not later.

## 4. Add the routes

One route takes the upload. `Storage.route` serves the saved files at `/files/{key*}`:

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/upload.controller.dart';

class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.post('/upload', (UploadController c) => c.store);
  }
}
```

```dart title="lib/routes/web.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';

class WebRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    // GET /files/{key*}, any file of the default disk
    Storage.route('files', signed: false);
  }
}
```

`signed: false` makes every file public. For private files, leave it out and use `Storage().signedUrl(path)` in place of `Storage().url(path)`.

## 5. Register the DTOs

Add the `dtos` list that `build_runner` writes. Skip this step if your `app.dart` already has `dtos: dtos`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
import 'package:my_app/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  dtos: dtos,
  // ...
);
```

## 6. Build and run

Build the code and start the server:

```bash
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
dox serve
```

## Check it

Upload a PNG:

```bash
curl -F image=@photo.png http://localhost:3000/api/upload
```

```json
{
  "path": "/images/074aa0d0-ce21-11f1-938a-57265e28c4a3.png",
  "url": "http://localhost:3000/files/images/074aa0d0-ce21-11f1-938a-57265e28c4a3.png"
}
```

Open the URL in the browser. The image shows.

Now upload a text file. You get 422:

```bash
curl -F image=@notes.txt http://localhost:3000/api/upload
```

```json
{"image":"The image must be an image"}
```

With no file, you also get 422, with `{"image":"The image is required"}`.

## Bigger files

A multipart body can be 100 MB by default. To change the limit, set `maxMultipartSize` in `AppConfig`. Set the same limit in your proxy too, like `client_max_body_size` in nginx.

## Next steps

- [Request: form data](../the-basic/request.md#form-data-file): read a `RequestFile`.
- [Validation rules: files](../the-basic/validation-rules.md#files): all the file rules.
- [File storage](../digging-deeper/file-storage.md): S3 and signed URLs.

# Pagination

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/guides/pagination/

# Pagination

Make a list route that takes `page` and `per_page` from the query string and returns one page of rows.

A table can have many thousands of rows, so the client asks for one page at a time.

## What you need

- A Dox app (`dox create my_app`). A new app has a database (SQLite), a `User` model and a `users` table.

## 1. Write the query DTO

The [DTO](../the-basic/dto.md) reads and checks `page` and `per_page`. With `source: Source.query`, it reads the query string, not the body:

```dart title="lib/app/dtos/list_users/list_users.dto.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'list_users.dto.g.dart';

/// GET /api/users?page=2&per_page=10
@Dto(source: Source.query)
class ListUsers {
  @Min(1)
  final int page;

  @Range(1, 100)
  final int perPage; // query key: per_page

  const ListUsers({this.page = 1, this.perPage = 20});

  static const DtoSchema<ListUsers> schema = $ListUsersDto;
}
```

Both fields have a default, so the client can leave them out. The field `perPage` reads the key `per_page`.

## 2. Write the controller

`paginate()` returns a `Pagination`. Return it as it is, and Dox sends its `toJson()`:

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/list_users/list_users.dto.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class UserController {
  /// GET /api/users?page=1&per_page=20
  Future<Pagination<User>> index(ListUsers query) async {
    return User()
        .orderBy('id', 'desc')
        .paginate(currentPage: query.page, perPage: query.perPage);
  }
}
```

Always add an `orderBy`. Without it, a row can show on two pages, or on none. To filter the rows, add a `where` before `paginate`.

## 3. Add the route

Add the list route to the API router:

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
Route.get('/users', (UserController c) => c.index);
```

## 4. Register the DTOs

Add the `dtos` list that `build_runner` writes. Skip this step if your `app.dart` already has `dtos: dtos`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
import 'package:my_app/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  dtos: dtos,
  // ...
);
```

## 5. Build and run

Build the code and start the server:

```bash
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
dox serve
```

## Check it

Ask for page 2, with 2 rows per page. With 3 users in the table, you get one user:

```bash
curl 'http://localhost:3000/api/users?page=2&per_page=2'
```

```json
{
  "total": 3,
  "per_page": 2,
  "last_page": 2,
  "current_page": 2,
  "data": [
    {
      "id": 1,
      "name": "User 1",
      "email": "user1@example.com",
      "created_at": "2026-10-22T14:01:07.843207Z",
      "updated_at": "2026-10-22T14:01:07.843207Z"
    }
  ]
}
```

The keys of the response are:

| Key | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `total` | rows that match the query, on all pages |
| `per_page` | rows per page |
| `last_page` | the number of the last page |
| `current_page` | the page you asked for |
| `data` | the rows of this page, from `toJson()` of the model |

A page after the last one gives an empty list in `data`.

Bad input gets 422:

```bash
curl 'http://localhost:3000/api/users?page=0&per_page=500'
```

```json
{
  "page": "The page must be greater than or equal 1",
  "per_page": "The per_page must be between 1 and 100"
}
```

## Change the shape of a row

To send only some fields, pass the rows to a serializer. Make one with `dox make:serializer User`. `page.data` gives the typed rows:

```dart
Future<Map<String, dynamic>> index(ListUsers query) async {
  Pagination<User> page = await User()
      .orderBy('id', 'desc')
      .paginate(currentPage: query.page, perPage: query.perPage);
  return <String, dynamic>{
    ...page.toJson(),
    'data': UserSerializer(page.data).toJson(),
  };
}
```

## Next steps

- [Query builder: paginate](../database/query-builder.md#paginating-results): all the paginate options.
- [DTOs: body and query string](../the-basic/dto.md#body-and-query-string): read the query string.
- [Serializer](../the-basic/serializer.md): change the shape of a model.

# JWT authentication

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/guides/jwt-auth/

# JWT authentication

Let users register and log in, give them a JWT token, protect routes with it, and read the user in a controller.

A JWT token is good for an API that a mobile app or a single page app calls. The client sends the token with every request, so the server needs no session.

## What you need

- A Dox app (`dox create my_app`). A new app has a database (SQLite), a `User` model and a `users` table with `name`, `email` and `password` columns.
- The `dox_auth` package. Add it:

```bash
dart pub add dox_auth
```

## 1. Hide the password in the model

Anyone with the token can read the user in it. So put the password in `hidden`. The model of a new app already does this:

```dart title="lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel(table: 'users', softDelete: true)
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @override
  List<String> get hidden => <String>['password'];

  @Column()
  String? name;

  @Column()
  String? email;

  @Column()
  String? password;
}
```

## 2. Set up the auth provider

The provider tells Dox how to make and check tokens, and how to find the user. Dox finds the provider by itself:

```dart title="lib/providers/auth_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

class AppAuthProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Auth.initialize(
      AuthConfig(
        defaultGuard: 'api',
        guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
          'api': AuthGuard(
            driver: JwtAuthDriver(
              // APP_KEY signs the tokens. A new key logs every user out.
              secret: SecretKey(env.appKey),
              // a token stops working after this time
              expiresIn: const Duration(days: 7),
            ),
            provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
          ),
        },
      ),
    );
  }
}
```

The secret must have at least 32 bytes, like a key from `dox key:generate`. A shorter secret stops the app in production.

## 3. Write the DTOs

Write one DTO for register and one for login. `@Unique` comes from `dox_orm`, so hide the `Schema` class of `dox_orm` in the import:

```dart title="lib/app/dtos/register_user/register_user.dto.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart' hide Schema;

part 'register_user.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class RegisterUser {
  @Length(min: 2, max: 50)
  @Trim()
  final String name;

  @Trim()
  @Lowercase()
  @Email()
  @Unique('users', column: 'email')
  final String email;

  @MinLength(8)
  final String password;

  const RegisterUser({
    required this.name,
    required this.email,
    required this.password,
  });

  static const DtoSchema<RegisterUser> schema = $RegisterUserDto;
}
```

```dart title="lib/app/dtos/login_user/login_user.dto.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'login_user.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class LoginUser {
  @Trim()
  @Lowercase()
  @Email()
  final String email;

  final String password;

  const LoginUser({required this.email, required this.password});

  static const DtoSchema<LoginUser> schema = $LoginUserDto;
}
```

## 4. Write the controller

The controller makes the user, logs in, and returns the user of a token:

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/auth.controller.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/login_user/login_user.dto.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/register_user/register_user.dto.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class AuthController {
  /// POST /api/auth/register
  Future<Map<String, dynamic>> register(RegisterUser body) async {
    User user = User()
      ..name = body.name
      ..email = body.email
      ..password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
    await user.save();

    String? token = Auth().login(user);
    return <String, dynamic>{'token': token, 'user': user};
  }

  /// POST /api/auth/login
  Future<Map<String, dynamic>> login(LoginUser body) async {
    Auth auth = Auth();
    String? token = await auth.attempt(<String, dynamic>{
      'email': body.email,
      'password': body.password,
    });
    if (token == null) {
      throw UnAuthorizedException(message: 'Wrong email or password');
    }
    return <String, dynamic>{'token': token, 'user': auth.user<User>()};
  }

  /// GET /api/auth/me (behind AuthMiddleware)
  User? me(DoxRequest req) {
    return req.auth?.user<User>();
  }

  /// POST /api/auth/logout (behind AuthMiddleware)
  /// By default a JWT is not cancelled on the server. The client deletes
  /// the token, and it still works until `expiresIn` passes. To cancel it,
  /// turn on revocation and call `Auth().revokeToken(req)`.
  Map<String, String> logout(DoxRequest req) {
    return <String, String>{'message': 'Delete the token on the client'};
  }
}
```

`auth.attempt` finds the user by email and checks the password hash. It returns null if the email or the password is wrong.

## 5. Add the routes

Put every protected route inside `AuthMiddleware`. It reads the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header. A missing or bad token gets 401:

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/auth.controller.dart';

class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.post('/auth/register', (AuthController c) => c.register);
    Route.post('/auth/login', (AuthController c) => c.login);

    Route.middleware(<dynamic>[AuthMiddleware()], () {
      Route.get('/auth/me', (AuthController c) => c.me);
      Route.post('/auth/logout', (AuthController c) => c.logout);
      // put every protected route here
    });
  }
}
```

## 6. Register the DTOs

Add the `dtos` list that `build_runner` writes. Skip this step if your `app.dart` already has `dtos: dtos`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
import 'package:my_app/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  dtos: dtos,
  // ...
);
```

## 7. Build and run

Build the code and start the server:

```bash
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
dox serve
```

## Check it

Register a user. You get a token and the user:

```bash
curl -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Ann","email":"ann@example.com","password":"secret123"}' \
  http://localhost:3000/api/auth/register
```

```json
{
  "token": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...",
  "user": {
    "id": 1,
    "name": "Ann",
    "email": "ann@example.com",
    "created_at": "...",
    "updated_at": "..."
  }
}
```

A login with a wrong password gets 401:

```json
{"error":{"code":"unauthorized","message":"Wrong email or password"}}
```

Now log in and use the token:

```bash
TOKEN=$(curl -s -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"ann@example.com","password":"secret123"}' \
  http://localhost:3000/api/auth/login | jq -r .token)

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://localhost:3000/api/auth/me
```

```json
{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "Ann",
  "email": "ann@example.com",
  "created_at": "...",
  "updated_at": "..."
}
```

Without the header, you get 401 with "Authentication failed".

The `{"error": ...}` shape comes from the handler in [Custom errors](custom-errors.md). Without it, the body is `{"code":"unauthorized","message":"Wrong email or password"}`.

## Logout and expiry

By default the server can not cancel one token. You can do this:

| You want | Do this |
| --- | --- |
| Log out on this device | The client deletes the token. That is all `logout` does. |
| Limit the damage of a stolen token | Keep `expiresIn` short, for example `Duration(hours: 12)`. |
| Log every user out at once | Change `APP_KEY`. Every old token stops working. |
| Block one user | Delete the user. `AuthMiddleware` loads the user on each request, so a deleted user gets 401. |

To cancel one token, or all tokens of a user, turn on [revocation](../security/authentication.md#revoke-tokens). Or use [access tokens](../security/authentication.md#access-tokens).

## Next steps

- [Authentication](../security/authentication.md): all the options of the guards and drivers.
- [Hashing](../security/hashing.md): make and check password hashes.
- [Middleware](../the-basic/middleware.md): run code before a route.

# Custom errors

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/guides/custom-errors/

# Custom errors

Give your app its own exception classes, send every error in one JSON shape, and log the unexpected ones.

A client is easier to write when every error has the same shape.

## What you need

- A Dox app.

## How Dox handles an error

This is what Dox does when a controller or a middleware throws:

| Error | Status | What Dox does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| an `IHttpException`, like `NotFoundHttpException` | its `code` | sends `{"code": ..., "message": ...}` |
| a validation error (bad DTO input) | 422 | sends the field errors: `{"field": "message"}` |
| any other exception or error | 500 | sends `{"code":"server_error","message":"Server Error"}`, or the error text when `APP_ENV` is development or local. Calls `report` |

`report` is a method of the [exception handler](../the-basic/errors.md). The `responseHandler` of `AppConfig` sees every response last, so this guide sets the error shape there.

## 1. Write your own exceptions

For a quick error, use `abort(403)` or `abort(409, 'The email is taken')`. See [HTTP exceptions](../reference/http-exceptions.md#any-status-abort-and-httpstatusexception).

For an error you throw in many places, extend `IHttpException`. Set `code` (the HTTP status), `errorCode` (a short text for the client) and `message`:

```dart title="lib/app/exceptions/app_exception.dart"
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// 409. Thrown when the row already exists or was changed by someone else.
class ConflictException extends IHttpException {
  ConflictException({String message = 'Conflict'}) {
    super.code = HttpStatus.conflict;
    super.errorCode = 'conflict';
    super.message = message;
  }
}
```

Throw them anywhere in a controller, a middleware or a service:

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/exceptions/app_exception.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class UserController {
  /// GET /api/users/{id}
  Future<User> show(int id) async {
    User? user = await User().find(id);
    if (user == null) {
      throw NotFoundHttpException(message: 'User $id not found');
    }
    return user;
  }

  /// DELETE /api/users/{id}
  Future<Map<String, bool>> destroy(int id) async {
    if (id == 1) {
      throw ForbiddenHttpException(
          message: 'The first user can not be deleted');
    }
    User user = await show(id);

    /// 0 rows: the user was deleted after show() found it
    if (await user.delete() == 0) {
      throw NotFoundHttpException(message: 'User $id not found');
    }
    return <String, bool>{'deleted': true};
  }
}
```

## 2. One JSON shape for every error

For an error, the content of the response is the exception. Turn it into your shape in the response handler:

```dart title="lib/app/http/response_handler.dart"
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// Gives every error the same JSON shape:
/// `{"error": {"code": "not_found", "message": "..."}}`.
/// A validation error (422) also has `"errors": {field: message}`.
class ResponseHandler extends ResponseHandlerInterface {
  @override
  DoxResponse handle(DoxResponse res) {
    dynamic content = res.getContent();

    if (content is ValidationException) {
      return res.statusCode(content.code).content(<String, dynamic>{
        'error': <String, dynamic>{
          'code': content.errorCode,
          'message': 'The input is not valid',
        },
        'errors': content.message,
      });
    }

    if (content is IHttpException) {
      return res.statusCode(content.code).content(<String, dynamic>{
        'error': <String, dynamic>{
          'code': content.errorCode,
          'message': content.message.toString(),
        },
      });
    }

    // any other exception: hide the details from the client
    if (content is Exception || content is Error) {
      return res.statusCode(HttpStatus.internalServerError).content(
        <String, dynamic>{
          'error': <String, String>{
            'code': 'server_error',
            'message': 'Something went wrong',
          },
        },
      );
    }

    return res;
  }
}
```

The last `if` gives a 500 your shape in every environment. Without it, development and local send the error text, which can show a SQL query or a file path.

## 3. Log unexpected errors

`report` runs for every 500, and for errors outside a request, like a timer. Log the error there:

```dart title="lib/app/error_handler.dart"
import 'dart:convert';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// Dox calls [report] for every unexpected error (a `500`, or an error
/// outside a request). It does not run for `IHttpException` errors
/// like `404` or `422`, because those are expected.
/// One JSON line per error. Send it to Sentry or Datadog from here.
class AppExceptionHandler extends ExceptionHandler {
  const AppExceptionHandler();

  @override
  void report(Object error, StackTrace stackTrace) {
    print(
      jsonEncode(<String, String>{
        'timestamp': DateTime.now().toIso8601String(),
        'status': 'error',
        'message': error.toString(),
        'error': <String, String>{'stack': stackTrace.toString()},
      }),
    );
  }
}
```

## 4. Register both

Add both handlers to `AppConfig`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
import 'package:my_app/app/error_handler.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/response_handler.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  responseHandler: ResponseHandler(),
  exceptionHandler: const AppExceptionHandler(),
  // ...
);
```

## Check it

Add a route that throws, only for this check:

```dart
Route.get('/boom', (DoxRequest req) => throw StateError('boom'));
```

| Request | Status | Body |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET /api/users/999` | 404 | `{"error":{"code":"not_found","message":"User 999 not found"}}` |
| `GET /api/users/abc` | 404 | `{"error":{"code":"not_found","message":"Not Found"}}` |
| `DELETE /api/users/1` | 403 | `{"error":{"code":"forbidden","message":"The first user can not be deleted"}}` |
| `POST /api/auth/register` with `{}` | 422 | `{"error":{"code":"validation_failed","message":"The input is not valid"},"errors":{"name":"The name is required", ...}}` |
| `GET /api/boom` | 500 | `{"error":{"code":"server_error","message":"Something went wrong"}}` |

After `GET /api/boom`, the server prints one line:

```json
{"timestamp":"2026-10-22T14:01:12.000Z","status":"error","message":"Bad state: boom","error":{"stack":"#0  ApiRouter.register.<anonymous closure> (package:my_app/routes/api.dart:41:44) ..."},"source":"error"}
```

Remove the `/boom` route when you are done.

A URL with no route gets the same shape: `{"error":{"code":"not_found","message":"GET /nothing not found"}}`.

- [Response: errors](../the-basic/response.md#errors): the built-in exceptions.
- [Response: change every response](../the-basic/response.md#change-every-response): the response handler.
- [Validation: the error response](../the-basic/validation.md#the-error-response): the 422 body.

# Background work

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/guides/background-work/

# Background work

Answer the request now and do the slow work later: after the response, on another thread, in a queue, or on a timer.

## What you need

- A Dox app (`dox create my_app`). A new app has the queue (`dox_queue`) and the scheduler (`dox_scheduler`).

## Pick the right tool

Pick a tool by the type of work, and by whether the work may get lost:

| You want | Use | Runs where | Lost when the process stops |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| small I/O work after the response (a log line, a cache update) | a `Future` you do not await | the same isolate, between requests | yes |
| CPU work (resize an image, parse a big file, compute) | `Isolate.run()` | a new thread | yes |
| work that must not get lost (an email, a payment call), with retries | a queue job | the queue worker process | no |
| work every N minutes (cleanup, sync) | a scheduled task | the schedule process | it runs again at the next tick |

## 1. Work after the response

For small I/O work, start the future with `unawaited` and return. An error of the future goes to `report` of the exception handler. This file has the code of steps 1, 2 and 3:

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/report.controller.dart"
import 'dart:async';
import 'dart:isolate';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/jobs/build_report.job.dart';

@Inject()
class ReportController {
  /// POST /api/reports
  /// Answers at once. The work runs after the response, in this isolate.
  Map<String, String> store(DoxRequest req) {
    String id = DateTime.now().microsecondsSinceEpoch.toString();
    unawaited(_build(id));
    return <String, String>{'id': id, 'status': 'queued'};
  }

  /// POST /api/reports/queued
  /// Saves a job in the jobs table and answers at once.
  /// The queue worker (`dox queue:work`) runs it, and tries again when
  /// it fails. The job is not lost when the server stops.
  Future<Map<String, String>> queue(DoxRequest req) async {
    String id = DateTime.now().microsecondsSinceEpoch.toString();
    String jobId = await BuildReport(reportId: id).dispatch();
    return <String, String>{'id': id, 'job': jobId, 'status': 'queued'};
  }

  /// I/O work (database, HTTP calls, email) is fine here. It shares the
  /// event loop with the requests, so it must not block the CPU.
  Future<void> _build(String id) async {
    await Future<void>.delayed(const Duration(seconds: 2));
    print('report $id is ready');
  }

  /// GET /api/primes/{limit}
  /// CPU work runs on another thread with `Isolate.run`.
  /// The request waits for the result, but other requests are not blocked.
  Future<Map<String, int>> primes(int limit) async {
    int count = await Isolate.run(() => countPrimes(limit));
    return <String, int>{'limit': limit, 'primes': count};
  }
}

/// Must be a top level or static function with plain arguments.
/// The new isolate has no Dox, no database and no providers.
int countPrimes(int limit) {
  List<bool> sieve = List<bool>.filled(limit + 1, true);
  int count = 0;
  for (int i = 2; i <= limit; i++) {
    if (!sieve[i]) continue;
    count++;
    for (int j = i * i; j <= limit; j += i) {
      sieve[j] = false;
    }
  }
  return count;
}
```

!!! warning "Do not block the event loop"
    `_build` shares the thread with the requests of this isolate, so a long loop makes them all wait. Put a long loop in `Isolate.run`.

## 2. CPU work on another thread

`Isolate.run` runs a function on a new isolate and sends the result back. Pass plain data in, like an integer, a string or bytes, and get plain data out.

If many requests do CPU work, use `Dox().compute`. It uses a pool of workers. See [Heavy CPU work](../digging-deeper/isolate.md#heavy-cpu-work).

`primes` above waits for the result. To not wait, combine both patterns:

```dart
unawaited(Isolate.run(() => countPrimes(limit)).then(saveResult));
```

## 3. A job that must not get lost

For work that must happen, use a queue job. `dispatch()` saves the job in the database. A worker runs `handle()`, and tries again if it fails.

Make the job:

```bash
dox make:job BuildReport
```

Write the work in `handle()`:

```dart title="lib/app/jobs/build_report.job.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';

/// Builds a report in the queue worker.
/// Dispatch it: `await BuildReport(reportId: id).dispatch();`
@Job()
class BuildReport extends DoxJob {
  BuildReport({required this.reportId});

  final String reportId;

  /// try 3 times, wait 10 seconds between tries
  @override
  int get tries => 3;

  @override
  List<Duration> get backoff => const <Duration>[Duration(seconds: 10)];

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    Logger.info('report $reportId is ready');
  }
}
```

Dox saves the fields of the job with it, so use plain values, like strings, numbers, dates, lists and maps. Save an id, not a model, and load the model in `handle()`.

Run `dart run build_runner build` after you add or change a job. The `queue` method of the controller dispatches the job.

Start the worker in a second terminal:

```bash
dox queue:work
```

`dox queue:failed` lists the jobs that failed every try. `dox queue:retry all` puts them back on the queue.

## 4. Work on a timer

Put a task that runs again and again in `lib/config/schedule.dart`:

```dart title="lib/config/schedule.dart"
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

/// `inProcess: false`: run `dox schedule:work` next to the server.
ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig();

/// The tasks. `dox schedule:list` shows them.
void schedule(Schedule s) {
  s.call('cleanup', cleanupUsers).hourly();
}

/// Removes the users that were soft deleted more than 30 days ago.
Future<void> cleanupUsers() async {
  DateTime limit = DateTime.now().subtract(const Duration(days: 30));
  List<User> old = await User()
      .withTrash()
      .where('deleted_at', '<', limit)
      .get();
  int removed = 0;
  for (User user in old) {
    removed += await user.forceDelete();
  }
  print('cleanup: removed $removed users');
}
```

Start the scheduler in a third terminal:

```bash
dox schedule:work
```

`dox schedule:list` shows each task and its next run. `dox schedule:test cleanup` runs the task now.

With many servers, set `ScheduleConfig(store: 'redis')`, so each task runs one time per tick. For a small app, you can [run the schedule inside the server](../digging-deeper/scheduler.md#run-inside-the-server).

## 5. Add the routes

Add the three routes to the API router:

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
Route.post('/reports', (ReportController c) => c.store);
Route.post('/reports/queued', (ReportController c) => c.queue);
Route.get('/primes/{limit}', (ReportController c) => c.primes);
```

Run `dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs` and `dox serve`.

## Check it

Start a report:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/reports
```

The response comes at once:

```json
{"id":"1792677668393002","status":"queued"}
```

Two seconds later, the server prints `report 1792677668393002 is ready`.

Start a queued report:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/reports/queued
```

```json
{
  "id": "1792677670112345",
  "job": "9f2c4e1a7b3d5f60a1c2e3f4a5b6c7d8",
  "status": "queued"
}
```

The worker terminal shows `report 1792677670112345 is ready`. When the worker is stopped, the job waits in the `jobs` table.

Count the primes:

```bash
curl http://localhost:3000/api/primes/100000
```

```json
{"limit":100000,"primes":9592}
```

# Static files and SPA

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/guides/static-files/

# Static files and SPA

Serve a folder of files, or a single page app (React, Vue, Flutter web), from the Dox app, with the right cache headers.

With the front-end in the same app as your API, you have one server to run and no CORS setup.

## What you need

- A Dox app.
- A `public` folder with the built front-end (`index.html`, `assets/...`).
- For the storage disk and the controller below: the `dox_storage` package, with its provider. See [File storage](../digging-deeper/file-storage.md#configuration).

## Serve a folder: one line

`Route.staticFiles` serves the files of a folder. Add it in `register()` of `WebRouter`:

```dart title="lib/routes/web.dart"
Route.staticFiles('/', 'public');
```

Now `/app.js` sends `public/app.js`. A route wins over a file with the same path. For a `Cache-Control` header, add `maxAge`. See [Routing: serve static files](../the-basic/routing.md#serve-static-files).

For a single page app, add a [fallback route](../the-basic/routing.md#fallback-route) that sends `index.html`.

### Or serve a storage disk

`Storage.route` serves every file of a disk. First add a `public` disk for the folder:

```dart title="lib/config/storage.dart"
StorageConfig storageConfig = StorageConfig(
  defaultDisk: env.storageDisk,
  disks: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
    'local': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'local', 'root': 'storage'},

    /// the front-end files
    'public': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'local', 'root': 'public'},
  },
);
```

Then add the route in `register()` of `WebRouter`:

```dart title="lib/routes/web.dart"
// GET /static/{key*}
Storage.route('static', disk: 'public', signed: false);
```

Now `/static/app.js` sends `public/app.js`. This route sends no `Cache-Control` header.

## Serve an SPA

A single page app (SPA) needs two things:

- `index.html` for every URL the SPA router handles, with no cache.
- The built assets with a long cache. Build tools put a hash in the file name (`app.3f9c2b.js`), so a new build has new names.

### 1. Write the controller

Write one method for the assets and one for `index.html`:

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/static.controller.dart"
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';

@Inject()
class StaticController {
  /// GET /assets/{path*}
  /// Built files have a hash in the name, so the browser may keep them
  /// for one year. The `public` disk rejects `..` in the path.
  Future<DoxResponse> asset(String path) async {
    StreamFile file = await Storage().disk('public').stream(path);
    return response(file).cache(const Duration(days: 365));
  }

  /// GET / and GET /{path*}
  /// Every other URL gets index.html, so the router of the SPA can
  /// handle it. Never cache it, so a new deploy shows at once.
  /// An unknown API URL stays a 404, it does not get the page.
  DoxResponse index(DoxRequest req) {
    if (req.uri.path.startsWith('/api/')) {
      throw NotFoundHttpException();
    }
    return response(File('public/index.html')).cache(Duration.zero);
  }
}
```

`cache(duration)` sets `Cache-Control: max-age=<seconds>`.

### 2. Add the routes

The catch-all route matches every URL, so it must come last. Put the API router before the web router in `AppConfig`:

```dart title="lib/routes/web.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/static.controller.dart';

class WebRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    // the SPA: assets with a long cache, every other URL gets index.html
    Route.get('/assets/{path*}', (StaticController c) => c.asset);
    Route.get('/', (StaticController c) => c.index);
    Route.get('/{path*}', (StaticController c) => c.index);
  }
}
```

Set the order of the routers:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  /// the SPA catch-all route is in WebRouter, so it must come last.
  /// Listed routers come first, in this order.
  routers: <Router>[ApiRouter(), WebRouter()],
  // ...
);
```

Keep the route for `/`, because `/{path*}` does not match the start page.

### 3. Put the build in `public`

Build the front-end and copy the files to `public`:

```bash
# React (Vite)
npm run build && cp -r dist/. public/

# Flutter web
flutter build web && cp -r build/web/. public/
```

Flutter web puts the files next to `index.html`, not in `assets/`. So for Flutter, change the asset route to match.

## Check it

The start page comes with no cache:

```bash
curl -i http://localhost:3000/
```

```text
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
cache-control: max-age=0
content-type: text/html
```

Any other page also gets `index.html`, and an asset gets a cache of one year:

```bash
curl -i http://localhost:3000/settings/profile   # same answer: index.html
curl -i http://localhost:3000/assets/app.js
```

```text
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
cache-control: max-age=31536000
content-type: text/javascript
```

`/assets/nope.js`, `/assets/..%2Fpubspec.yaml` and `/api/nothing` answer 404.

## In production

Put a [proxy](../digging-deeper/deployment.md#https-put-a-proxy-in-front) in front of Dox, and let it do gzip. For a big site, serve `public` from the proxy or a CDN.

## Next steps

- [Routing: serve storage files](../the-basic/routing.md#serve-storage-files): all the options of `Storage.route`.
- [Response: files and big responses](../the-basic/response.md#files-and-big-responses): send a file.
- [File storage](../digging-deeper/file-storage.md): disks and drivers.

# CORS for a browser front-end

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/guides/cors-for-spa/

# CORS for a browser front-end

Let a web app on another origin (`http://localhost:5173` in development, `https://my.app` in production) call your API.

A browser blocks a call to an API on another origin. **CORS** headers tell the browser which origins may call.

## What you need

- A Dox app.
- A front-end that runs on its own origin, like Vite, Next.js or Flutter web.

## 1. Write the config

A new app has `lib/config/cors.dart` with `enabled: false`. Replace the whole file with this one:

```dart title="lib/config/cors.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

/// `enabled` is true by default, so every route sends the headers.
CORSConfig cors = CORSConfig(
  /// One origin, or a list of origins. Set CORS_ORIGIN to the real
  /// front-end URL in production.
  origin: env.corsOrigin,

  methods: <String>['GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'PATCH', 'DELETE'],

  /// the request headers the front-end sends
  headers: <String>['Content-Type', 'Authorization'],

  /// the response headers the front-end may read
  exposeHeaders: <String>['Content-Disposition'],

  /// true only when the front-end sends cookies. Not needed for a
  /// `Authorization: Bearer` token.
  credentials: false,

  /// the browser keeps the preflight answer for 10 minutes
  maxAge: 600,
);
```

`AppConfig` in `lib/config/app.dart` already uses it with `cors: cors`.

## 2. Set the origin per environment

Read the front-end URL from a new key, `CORS_ORIGIN`. Add a getter for it to the `AppEnv` class:

```dart title="lib/config/env.dart"
  /// the front-end URL that may call the API
  String get corsOrigin => 'http://localhost:5173';
```

Run `dart run build_runner build`. Then set the value in `.env`:

```ini title=".env"
CORS_ORIGIN=http://localhost:5173
```

In staging and production, set `CORS_ORIGIN` as an environment variable, like `https://my.app`. The origin is the scheme, host and port only, with no `/` at the end.

## 3. Choose `credentials`

The right `origin` and `credentials` depend on how the front-end logs in:

| Your front-end sends | `origin` | `credentials` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| a token in `Authorization: Bearer` (see [JWT authentication](jwt-auth.md)) | your front-end URL | false |
| cookies (`fetch(url, {credentials: 'include'})`) | your front-end URL, never `*` | true |
| nothing, a public API | `'*'` | false |

For two or more front-ends, set `origin` to a list, like `['https://a.com', 'https://b.com']`.

## Check it

Before a POST with JSON, the browser sends an OPTIONS request, the **preflight**. Dox answers it by itself:

```bash
curl -i -X OPTIONS http://localhost:3000/api/users \
  -H 'Origin: http://localhost:5173' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: POST' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Headers: Authorization'
```

```text
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
access-control-allow-origin: http://localhost:5173
access-control-allow-methods: GET,POST,PUT,PATCH,DELETE
access-control-allow-headers: Content-Type,Authorization
access-control-expose-headers: Content-Disposition
access-control-allow-credentials: false
access-control-max-age: 600
```

A normal request gets the origin header too:

```bash
curl -i http://localhost:3000/api/ping -H 'Origin: http://localhost:5173' \
    | grep -i access-control-allow-origin
```

```text
access-control-allow-origin: http://localhost:5173
```

In the browser, open the front-end and call the API with `fetch`. The console shows no CORS error.

## When it still fails

| The console says | The fix |
| --- | --- |
| `No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header` | `CORS_ORIGIN` does not match the page origin exactly. Check `http` or `https`, and the port. |
| `The value of ... header is 'a.com,b.com'` | `origin` is one text with commas. Use a `List<String>` instead. |
| `Request header field x-foo is not allowed` | Add the header to `headers`. |
| `credentials mode is 'include'` with `*` | Set `origin` to the front-end URL and `credentials: true`. |

## Turning CORS off for some routes

A call from another server, like a Stripe webhook, does not use CORS. Turn CORS off for such routes:

```dart
Route.disabledCors(() {
  Route.post('/webhooks/stripe', (WebhookController c) => c.handle);
});
```

## Next steps

- [CORS](../security/cors.md): every option.
- [JWT authentication](jwt-auth.md): log in with a token.

# Environments

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/guides/environments/

# Environments

Run the same app in development, staging and production with different config, and keep secrets out of git and out of the image.

Each place needs other values, like another database or front-end URL. Dox reads them from the environment, not from the code.

## What you need

- A Dox app.
- `build_runner` for the typed env class (a new app has it).

## How Dox reads config

Dox looks for each key in two places:

1. A real environment variable (from the shell, Docker or systemd). This one wins.
2. The `.env` file in the folder where the app starts.

So use a `.env` file on your machine, and real environment variables on a server.

## 1. The typed env class

The `AppEnv` class in `lib/config/env.dart` lists every key, with its type and its default. This guides app adds `corsOrigin` and `appUrl`:

```dart title="lib/config/env.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'env.g.dart';

/// The env of the app, typed. Made by `dox env:generate`.
/// -------------------------------
/// Each getter reads one key: `appName` reads `APP_NAME`.
/// A getter body is the default. A nullable getter is optional.
/// Other getters are required: the app stops at startup when one is
/// missing.
/// Run `dart run build_runner build` after you change this class.
@DoxEnv()
abstract class AppEnv {
  /// reads and checks every key once
  static AppEnv load([EnvReader? reader]) {
    return _$AppEnv.load(reader);
  }

  String get appName => 'dox';

  /// development, staging or production. Not set: production.
  String get appEnv => 'production';

  int get appPort => 3000;

  /// required: used to sign tokens and encrypt cookies
  String get appKey;

  /// isolates (threads) of the HTTP server.
  /// Null: one per CPU the process may use.
  int? get appTotalIsolate;

  String get logLevel => 'info';

  /// memory, file or redis
  String get cacheStore => 'file';

  /// local, s3, azure or memory
  String get storageDisk => 'local';

  /// sqlite, postgres or mysql
  String get dbConnection => 'sqlite';

  /// the database name. For SQLite: the file path.
  String get dbName => 'db/dox.sqlite';

  String get dbHost => 'localhost';

  /// null: 5432 for Postgres, 3306 for MySQL
  int? get dbPort;

  String get dbUsername => 'postgres';

  String get dbPassword => '';

  /// the front-end URL that may call the API
  String get corsOrigin => 'http://localhost:5173';

  /// the public URL of this app, used in file links
  String get appUrl => 'http://localhost:3000';
}

/// The env of the app. Read and checked once, on first use.
final AppEnv env = AppEnv.load();
```

Each getter reads its name in upper snake case, so `dbPort` reads `DB_PORT`:

- A getter with a body has a default: `int get appPort => 3000;`.
- A nullable getter with no body is optional: `int? get dbPort;` is null when the key is not set.
- Any other getter with no body is required: `String get appKey;`.

If a required key is missing, the app stops at start and lists all the problems.

## 2. Add a key

For a new value, add a getter to `AppEnv`, like this mail host:

```dart
  /// the SMTP server for mails
  String get mailHost => 'localhost';
```

Then run `build_runner` again:

```bash
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
```

Now `env.mailHost` reads `MAIL_HOST`. Add the key to `.env.example` too.

## 3. Use it in the config files

The config files read the typed getters. For a setting that changes per environment, use `APP_ENV`, like `prettyPrint` and `debug` here. Development is an `APP_ENV` of development, local, test or testing. Any other value is production:

```dart title="lib/config/logger.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

LoggerConfig logger = LoggerConfig(
  name: env.appName,
  enabled: true,
  level: env.logLevel,
  // colors on your machine, one JSON line per log in staging and
  // production.
  // Env.appEnv, not appConfig.isDevelopment: appConfig is built from
  // this logger, so reading appConfig here would loop.
  prettyPrint: Env.appEnv == 'development',
);
```

The database prints every query in development only:

```dart title="lib/config/database.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: env.dbConnection,
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'postgres': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.postgres,
      host: env.dbHost,
      port: env.dbPort ?? 5432,
      user: env.dbUsername,
      password: env.dbPassword,
      database: env.dbName,
      // print every query on your machine only
      debug: appConfig.isDevelopment,
    ),
    'sqlite': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.sqlite,
      database: env.dbName,
      debug: appConfig.isDevelopment,
    ),
  },
);
```

## 4. Write the env files

Commit `.env.example` with every key and a safe value. Never commit `.env`, because it holds your real secrets:

```ini title=".env.example"
APP_NAME=my_app
APP_ENV=development
APP_PORT=3000
# run `dox key:generate`
APP_KEY=
APP_URL=http://localhost:3000

DB_CONNECTION=postgres
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432
DB_NAME=my_app
DB_USERNAME=postgres
DB_PASSWORD=postgres

CORS_ORIGIN=http://localhost:5173
LOG_LEVEL=debug
```

To start on a new machine, copy the example and make a key:

```bash
cp .env.example .env
dox key:generate   # writes a new APP_KEY into .env
```

Keep every `.env` file out of git, except the example:

```text title=".gitignore"
.env
.env.*
!.env.example
```

The values live in a different place in each environment:

| Environment | Where the values live | `APP_ENV` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| your machine | `.env` | development |
| staging | real env variables (compose `environment:`, a secrets manager) | staging |
| production | real env variables | production |

On a server you can also keep a `.env` file next to the binary, with `chmod 600`. See [Deployment](../digging-deeper/deployment.md#keep-it-running).

## 5. `APP_KEY`

`APP_KEY` is your most important secret. It encrypts cookies and signs JWT tokens and local signed URLs.

- Make one key per environment with `dox key:generate`. Never share the production key with staging.
- The key must be exactly 32 characters.
- In production a bad key stops the app at start. A bad key is empty, not 32 characters, or a public sample key.
- A new key stops every cookie, token and signed URL, so every user is logged out.

## 6. Check the env before a deploy

`dox env:check` prints every missing or bad key. On a problem it exits with code 1, so CI stops:

```bash
dox env:check
```

## Check it

Start the app with a key missing:

```bash
APP_KEY= dart run bin/server.dart
```

```text
Unhandled exception:
EnvException: the env is not valid
  - APP_KEY is missing
```

Now start it as staging on another port. The real variables win over `.env`:

```bash
APP_ENV=staging APP_PORT=4000 dart run bin/server.dart
```

The app listens on port 4000. `env.appEnv` is staging, and `appConfig.isDevelopment` is false.

## Things that differ per environment

Most apps change these settings between environments:

| Setting | Development | Staging and production |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `prettyPrint` of the logger | true | false (one JSON line per log) |
| `debug` of the database | true | false |
| `totalIsolate` | 1 or 2 is enough | one per core (the default) |
| `CORS_ORIGIN` | `http://localhost:5173` | the real front-end URL |
| the server | `dox serve` (JIT) | the `dox build` binary (AOT) |

## Next steps

- [Environment variables](../digging-deeper/env.md): all the types and rules of the env class.
- [Docker](docker.md): set the env in a container.
- [Deployment](../digging-deeper/deployment.md): run the app on a server.
